narrate.summary: This paper develops tractable bounds for expected information gain (EIG) in Bayesian experimental design for nonlinear models and non-Gaussian probability distributions. Instead of repeatedly estimating the EIG with nested sampling, the authors express lower and upper bounds as signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) based on covariance and Fisher information matrices. They define conservative criteria for retaining information from the full dataset and incremental criteria for choosing observations sequentially. The matrices can be estimated from samples, approximations to conditional expectations, or model gradients; the gradient-based approach provides certified bounds. The bounds are exact for linear models with Gaussian distributions, while their gap grows with nonlinearity and non-Gaussianity.
narrate.key_results: In the linear-Gaussian setting, the proposed bounds coincide with the exact EIG. In the simulated viscous Burgers equation example, the model used 200 spatial points and 10^4 samples, and designs were evaluated for up to 15 observations. As nonlinearity increased, the certified intervals widened; incremental intervals were comparatively tight at small observation budgets, while conservative intervals widened more rapidly. The diagnostic matrices separate model evaluation from design optimization: matrix assembly scales linearly with the sample count, whereas the paper notes that standard nested estimators typically require O(N^2) forward-model evaluations per candidate design; estimating full-data EIG for the conservative bounds used 1000 samples at each of two nested levels.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that a detailed error analysis for approximation-based diagnostic matrices, including sampling, reconstruction, and discretization errors, is beyond the paper's scope. Gradient calculations can also be prohibitively costly for some large problems, while approximation-based matrices do not certify the bounds unless approximation error is accounted for.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation centers on one simulated Burgers-equation problem, so performance across other physical models, noise structures, and design constraints is not established. The experiments use greedy selection of point observations, and do not provide a broad numerical comparison against alternative optimization algorithms or report a quantified computational benchmark against competing EIG methods.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing efficient diagnostic-matrix computations for very large observable spaces, including examples with about one million observables, and using such problems to further compare the conservative and incremental bounds. They also suggest reversing the roles of the parameter and data, and using transport-based methods to make their joint distribution more Gaussian and improve bound tightness.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test these criteria on real experiments and on practical designs with costs, safety limits, or other operational constraints. It could also develop sequential updates to the diagnostic matrices and compare greedy selection with alternative design optimizers across multiple application models.

narrate.summary: This paper compares practical parameter-identifiability assessments for the Integrated Inflammatory Stress (ITIS) model, a nonlinear model of inflammation coupled to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal system. The goal is to determine which model parameters can be estimated from different combinations and sampling schedules of measured states. The authors generate synthetic data from the model and compare a local Fisher information matrix assessment, repeated optimization with confidence intervals, and profile-likelihood analysis. They examine six designs formed from three measurement combinations and two sampling schedules, with and without added measurement noise. The main finding is that local information-matrix methods identify more parameters than profile-likelihood analysis, and identifiability changes when the observation design changes.
narrate.key_results: The six designs measured cortisol and adrenocorticotropic hormone, with tumor necrosis factor alpha and then interleukin 10 added in the larger measurement sets; each used either 13 or 25 time points over 24 hours. The local Fisher information matrix test retained all sensitivity-screened parameters for every design using a condition-number threshold of 1,000,000, whereas profile-likelihood identified between 2 and 7 parameters in the noisy-data cases. The largest profile-likelihood set contained 7 parameters for the design with four measured states and 25 time points; the other five designs yielded sets of 6, 4, 5, 2, and 4 parameters. Repeated optimization used 20 initializations per case and judged parameters by 90% confidence-interval coverage and a bias within 10%; its conclusions did not consistently match profile-likelihood results. The study reports no general efficiency or prediction-accuracy ranking, but finds that a profile-likelihood assessment should be redone when the observation design changes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that they used sensitivity-based parameter screening before identifiability analysis and did not assess structural identifiability. They considered noise-free data and independent Gaussian noise, so their analysis does not cover multiplicative noise or model discrepancy. They also used a relatively simple set of experimental designs; broader design comparisons and iterative profile-likelihood subset reduction would require substantially more computation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The data are synthetic and generated from the same model used for estimation, so the results do not test whether the conclusions hold with real measurements or model mismatch. The analysis also uses nominal parameter values and a single endotoxin-challenge scenario, leaving uncertainty about identifiability across subjects, parameter values, and other challenge conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose examining a more exhaustive range of designs and using information criteria, such as expected information gain, to select observation operators. They also suggest repeated profile-likelihood analysis with iterative parameter-subset reduction, and surrogate models or emulation to reduce the resulting computational burden.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to optimize measurement times and measured states jointly under practical limits on sampling, assay cost, and subject burden, then compare the selected designs with the six designs studied here. The conclusions should also be validated using experimental data and tested across subjects or challenge conditions rather than only the paper’s synthetic scenario.

narrate.summary: This theoretical paper compares uniform-norm recovery using function values with recovery using arbitrary bounded linear measurements. It considers functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space with a bounded kernel and seeks a worst-case prediction error bound. The authors relate sampling to selecting kernel translates, then use a maximal Gram-determinant, or D-optimal, selection and a Hilbert-space subset-selection bound. The result shows how using more sampling points than measurements improves the comparison. The leading bound is sharp in the sense that examples can approach it arbitrarily closely.
narrate.key_results: For every bounded-kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space and integers m at least n at least 1, the linear sampling width is at most (m + 1) divided by (m - n + 1) times the Gelfand width. When m equals n, this gives the factor n + 1; when m equals 2n, the factor is at most 2. More generally, for any fixed oversampling ratio b greater than 1, the paper gives a bound with factor b divided by (b - 1). The authors construct examples showing that the leading factor cannot be reduced uniformly: the ratio approaches (m + 1) divided by (m - n + 1).

narrate.limitations_unstated: The main theorem is an existence result based on a near-maximal Gram determinant, but the paper does not give a practical algorithm or computational-cost analysis for finding such a set. Further work could also test the bounds in real experiments and examine whether similar results hold for other prediction criteria or for sequential design.

narrate.summary: The paper designs random-duration switchback experiments for estimating the average effect of assigning an entire system to treatment rather than control. It assumes outcomes may depend on treatment during a finite carryover period and seeks designs that protect against arbitrary bounded changes in outcomes over time. Treatment and control alternate after durations drawn from a chosen distribution, and the design is evaluated through the frequency patterns of treatment-control imbalance and contaminated exposure. The authors optimize a simple rule with one switching rate early in a run and a higher rate after a changepoint. Their optimized rule has a lower worst-case error certificate than the standard independently randomized fixed-block design, with an asymptotic improvement of at least 32.2 percent.
narrate.key_results: The optimized two-rate design has a spectral criterion of about 10.843, compared with 16 for the standard regular switchback with block length equal to the carryover horizon; this corresponds to at least a 32.2 percent reduction in asymptotic worst-case mean squared error. The optimized design uses early and later switching-rate parameters of about 0.182 and 0.885, with a changepoint at about 1.045 carryover horizons. Its mean run duration is 1.886 carryover horizons and its pure-exposure probability is 0.258, compared with 2.000 and 0.250 for the regular switchback. The optimized one-rate design has a larger criterion of 17.244, showing that continuous random switching alone does not provide the improvement. In a numerical illustration with a 50-unit experiment horizon, the two-rate design has lower estimated error across the outcome frequencies considered; alternating fixed blocks show large error spikes at frequencies aligned with their periodic assignment pattern.

key_equations.name: Probability of pure exposure
key_equations.explanation: The symbol p_G is the pure-exposure probability, G is the run-duration distribution, E_G is expectation under that distribution, R is run duration, m is the carryover horizon, and (R-m)_+ is the positive part of R minus m.

key_equations.name: Worst-frequency design criterion
key_equations.explanation: J is the design criterion for duration distribution G, x is normalized frequency, f_X is the spectrum of treatment-control imbalance, and f_H is the spectrum of contamination.

key_equations.name: Two-rate switching hazard
key_equations.explanation: Lambda is the switching hazard at run age r, c_1 and c_2 are the early and later rate parameters, m is the carryover horizon, and theta sets the changepoint as a multiple of that horizon.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the spectral criterion is a conservative upper bound for pointwise-bounded outcomes in general, because a bounded outcome path may not be able to concentrate all its variation at the most unfavorable frequency. The bound is asymptotically sharp when its maximum occurs at zero frequency. They optimize only within a simple two-rate family rather than over all possible duration distributions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantee relies on finite carryover, non-anticipation, and bounded outcomes, so performance under longer or misspecified carryover is not established. The numerical comparison uses a stylized periodic outcome model and a finite set of design benchmarks; it does not establish how the rule performs in field experiments or under operational constraints on switching.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Assess the design under non-finite or misspecified carryover, irregular operating constraints, and outcome patterns beyond the periodic model used in the numerical illustration. Field validation and practical implementation tools could also test whether age-dependent switching is feasible and beneficial in real platform experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops the Bid-Aware Filter Family (BAFF) for reducing training-data interference in real-time bidding (RTB) A/B tests. The method controls how much data from the other model is retained, using separate tolerances for ad-ranking disagreement and bid-price disagreement. It also proposes a three-stage online experiment that compares candidate strategies with a model trained on data from its own serving. A ridge-regression analysis motivates the filtering approach, and simulations and a production deployment evaluate it. In both evaluations, some filters stay closer to the reference model than either unfiltered data sharing or using only each model’s own data.
narrate.key_results: In simulation, log-splitting had a mean Kullback-Leibler divergence of 0.80 × 10^-3 from the reference policy, compared with 6.61 × 10^-3 for unfiltered log-sharing. The best strict ad-selection filter had divergence of 0.51 × 10^-3 and outperformed log-splitting across the 10 seeds, with reported p values at most 0.008. In the live experiment, the bid-price-only filter’s cost per click (CPC) differed from the reference by 0.44, compared with 8.84 for log-splitting and 9.85 for unfiltered sharing; the joint filter differed by 5.37. For click-through rate (CTR), the joint and bid-price-only filters differed from the reference by 0.40 and 0.78 percentage points, respectively, compared with 1.38 for log-splitting and 1.94 for unfiltered sharing.

key_equations.name: Reference-preservation measure
key_equations.explanation: Here TE_s is the treatment effect for strategy s, m is a measured metric, B_s is the model trained under strategy s, and B_ref is the interference-free reference model.

key_equations.name: Ridge-regression surrogate
key_equations.explanation: Here theta_P* is the fitted parameter vector for training pool P, y is the label, z is the feature vector, the expectation is over pool P, and lambda is the ridge penalty.

narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical result uses population quantities for a ridge-regression surrogate and does not directly extend to the non-convex, finite-sample multilayer perceptron models; the bound’s tightness for deep models remains open. The live study covered one advertiser–supply-side platform pair for 2 days of reference training, 2 days of mixed-log generation, and 3 days of comparison, froze the reference model during the later stages, and tested only one interior filter setting. The authors also note limited statistical precision, the narrow setting’s external-validity limits, and the open question of constructing a reference model without a dedicated full-traffic serving stage.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The bid-price disagreement score is one-sided: it records cases where the control model bids more than the treatment model, so it may not capture other meaningful forms of bid difference. The filtering procedure also requires replaying counterpart-model logs through the treatment model at retraining time, and the paper does not quantify the resulting computational or operational burden.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for replication across advertisers, supply-side platforms, and advertiser goals, and note that a longer reference-training period is feasible. They also identify as future work finding a way to construct the reference model without dedicating full traffic to a separate serving stage. They recommend sweeping the tolerance grid in each deployment to locate a suitable operating point.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test versions of the disagreement scores that capture bid differences in both directions and assess whether alternative measures of ad-ranking disagreement improve reference preservation. It could also study adaptive threshold selection as market conditions change and evaluate filters under practical traffic, budget, and retraining constraints.

narrate.summary: The paper develops rerandomization methods for estimating main effects and interactions in two-level factorial experiments. Its oracle method uses researchers’ priorities for effects and the covariates’ relevance to each effect to target precision improvements. Because that relevance is generally unknown, the data-adaptive method estimates it from a randomly selected subset of the experiment and uses the estimate to guide rerandomization in the remaining units. The method uses one dataset rather than requiring a separate auxiliary dataset. The authors’ theory and numerical studies show improved precision over existing rerandomization approaches, while the data-adaptive method approaches the oracle method as the learning subset becomes small under the stated conditions.
narrate.key_results: In model-generated studies with three factors, five covariates, and 800 units, the authors generated 100 datasets per setting and evaluated 1,000 accepted assignments for each method and dataset. With equal effect priorities in the linear setting, the data-adaptive method with a 0.3 learning share reduced variance by 37.25% for one main effect, compared with 26.28% for ReFM; the oracle method achieved 46.84%. With higher priority for main effects, the data-adaptive method at a 0.3 learning share reduced variance by 41.25% for one main effect and 29.85% for one interaction, compared with 31.41% and 14.78% for ReFMTF. In the analysis using the Student Achievement and Retention Project data, the equal-priority adaptive method at a 0.3 learning share reduced variance by 32.23% for one main effect, compared with 25.53% for ReFM; the higher-priority adaptive method reduced it by 32.79%, compared with 26.30% for ReFMTF. The reported confidence-interval coverage was at least 95% in the real-data-based study, and all methods attained the nominal 95% level in the model-generated studies.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the procedure estimates covariate importance from a subset and suggest that using richer information from that subset could yield further precision gains. They also state that the best learning-subset proportion remains unresolved.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method depends on suitable covariate and effect-importance estimates, and its theory requires regularity conditions including a full-rank projected importance structure; these requirements may be difficult to meet with many covariates or limited sample sizes. The numerical comparisons cover a small set of simulated settings and one real-data source whose unobserved potential outcomes were imputed, so they do not establish performance across a broad range of practical factorial experiments or operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying how to use additional information from the learning subset, combining the method with regression adjustment, and developing a more refined theory for choosing the learning-subset proportion.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method under practical assignment constraints, such as restricted treatment combinations or fixed blocks, and test it in prospective experiments without imputed potential outcomes. It would also be useful to develop implementation software and assess sequential or repeated use when new units or outcome information become available.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Covariance-Optimized Spatiotemporal Treatment Allocation (COSTA), a design for experiments that assign treatments to networked units over multiple time blocks. Its objective is to estimate the global average treatment effect (GATE), comparing sustained treatment of all units with sustained control, despite network spillovers and temporal carryover. COSTA chooses a joint Bernoulli assignment distribution by optimizing treatment correlations on important network and time-exposure pairs, with additional controls for treatment balance and switching. The design is constructed with thresholded Gaussian variables and shared unit and time factors, allowing the covariance pattern to scale without building a full assignment covariance matrix. In semi-synthetic experiments using RetailRocket and MovieLens data, COSTA substantially reduced estimation error relative to several established designs, while the authors show that valid inference also requires separate checks for dependence, causal centering, and variance estimation.
narrate.key_results: In the default setting with 10,000 items, 8 time blocks, and treatment probability 0.5, COSTA’s weighted Horvitz–Thompson root mean squared errors on RetailRocket were 0.066, 0.071, and 0.056 for the linear, nonlinear, and demand models; the corresponding independent-randomization results were 0.185, 0.239, and 0.125. On MovieLens, COSTA’s errors were 0.102, 0.111, and 0.108, compared with 0.185, 0.235, and 0.123 under independent randomization. The COSTA variant with a penalty on sampled distant-pair covariances had errors of 0.088, 0.112, and 0.082 on RetailRocket and 0.143, 0.161, and 0.130 on MovieLens. In the inference study, design-centered coverage for the design-aware variance procedure ranged from 0.888 to 0.932 at a nominal 90% level, while raw-GATE coverage ranged from 0.696 to 0.909; intervals for the penalized variant were 25%–38% narrower than COSTA intervals across the six dataset-and-outcome comparisons.

key_equations.name: Exact bias under the linear exposure model
key_equations.explanation: Bias is the design expectation of the estimator minus the target; theta is the exposure-effect coefficient; M is the number of outcome cells; a and c index assignment cells; H assigns exposure weights; and R is normalized treatment covariance.

narrate.limitations_stated: The exact bias identity applies to the stated linear exposure model with common treatment marginals; nonlinear outcomes and demand substitution are robustness evaluations rather than extensions of that identity. The low-rank Kronecker assignment construction is not automatically covered by the paper’s inference conditions, and its sampled pairwise locality penalty is not an inference certificate. The reported design objective is unweighted even though the headline empirical estimand and estimator use traffic weights.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses semi-synthetic outcomes built around historical RetailRocket and MovieLens data, rather than a live randomized experiment, so it does not establish operational performance under real treatment launches. Empirical validation centers on recommendation-item settings and estimated competition graphs, leaving performance in other application domains and under substantially different graph structures less established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify model-assisted correction of design bias, bias-aware intervals, and alternative exposure targets as ways to address cases where the estimator is not centered on the GATE. They also point to developing nonlocal common-factor limit theory for global assignment structures that do not satisfy their local dependence conditions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the design in live experiments and assess how graph estimation error, changing networks, and practical assignment constraints affect results. It would also be useful to test sequential or adaptive versions of the design and to compare robust objectives that explicitly account for uncertainty in exposure effects and outcome models.

narrate.summary: This paper treats the allocation of a fixed pretraining token budget across data domains as a mixture experiment for large language models (LLMs). It models validation loss over the simplex of feasible domain shares using sparse second-order Scheffé response surfaces, which represent both additive domain contributions and pairwise interactions. It also constructs model-robust I-optimal designs to select proxy-training mixtures that are informative for prediction under both first-order and second-order models. In the RegMix case study, the fitted interactions show that domain value can depend strongly on which other domains are mixed with it, especially web-derived text. In a simulation based on the fitted response surface, the designed experiments recover mixture rankings with about 25% fewer proxy runs than the original design.
narrate.key_results: The analysis used 512 proxy runs across 17 domains, with proxy models trained on 1 billion tokens, and found that pairwise terms improved the fitted surface over the first-order model (F = 6.5145, p < 0.001). The sparse second-order model retained 80 terms, including 63 interactions; its Spearman rank correlations at the 1 million, 60 million, and 1 billion model scales were 0.937, 0.939, and 0.975, compared with 0.902, 0.892, and 0.879 for the first-order model. The flexible LightGBM predictor had higher correlations at the 1 million and 60 million scales, while the two predictors were comparable at the 1 billion scale, where the evaluation set contained 64 mixtures. At 512 runs, random Dirichlet designs had relative I-efficiencies concentrated around 0.07 to 0.08 compared with the model-robust I-optimal design. In the simulation study, designs with roughly 350 runs matched or exceeded the original 512-run reference on both ranking measures, corresponding to about 25% fewer runs.

key_equations.name: Feasible mixture

key_equations.explanation: The expected response E(Y given x) is the sum of each domain share x_i multiplied by its additive coefficient beta_i, plus pairwise products x_i x_j multiplied by interaction coefficients beta_ij, for domains indexed by i and j among K domains.

key_equations.name: Model-robust I-optimal criterion
key_equations.explanation: The model-robust criterion I_rob for design X is the equally weighted average of the I-optimal criteria I_1 and I_2 under the first-order and second-order candidate models.

narrate.limitations_stated: The empirical analysis relies on one publicly available proxy-training dataset, and the design comparison is simulation-based using the fitted sparse Scheffé surface as the data-generating mechanism. A sparse quadratic model may be too restrictive if higher-order interactions, threshold effects, or strong local irregularities dominate. The designs also assume that any point in the simplex is feasible and that every proxy run has the same cost, whereas practical studies may face feasibility, data availability, licensing, preprocessing, and unequal-cost constraints.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The reported interactions and ranking performance may depend on the particular Pile domains and validation objective used in the case study, so they may not transfer to other domain taxonomies or training goals. The boundary-concentrated designs include extreme mixtures that may be impractical or unrepresentative of intended pretraining, and the claimed run savings have not been confirmed in a newly conducted proxy experiment.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adding model scale and training conditions as process variables in mixture-process response models. They also suggest sequential or adaptive designs that use early proxy results to choose later runs, and extending the framework to multimodal, domain-adaptive, multilingual, and instruction-tuning data mixtures.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A prospective study could implement an optimal design and a random-sampling baseline under the same practical data and compute constraints, then compare their observed ranking performance and costs. Further work could test alternative response models and objectives, including uncertainty-aware prediction and designs that account directly for unequal run costs or restricted feasible mixtures.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a sequential Bayesian optimal experimental design method that aims to reduce the chance of misleading evidence about a model parameter. Rather than optimizing expected information gain alone, it uses the bias against criterion, defined as the probability that the data do not provide evidence in favor of the true parameter. The authors derive an upper bound on this probability and show that minimizing the bound is equivalent to maximizing expected information gain with a penalty for variability in the log relative belief ratio. They use a deep adaptive design policy and Monte Carlo estimates with stochastic gradient optimization to learn adaptive designs. In three simulated examples, the learned designs generally reduce the estimated bias-against bound while retaining similar mean information gain to expected-information-gain designs.
narrate.key_results: The paper evaluates policies in three simulated problems: source location with 30 experiments, hyperbolic temporal discounting with 20 experiments, and pizza choice with 12 choice tasks. In all three, bias-against policies generally lower the estimated variability of the log relative belief ratio and improve its mean-to-standard-deviation ratio compared with expected-information-gain policies, while the reported mean information-gain estimates are similar or only modestly lower. In the pizza-choice example, the frequency of designs with at least one dominated option was 0.4800 for the bias-against policy and 0.4182 for the expected-information-gain policy. The authors report that the bias-against policy achieves this pattern while maintaining comparable mean information gain; they do not provide a single numeric overall improvement in the bias-against probability.

key_equations.name: Bias-against criterion

key_equations.explanation: The bias against for design x is the probability, over parameter θ drawn from its prior and data y generated under that parameter, that the log relative belief ratio is not positive; p denotes the prior or data density and P denotes probability.

key_equations.name: Upper bound on bias against
key_equations.explanation: The bias against for design x is bounded above by the variance of log relative belief ratio Z divided by that variance plus the square of expected information gain for design x.

key_equations.name: Variance-penalized design objective
key_equations.explanation: The objective for design x is expected information gain minus the penalty α times the variance of the log relative belief ratio Z.

key_equations.name: Log relative belief ratio

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the stochastic-gradient estimator has biased gradients for finite outer and contrastive Monte Carlo sample sizes, with the bias vanishing as those sample sizes increase. For discrete outcomes, training uses a differentiable relaxation, so the optimization objective is an approximation to the intended discrete-data objective; final design evaluations use the original discrete simulator.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method assumes that the specified Bayesian model and prior adequately describe the experiment, but the evaluations use simulated data and do not test robustness to model or prior misspecification. The bias-against probability is optimized through an upper bound rather than directly, and the reported comparisons do not include real experiments, broad alternative design methods, or measured computational cost. Practical constraints such as limited or costly design choices are not evaluated in the examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose combining bias against with the complementary bias-in-favour criterion. This would allow design to account for which differences from the true parameter are practically significant to detect.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method on real experiments and assess how its designs perform when the assumed model or prior is imperfect. It could also extend the policy to operational constraints on allowable settings and costs, and compare direct probability-based, threshold-based, or other risk criteria against the proposed bound.

narrate.summary: This paper designs extensible point sequences for space-filling computer experiments, without assuming a response model. Its objective is to keep the mesh ratio bounded in every two-coordinate projection, rather than only in the full design space. One construction uses a cubic number field to generate an infinite Kronecker sequence; the other uses a real quadratic field and compatible prime-power calculations to produce nested rank-one lattice designs. Distinct rational projective directions specify the coordinates, and algebraic norm bounds establish the projection properties. The paper proves uniform quasi-uniformity for all two-coordinate projections and shows that selected coefficient configurations improve worst-projection mesh ratios in numerical comparisons.
narrate.key_results: The theory establishes covering and separation radii of order N to the power negative one-half for every two-coordinate projection of the cubic construction, and the corresponding order for nested lattice designs at each nesting level. In dimension 8, the optimized cubic construction had maximum periodic and Euclidean mesh ratios of 10.28 and 16.35 over the six tested run sizes, compared with 36.30 and 59.49 for the reference configuration. For the dimension 8 nested lattice construction, the maximum periodic mesh ratio across levels 1 through 7 fell from 14.15 for the Hensel–Korobov reference to 6.12 for the optimized configuration; at level 4, the evaluated Euclidean ratios were 12.16 and 28.24, respectively. The level 4 lattice contains 14,641 points, and the paper also reports evaluating periodic objectives through level 7, corresponding to 19,487,171 points.

key_equations.name: Cubic-field Kronecker construction
key_equations.explanation: Here x_n is the design point with index n, braces denote fractional parts taken coordinate by coordinate, alpha_j is the value for coordinate j, d is the dimension, and a_j, b_j, and theta specify the cubic-field construction.

key_equations.name: Nested quadratic-field generating coordinates
key_equations.explanation: Here beta_j is the quadratic-field value for coordinate j, a_j and b_j are its integer coefficients, omega generates the field, z_m,j is the generating coordinate at nesting level m, iota_p is the chosen p-adic embedding, and p is the split prime.

narrate.limitations_stated: The paper focuses exclusively on two-dimensional coordinate projections. It notes that the constructions do not ensure quasi-uniformity for higher-dimensional projections and leaves extensions using higher-degree fields and larger coefficient configurations for future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical optimization uses bounded-height candidate pools and finite ranges of run sizes or nesting levels, so its reported rankings do not establish which configurations are best under every finite-budget condition. Ordinary-square geometric checks are also limited for the nested design, including a level-4 check of only the pair that was worst under the periodic criterion for dimension 8.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying higher-dimensional projections using number fields of higher degree and higher-dimensional projective coefficient spaces. They identify proving the associated Diophantine and lattice-geometric bounds, and finding effective constructions with favorable mesh-ratio constants, as work beyond this paper.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A practical next step would be to evaluate these sequences under constraints common in experiments, such as non-power-of-prime run budgets, restricted input ranges, or required randomization, and to provide accessible implementation software. Testing whether the improved projection geometry benefits prediction or optimization on real simulator outputs would also assess its value beyond geometric criteria.

narrate.summary: This paper studies the engagement cost of symmetric two-sided isolation, a design that assigns matched fractions of creators and viewers to separate treatment and control markets. Its objective is to help estimate treatment effects without cross-arm marketplace interference, while measuring how isolation itself changes the experience being measured. The authors model each viewer’s best available content match as the maximum of candidate match qualities, then relate the loss from reducing the candidate pool to the distribution’s upper tail. Their theory, production experiments, and simulations show that isolation’s cost may decline with platform size, but can remain substantial and can make a design infeasible under a chosen loss tolerance.
narrate.key_results: In a production experiment with the viewer share held at 10 percent, reducing the creator catalog from 70 percent to 10 percent reduced exploration view time by 12.27 percent and story completions by 19.03 percent; the 2 percent cell showed losses of 29.76 percent and 41.82 percent, respectively. In a separate catalog-ablation experiment, removing 10 percent of the catalog reduced whole-feed view time by 1.18 percent, with a reported 95 percent interval half-width of 0.71 percentage points. The calibrated heavy-tail indices for deeper engagement metrics were about 9 to 15, and the resulting predictions for view time, story completion, and sending fell inside the ablation experiment’s reported 95 percent intervals. For a 5 percent loss tolerance, the authors’ calibration required 47 percent of each population for view time and found no feasible two-arm design for story completion; a 10 percent tolerance required 21 to 38 percent.

key_equations.explanation: L(p) is the relative loss, p is the retained fraction, and alpha is the heavy-tail index; in this regime the loss does not vanish as the full pool grows.

key_equations.name: Preflight traffic fraction
key_equations.explanation: The selected minimum fraction p star is the largest of the supply, loss-tolerance, and statistical-power requirements; each component is the minimum fraction that meets its named constraint.

narrate.limitations_stated: The model assumes independent match qualities and selection of the top item; the authors note that strong dependence could change the scaling. The production study measures identical-policy experiments and draws implications for treatment experiments indirectly, and its calibrated tail index does not identify the underlying tail class or remain constant across changes in the serving system. The authors also do not separately identify serving effects such as deeper-scanning latency, and leave creator-retention outcomes and their causal decomposition to a companion study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from one production content platform, so the measured costs and calibrated indices may not transfer to platforms with different content, recommendation systems, or audience behavior. The proposed preflight sizing relies on calibrated loss estimates, but the paper does not provide a general procedure for propagating uncertainty in those estimates into the selected traffic fraction.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify creator retention and the causal decomposition of creator-side outcomes as topics for a companion study. They also state that a denser sweep of catalog fractions would sharpen the scaling estimate, while noting that such a sweep consumes scarce creator supply and viewer traffic.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the preflight method across multiple platforms, content categories, and actual treatment launches, and report how often its predicted loss and traffic requirements hold. They could also add uncertainty bounds for the calibrated tail index and compare the recommended fallback designs under common operating constraints.

narrate.summary: This paper develops ScoreBED, a method for sequential Bayesian experimental design that chooses experiments to maximize expected information gain about unknown parameters. It targets adaptive policies, which select each design using the previous observations and designs. The method first trains a score network using simulated parameter, design, and observation samples, then reuses that network to train one or more policies without repeatedly estimating the marginal likelihood. The authors evaluate it on simulated source-location, dynamical-system, and gravimetry problems, comparing it with contrastive and variational approaches. Under equal likelihood-evaluation budgets, ScoreBED is competitive overall and gives the strongest reported results on the more challenging source-location setting.
narrate.key_results: On the source-location problem with 3 spatial dimensions and 10 sources, using a total budget of 6.144 × 10^9 likelihood evaluations, ScoreBED’s lower information-gain bound was 9.45 with standard error 0.03 for one policy and 9.37 with standard error 0.04 for five policies; the corresponding results were 8.82 with standard error 0.02 for prior contrastive estimation and 8.18 with standard error 0.04 for the jointly trained variational posterior. On the 2-dimensional, 2-source problem, ScoreBED reached 10.81 with standard error 0.06 for one policy, below the jointly trained variational posterior’s 11.52 with standard error 0.05. In the dynamical-system comparisons, with a budget of 1.024 × 10^10 likelihood evaluations, ScoreBED with 50 policies achieved lower bounds of 7.17 for cart-pole and 11.78 for the double link, compared with 7.22 and 11.99, respectively, for the best reported competing method in each case. The design trains a score network once and reuses it across policy restarts, so its upfront cost is amortized; this allows multiple policies to be trained within the fixed budgets, although the numerical results do not show ScoreBED winning every benchmark.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that ScoreBED relies on explicit likelihoods with differentiable reparameterizations and requires continuous design and observation spaces so that the relevant score functions exist. They also report instability in score-network training on some dynamical-system tasks and address it by splitting the score-training budget across multiple network seeds.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The score network is trained using a selected design-sampling distribution rather than the policy’s changing distribution, so inadequate coverage of designs visited during policy training could produce inaccurate gradients. The method also depends on a large transformer score network and differentiating through its score; the paper notes that its conservative network wrapper considerably increases evaluation cost, which could reduce the practical savings when policies are not retrained many times.

Further work could also develop adaptive design-sampling distributions that track policy exploration, and evaluate the approach in real experiments or sequential deployments rather than simulations alone.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to obtain more stable exploratory landscape analysis descriptors when the number of objective evaluations is limited. It proposes generating samples in randomly oriented lower-dimensional linear subspaces, instead of spreading all samples across the full search space. The authors compare several ways of allocating samples across subspaces and computing features in the original or reduced space. They test the designs on noiseless benchmark functions in 20 dimensions and compare feature distributions with higher-budget estimates. The best overall results come from using several subspaces with moderate compression, although which design works best depends on the feature and problem.
narrate.key_results: The experiments used 24 benchmark functions in 20 dimensions, with a budget of 10 times the dimension, repeated 40 times, and a reference based on 2,000 samples. In the authors’ consensus ranking, multiple-subspace sampling at compression ratio 0.5 ranked 3.3, compared with 3.5 for full-space sampling and 3.7 for single-subspace sampling with features computed in the reduced space. Ratios of 0.25 and 0.1 were consistently dominated by the moderate ratio, while dispersion and information-content features often benefited from subspace sampling; linear meta-model features generally favored full-space sampling. No method was statistically superior across all settings, and the authors report that the advantage of subspace sampling varies by feature and problem.

narrate.limitations_stated: The study is limited to a 20-dimensional benchmark setting and one family of random linear embeddings. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose testing the approach on benchmarks with low intrinsic dimensionality and on real-world problems. They also propose evaluating whether the sampling strategies improve downstream algorithm selection and configuration.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs under measurement noise, nonlinear or constrained feasible regions, and budgets that differ from the fixed budget used here. narrate.summary: The paper develops an experimental design and analysis framework for evaluating autonomous model discovery by large language model (LLM) coding agents. It studies Codex and Claude Code on networked anagram-game data, using one task to predict players’ next actions and another to build a simulator of complete game sessions. A full factorial experiment varies reasoning effort, discovery fold, and training-data regime within combinations of agent, task, and target metric. The analysis jointly considers model performance, monetary and time costs, and measures of the agents’ modeling process, and introduces a utility-aligned canonical decomposition (UACD) to describe the direction of effort-related changes. In this testbed, higher requested effort consistently increased resource use and process complexity, but did not reliably improve the prespecified combination of performance and cost.
narrate.key_results: The design scheduled 144 runs, with no repeated configurations; 140 runs passed the simulation-validity screen and were analyzed. The linear effort effect on the prespecified utility was negative in all eight agent-by-task-by-metric strata, and was statistically significant after Holm correction in seven of them. The leading canonical direction accounted for 0.84 to 0.99 of the canonical effect and had negative utility alignment in all eight strata; the authors treat this alignment pattern as descriptive because that direction is weakly identified within a stratum. Median fresh-token use rose from 29.4 thousand to 91.6 thousand for Claude Code and from 69.6 thousand to 170.5 thousand for Codex between the lowest and highest effort settings, while median reported costs were USD 4.19 and USD 0.60, respectively; the Codex cost was imputed rather than metered. The agents achieved comparable primary-metric quality overall, and effort effects on the primary metric alone were weak; the omnibus multivariate test was significant in four strata before correction and none after correction.

narrate.limitations_stated: The study has no replicated configurations, so uncertainty estimates may be unstable and larger replicated studies are costly. It examines only two agents and one family of discovery tasks; Codex costs are imputed from token counts rather than directly metered. The leading canonical direction is weakly identified within each stratum, so its utility-misalignment pattern is treated as descriptive.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The utility direction assigns fixed weights to performance and monetary cost while assigning no weight to wall-clock time or process complexity, so conclusions about what effort is “useful” depend on a narrow, prespecified trade-off. The per-stratum multivariate analysis relies on a small number of runs and a multivariate normal error model; the paper does not report a robustness analysis for that model assumption. The study also does not describe randomization of run order, leaving possible time-related changes in agent or service behavior unexamined.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose testing a wider range of agents and discovery domains, recording directly metered costs, and analyzing run traces in more detail to understand how extra effort is spent. They also call for further joint analyses of agent behavior, performance, quality, cost, and process.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future experiments could compare alternative utility weights and explicit resource constraints, including limits on run time or cost, to identify effort settings that are useful under different operating priorities. Replicated or sequential experiments could also estimate run-to-run variability more directly and check whether results persist when agent versions or service conditions change.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a design method for estimating a causal treatment effect when complete observations are more costly than observations of only an instrument and treatment. It studies a linear Gaussian model with an instrument, a potentially confounded treatment, and an outcome. The method uses the model’s asymptotic estimator variance to decide how to divide a fixed additional budget between complete and partial observations. It also gives calculations for testing whether the effect is positive, including significance level and power. The authors show that partial observations can improve precision for some parameter configurations and report favorable variance comparisons in two applications using real datasets.
narrate.key_results: In the paper’s numerical example, the floored optimal allocation gives an estimator variance of about 17.12%, compared with about 17.13% when requesting only complete observations; matching the partial-observation plan’s variance using complete observations alone would require 14.8% more budget. In the aggressive-driving application, the estimated variance was 1.012 with the optimized plan and 1.274 with the baseline, a reported 21% reduction; the corresponding theoretical variances were 7.329 and 7.526. In the intensive-care medication application, the estimated variances were 8.879 × 10⁻⁹ and 2.809 × 10⁻⁸, a reported 68% reduction; the corresponding theoretical variances were 1.098 × 10⁻⁷ and 1.1038 × 10⁻⁷. In a power example, an effect level above 0.75 at a significance level of 0.05 gave power above 0.8, and simulations with 5,000 replications were reported to agree well with the asymptotic approximation.

key_equations.explanation: The design chooses m1 additional complete observations and m2 additional partial observations to minimize the asymptotic variance per complete-observation count, where n is the existing complete-observation count, v is the asymptotic variance function, c1 and c2 are the costs per complete and partial observation, and b is the available additional budget.

narrate.limitations_stated: The paper does not provide a separate limitations section. Its derivations rely on the specified linear Gaussian model and an identifiable causal effect; its criterion for when partial observations help depends on the model parameters and relative observation costs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data applications use subsampling to estimate variances and assume specified sample costs and allocations; they do not report a prospective experiment that actually gathers data according to the optimized plan. The recommendations may also be sensitive to violations of the instrumental-variable assumptions or the Gaussian model, and the paper does not evaluate those sensitivities.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that the budget-and-variance framework could be derived for more complex causal graphs when the target effects are identifiable. They also note that it may be possible to relax the Gaussian assumption by comparing asymptotic normality of maximum-likelihood estimators based on partial datasets.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess how allocation decisions change under model misspecification and under practical constraints on which variables can be measured together, or on how many observations can be collected. Prospective validation could test whether the predicted variance savings hold when real data collection follows the optimized plans.

narrate.summary: The paper develops designs for incomplete stepped wedge clinical trials, where researchers collect data in some cluster-periods but not others. It seeks to minimize the variance of the treatment-effect estimate, or equivalently the number of cluster-periods needed for a specified precision, assuming equal data-collection cost per cluster-period and the same number of participants at each collected period. For two periods, the authors derive optimal allocation patterns under an exchangeable correlation model and show that the pattern changes at a correlation of about 0.866. For more than two periods, they use a greedy search to propose a general pattern, but do not prove it is optimal. Their results show that data collection can be targeted to particular sequences rather than conducted in every cluster-period.
narrate.key_results: For two-period trials, the optimal design changes form at rho equal to 3^(1/2)/2, about 0.866: below this value the minimum variance is sigma-squared divided by N times one plus the square root of one minus rho; above it the minimum variance is four sigma-squared divided by N times one plus rho squared times the square root of one minus rho. The authors also show that simple designs can remain close to optimal: a 1:1:1 dog-leg for rho below 0.5, a 2:1:2 dog-leg for rho between 0.5 and 0.875, and a 1:1 controlled before-after design for rho above 0.875. In the motivating school example, a previously reported calculation at rho 0.4040 required 63 schools and 84 visits for a 1:1:1 dog-leg, compared with 88 schools and 176 visits for a 1:1 controlled before-after design. For trials with more than two periods, greedy searches suggested a generalized pattern, but this result is a conjecture rather than a proven optimum.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces ShaplEIG, a sequential design method for estimating Shapley values when evaluating coalitions is expensive. It models the coalition value function with a Gaussian process using a Hamming-distance kernel, then selects the next coalition according to its expected information gain about all the Shapley values. The method exploits the fact that Shapley values are a linear transformation of coalition values, allowing the information-gain calculation to be expressed in closed form. The authors also use elementary symmetric polynomials to make the calculation polynomial rather than exponential in the number of players. Across a range of machine-learning applications, the method generally estimates Shapley values more accurately than the compared approaches when evaluation budgets are limited.
narrate.key_results: The experiments cover games with 8 to 101 players, use an initial design of players-plus-one coalition evaluations, and run for up to 512 evaluations; repetitions number 100 or 30, depending on the game. Across the tested tasks, ShaplEIG generally achieves lower mean squared error than permutation sampling, Kernel SHAP, Leverage SHAP, and Regression MSR, with Regression MSR the most often competitive baseline. In an illustrative asymmetric three-player game, one ShaplEIG-selected evaluation reduces the estimation error from 0.024 to 5.485e-06, compared with 8.75e-4 for the cited size-based sampling outcome. For games with up to 16 players, information-gain computation takes less than a second, while Gaussian-process hyperparameter fitting can take up to about 2 minutes per iteration; for games with up to 100 players, information-gain computation stays below 30 seconds, while fitting can take up to about 25 minutes per iteration.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test alternative surrogate kernels and assess how sensitive selection is to errors in the fitted value-function model. narrate.summary: This paper introduces Constrained Online Planning for Experimental design (COPEx), a method for sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) when experiments must obey changing constraints. It targets information gain about unknown model parameters and, in an active-learning setting, reduction in uncertainty about predictions. COPEx combines offline-trained posterior and design-policy networks with online multi-step planning over a tree of possible future observations, optimizing the planned designs subject to constraints. The authors evaluate it in simulated source-location, consumer-preference, and active-learning tasks with movement, budget, and spatial cost constraints. Across these tasks, COPEx generally obtains more informative designs or better predictions than the tested baselines, at the cost of additional planning time.
narrate.key_results: In the source-location task, evaluated over 100 runs of 30 steps, COPEx outperformed the variational and amortized-policy baselines at all tested movement limits; planning beyond horizon 2 or 3 brought little further information gain while increasing runtime. In the consumer-preference task, COPEx with horizon 1 achieved information-gain values of 7.03 ± 0.55 and 7.47 ± 0.55 at total budgets of 100 and 150, respectively; the myopic version scored 5.26 ± 0.39 and 6.12 ± 0.45, while the reported runtimes were about 19.47 seconds and 10.05 seconds. The horizon-3 version scored 6.36 ± 0.59 and 6.94 ± 0.54, with a runtime of 28.81 ± 2.03 seconds. In active learning, COPEx generally achieved lower prediction error than the tested Gaussian-process baselines at the same accumulated cost; longer planning helped most when the budget was small, and the paper reports results averaged over 100 runs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that COPEx depends on amortized posterior or predictive networks, whose approximation errors can accumulate over longer fantasy rollouts. Scenario trees grow exponentially with planning depth, and the gradient-based optimizer is best suited to continuous designs. The method also assumes the model captures the true data-generating process, so model misspecification is a limitation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is entirely on simulated benchmark tasks, including the economics-inspired preference task, and does not establish performance in actual laboratory, manufacturing, or clinical experiments. Practical deployment may also require reliable cost and constraint models and sufficient offline simulation data, neither of which is validated with real operational data here.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest using more expressive conditional generative models, such as diffusion or flow-matching models, to reduce surrogate bias. They also propose more efficient planning methods, alternative optimizers for discrete designs, and integration with robust methods to address model misspecification.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test COPEx in real experiments and measure whether its information or prediction gains justify the added computation and offline training. Further work could also study safety, feasibility, and resource constraints estimated from uncertain or changing operational data, rather than supplied as known functions.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a staged factorial screening workflow for short-budget language-model micro-pretraining, seeking to identify recipe factors that affect validation performance before spending more training time. At 60 minutes, the bridge anchor had mean val_bpb of 0.974511, compared with 0.981837 for the greedy winner; at 24 hours, the bridge had the lowest sample mean on both hosts, although the ordering of the other anchors differed by host.

narrate.summary: This paper extends hyper-differential sensitivity analysis with respect to model discrepancy (HDSA-MD), which uses a few high-fidelity simulations to improve an optimizer obtained from a cheaper low-fidelity model. The method represents discrepancy with an affine function of the optimization variable and estimates its parameters using a Bayesian model with a Gaussian prior and noise. It selects additional simulation inputs sequentially by minimizing an A-optimal uncertainty criterion focused near the current estimated optimizer, with a batch option for parallel runs. It also uses pseudo-time continuation to update the optimizer more accurately than a single linear sensitivity step. Numerical examples in diffusion-reaction control and contaminant source identification show improved solutions using only a few high-fidelity evaluations.
narrate.key_results: In the diffusion-reaction example, three to four continuation steps were usually sufficient, and three continuation steps substantially reduced error compared with a single post-optimality linearization. With two or three high-fidelity evaluations, the updated solutions were reported as 90% closer to the best attainable objective than the low-fidelity solution. The proposed sequential design achieved greater uncertainty reduction near the estimated optimizer than random designs and produced lower objectives on average; two sequential evaluations outperformed six evaluations collected in parallel upfront in the reported batch comparison. In contaminant source identification, at most five high-fidelity evaluations reduced the objective by two orders of magnitude relative to the low-fidelity optimizer, with an average 42% objective improvement at each step.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a robust and adaptive experimental design method for estimating unknown parameters in linear, discrete-time state-space models with Gaussian process and measurement noise. The design objective is pseudo-Bayesian D-optimality, which seeks inputs that yield high information about the parameters across a prior distribution of possible parameter values. The method uses a Kalman filter to account for uncertain system states, and uses Monte Carlo parameter draws to approximate the prior-based criterion. As measurements arrive, it updates the parameter weights and observed information, then optimizes the next short horizon of inputs. In simulated examples, the designed inputs estimated parameters more effectively than random inputs, and the adaptive design improved on a non-adaptive strategy in the mass-spring-damper example.
narrate.key_results: In the mass-spring-damper simulation, an adaptive design with 100 prior draws, a 3-step control horizon, and 100 total time steps brought estimates close to the true parameters after about 50 time steps; the random-input experiment did not correctly estimate them after 100 time steps. Across 100 repeated simulations, reducing the horizon from 3 steps to 1 made performance nearly as poor as random inputs, while increasing it to 6 did not improve results, which the authors attribute to limited optimization evaluations. Increasing the number of prior draws from 100 to 400 added little apparent value, while a non-adaptive design estimated the damping parameter less accurately later in the experiment and took much longer to optimize. In the two-compartment simulation, using 1,000 prior draws and a 3-step horizon gave precise estimates after roughly 150 time steps; the random experiment did not correctly estimate the parameters after 200 time steps.

key_equations.explanation: The design selects the next e inputs to maximize the posterior average of the determinant of the sum of J, the observed information from existing data, and I, the expected information from future data; θ is the parameter vector, y and u are outputs and inputs, k is the current step, and p is the updated parameter distribution.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method reuses the same parameter draws throughout the experiment, so it cannot shift draws toward increasingly likely regions; the authors note that making such updates efficient enough for online design remains a challenge. They also report that likelihood values can overflow to negative infinity, which can prevent the algorithm from selecting a maximum-likelihood estimate, and suggest an early stopping criterion.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method assumes linear dynamics and Gaussian process and measurement noise, so its performance may not carry over when those assumptions are substantially violated. Its empirical evaluation uses simulated examples and bounded input choices, without demonstrating performance under real operating constraints or in a real experiment; repeated online optimization may also be burdensome for systems with tight computation limits.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to nonlinear dynamics using other Bayesian filters, and investigating continuous-time stochastic systems. They also propose comparing the approach with the mixture Kalman filter and improving parameter sampling through efficient jittering or quasi-Monte Carlo methods; they mention adding early stopping for likelihood overflow.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess robustness under model misspecification and non-Gaussian noise, and compare alternative design criteria beyond determinant-based parameter precision. The method could also be tested with practical input constraints and validated in real process or quality-engineering experiments, including studies of how computation affects online deployment.

narrate.summary: This paper studies whether the coordinate-exchange algorithm produces optimal experimental design points in a random run order. The authors examine a D-optimal design for a linear regression model with two quantitative factors, including their main effects and interaction, and a quadratic effect for the first factor. The algorithm begins with a random feasible design and sequentially optimizes each factor level, observation by observation, until a full pass yields no improvement. Across repeated executions, the resulting orders of the six design points are strongly uneven rather than random. The authors conclude that experimenters should randomize the complete design output before conducting the experiment.
narrate.key_results: In 56,000 executions, the algorithm produced all 720 possible orders at least once, but the order frequencies were not uniform; a Pearson chi-squared test gave a p-value below 0.001. The 96 orders that start with four factorial points or with three factorial points followed by the other factorial point accounted for 36% of executions, while the other 624 orders accounted for 64%. Specifically, 12,779 executions started with all four factorial points, and 7,608 placed the factorial points in positions 1, 2, 3, and 5. Tests using two other initial seeds, a different random number generator, and A-optimality also gave p-values below 0.001; the paper reports no comparison of design efficiency or parameter estimation accuracy.

key_equations.name: D-optimal design criterion

narrate.limitations_unstated: The main frequency experiment concerns one six-point design for one two-factor model, so it does not establish how strongly run order is biased across a broad range of models, run sizes, or design constraints. The results also concern a particular sequential coordinate-optimization implementation; different optimization settings or algorithm variants may produce different order distributions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest adapting the algorithm to visit design rows in a random order instead of sequentially. They note that this is more cumbersome than randomizing the completed design output.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further studies could measure the order bias across a wider range of models, run sizes, optimality criteria, and practical constraints, including blocked and multi-stratum designs. It would also be useful to compare row-randomized algorithm variants with post-generation randomization and validate the consequences in conducted experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential experimental-design method for learning unknown physical relationships in dynamic process models. It combines a universal differential equation, which represents missing physics with a neural network, with symbolic regression, which proposes interpretable candidate equations. At each stage, the method chooses a feed-control profile to make the candidate models disagree in their predicted measurements, then uses the resulting data to update the candidates. The authors demonstrate the method in simulation on a fed-batch bioreactor whose unknown growth-rate relationship follows Monod kinetics. In this example, the sequential designs led symbolic regression to identify the Monod model, while the tested random experiments did not.
narrate.key_results: The bioreactor simulation used 15 hourly substrate-concentration measurements per time series. After three experiments, the Monod kinetics had the highest symbolic-regression score, reported as 3.604e+01. In comparison, none of five random experiments, each consisting of three time series, recovered the Monod equation. The paper reports no numerical measure of design efficiency or prediction accuracy, but concludes that the optimal-design approach provided information that the random experiments did not.

key_equations.explanation: The score averages, over pairs of candidate model structures, the largest squared difference in their predicted outputs at the measurement times.

key_equations.name: Sequential control selection
key_equations.explanation: The next feed control is the feed-rate profile that maximizes the model-discrimination score.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the method’s hyperparameters are fixed throughout the experiments; automatic tuning would be needed for a fully online design method. They also note that the example optimizes only the control signal, while measurement times, experiment duration, and initial conditions could also be optimized.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is a simulation of one bioreactor with a known Monod relationship, so it does not establish performance with real process data or with substantial model misspecification. The comparison with random designs is limited to five random experiments in this example, and the paper does not report a numerical measure of efficiency or uncertainty in the recovered structure.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify automatic tuning of the method’s hyperparameters as an important direction for future work. They also describe incorporating additional design variables, such as measurement times and initial conditions, and combining missing-physics discovery with precise parameter estimation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the sequential strategy in real bioreactor experiments and assess its robustness to measurement noise and incorrect candidate-model sets. Further studies could also evaluate operational constraints on feed profiles and compare the criterion with alternative design objectives across multiple process systems.

narrate.summary: This theory paper develops structural results for mixed orthogonal arrays, which are arrays used in experimental design when columns can have different numbers of levels. It derives a Singleton-type bound using the array’s column alphabet sizes and minimum Hamming distance, and identifies conditions for maximum-distance and almost-maximum-distance arrays. For arrays whose rows form a linear space over a finite field, it constructs a trace-based duality and relates array strength to the distance of an associated error-block code. It also studies irredundant mixed orthogonal arrays and proves a connection to error-block codes and to absolutely maximally entangled quantum states with minimal support.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves that an array with strength t and minimum Hamming distance d_H has size between the product of the largest t column alphabet sizes and the product of the alphabet sizes from column d_H through column s, with a further upper bound given by the product for the first s − d_H + 1 columns. For linear arrays, the associated error-block code’s dual distance is at least t + 1, and the array obtained from a code has strength equal to the code’s dual distance minus 1. When t equals the floor of s divided by 2 and the stated condition on the block sizes holds, an irredundant array is maximum distance separable exactly when its minimum index is 1. The paper provides theoretical examples, including an 8-row mixed array, but reports no empirical efficiency or prediction comparisons.

key_equations.name: Index for a subset of columns
key_equations.explanation: The index lambda for columns i_1 through i_t is the number M of array rows divided by q raised to the sum of the corresponding column sizes n_i, where q is the base field size.

key_equations.name: Singleton-type bound
key_equations.explanation: The array size M is bounded below by the product of the alphabet sizes for the first t columns and above by products determined by the number s of columns and the minimum Hamming distance d_H; q is the base field size and n_i is the size of column i.

key_equations.name: Strength from a linear code
key_equations.explanation: The array obtained from a linear error-block code C has strength t equal to one less than the minimum block distance d_pi of the dual code C-perp.

key_equations.name: Irredundancy condition
key_equations.explanation: An array is irredundant exactly when its minimum Hamming distance d_H is at least one greater than its strength t.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors explain that mixed arrays do not generally have the usual Euclidean duality or one intrinsic global index, and that familiar bounds and tools from the symmetric setting do not directly apply. These differences motivate the paper’s new structural tools.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results are theoretical and do not evaluate how useful the bounds or constructions are in actual experiments. The linear duality results also rely on a finite-field structure, and some duality-preservation statements require conditions on the field or block sizes, limiting their direct reach beyond those settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test whether the bounds and irredundant-array constructions yield practical experimental designs under run-size, randomization, and factor-level constraints. Further work could also examine nonlinear mixed arrays or additional design criteria and compare resulting designs using real experimental data.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an adaptive model-based design of experiments method for dynamical systems whose governing equations are known but whose parameters are uncertain. It aims to improve information about selected target parameters while accounting for nuisance parameters, such as measurement noise or uncertain initial conditions. The method trains a neural-network policy offline using simulations that differentiate through the mechanistic model, a nuisance-aware extension of sequential contrastive estimation, and a transformer that represents the order of observations. The policy then chooses each experimental input from the observations collected so far. Simulations on four systems show improved estimation or information scores over the tested alternatives, with especially fast per-step computation for a simulated DC motor.
narrate.key_results: For the Monod bioreactor, the adaptive policy scored 3.68 on the sequential contrastive objective, compared with 3.34 for the static design optimized with that objective and 3.45 for the Bayesian D-optimal baseline; the paper reports a posterior root mean square error reduction of about 30% versus the best static design. Its reported posterior root mean square errors, multiplied by 1,000, were 3.1 and 24.9 for the two target parameters, compared with 5.6 and 41.5 for the static contrastive design and 4.4 and 34.3 for the Bayesian D-optimal design. In the DC motor simulation, the adaptive policy scored 2.96 compared with 2.56 for adaptive Bayesian D-optimal design, and its corresponding reported errors, multiplied by 1,000, were 20.6 and 2.9 compared with 35.1 and 4.6. The policy took a median of 24 microseconds per step, compared with 7.4 milliseconds for adaptive Bayesian D-optimal design; in the pharmacokinetic architecture ablation, removing positional encoding reduced the score by 0.35, while replacing attention with a similarly sized multilayer perceptron reduced it by 0.03.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the policy is trained for a specific prior distribution, so significant prior shifts require retraining. They also state that model misspecification is not addressed, stochasticity is limited to the measurement equation, and training requires graphics-processing-unit hours on a supercomputer, although deployment is lightweight.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The reported evaluations are simulations, and the paper does not validate policy performance on a physical experiment; the DC motor result demonstrates simulated computation time rather than hardware deployment. The comparisons are also limited: the principal numerical comparisons use particular static or myopic Bayesian D-optimal baselines, so they do not establish performance against a broad range of adaptive design methods or practical operating constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose combining the method with Bayesian model selection to handle model uncertainty, extending it to process noise through Bayesian filtering, and deploying a learned policy on physical hardware with closed-loop feedback.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test robustness under realistic deviations from the assumed dynamics and prior distributions, including constraints on allowable inputs and measurement schedules. The method could also be assessed in real process experiments and developed for updating or retraining policies as new observations become available.
