narrate.summary: This paper develops a robust method for Bayesian experimental design when the assumed model may not match the data-generating process. It considers experiments that use a prior over unknown parameters and a likelihood for observed outcomes, with the goal of selecting designs that provide information while remaining robust to misspecification. The authors formulate the problem as a worst-case game in which nature can perturb the nominal joint model subject to an information-theoretic constraint. This construction yields Sibson’s alpha-mutual information as the robust design criterion and an alpha-tilted posterior as the corresponding belief update. The paper also uses PAC-Bayes bounds to optimize stochastic design policies despite noisy, biased Monte Carlo estimates, and reports better calibration and lower regret than the compared nominal or naive approaches in its simulations.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 10^4 experiments, the robust optimal design at alpha 0.056 had posterior-mean root mean squared error of 0.247 in linear regression, compared with 0.257 for the nominal optimal design; in the conversion-rate experiment, the robust design at alpha 0.115 had error 0.0713, compared with 0.106 at alpha 1. The authors also report that the robust posterior improves empirical coverage as alpha decreases, while the nominal posterior undercovers. For the noisy-estimator optimization comparison with inner sample size 16 and outer sample size 16, mean regret was 0.077 for the PAC-Bayes policy and 0.327 for the naive optimizer. At outer sample size 256, mean regret was 0.018 for the PAC-Bayes policy and 0.282 for the naive optimizer; the reported advantage persisted across the tested alpha values.

key_equations.name: Nominal generative model
key_equations.explanation: Here p is a probability density, θ is the unknown parameter, x is the outcome, and ξ is the design; the equation factors the nominal joint density into a prior and a conditional likelihood.

key_equations.name: Robust design criterion
key_equations.explanation: Here I^S_α is Sibson’s alpha-mutual information for design ξ, α is the robustness order, p is the nominal density, θ is the parameter, and x is the outcome; the integrals average over parameters and outcomes.

key_equations.name: Worst-case posterior update
key_equations.explanation: Here q* is the worst-case posterior, θ is the parameter, x is the observed outcome, ξ is the design, p is the nominal prior and likelihood, and α controls the likelihood’s power; proportionality indicates that the expression must be normalized.

key_equations.name: PAC-Bayes stochastic policy
key_equations.explanation: Here π* is the optimized policy over designs ξ, π₀ is the prior design policy, exp is the exponential function, λ is the precision parameter, and the estimated robust information gain is denoted by the tilde-marked I^S_α; proportionality indicates normalization.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the maximin formulation can produce overly conservative designs. They also identify calibration of the robustness order alpha as experimental data accumulates as an open challenge.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence comes from simulated linear-regression and conversion-rate examples, so it does not establish how the method performs in real experiments or across a broad range of engineering systems. Its nested Monte Carlo estimation and stochastic policy optimization may also be costly, and the randomized policies may not fit experiments that require fixed allocations or operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest exploring robust decision-making approaches that may avoid excessive conservatism and methods for calibrating alpha as data accumulate. They also propose extending the framework to robust sequential experimental design over a horizon of experiments.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method in real engineering experiments and benchmark it against robust design methods using practical limits on factors, resources, and allowable run allocations. Further work could also develop computationally efficient estimators and test sensitivity to different forms of misspecification beyond the two simulated settings.

narrate.summary: The paper compares fixed route assignments with temporal switchback designs for estimating the effect of airline seat-pricing changes when routes, rather than individual passengers, are the experimental units. In a switchback design, each route alternates between treatment and control on a preset schedule, either daily or weekly. The authors use the same two-way fixed-effects model to compare designs, and evaluate them with simulated data and 2024 operational data from 80 LATAM routes. Their results show substantially lower standard errors for switchbacks than for fixed route assignments. Daily switching tends to help most over short experiment durations, while weekly switching also provides large gains and may be simpler to operate.
narrate.key_results: In the real route data, weekly switching reduced standard errors relative to fixed route assignments by 32.5%, 50.2%, and 67.7% at 2, 8, and 16 weeks; daily switching reduced them by 39.5%, 54.0%, and 67.1%. In the synthetic scenarios, the largest reported reduction was 71.2% for daily switching at 16 weeks in the stronger-seasonality scenario. For a simulated 3% uplift, daily switching reached at least 80% power by 8 weeks in every scenario, while fixed assignments remained below 43% power even at 16 weeks. The authors report that false-positive rates were generally near the nominal 5% level, with some over-rejection for daily switching at 2 weeks: 8.2% in the synthetic baseline and 7.6% in the real-data evaluation.

key_equations.name: Two-way fixed-effects outcome model
key_equations.explanation: Y_it is the outcome and D_it the treatment indicator for unit i at time t; beta is the average contemporaneous treatment effect; Gamma_i is the unit effect, Theta_t is the common time effect, and epsilon_it is the residual.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their study does not explicitly model temporal interference, such as treatment effects that carry over to later periods or spillovers through shared capacity, inventory, or congestion. They note that this concern is limited for the ancillary pricing application but can change the appropriate estimand and switching cadence in other operational settings.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation centers on one airline, one ancillary product context, and a single year of data from 80 routes, so the results may not transfer to other transport businesses or operational settings. The paper evaluates proposed schedules using historical data and simulated treatment effects rather than reporting a prospective randomized pricing deployment, leaving their real-world operational performance unverified.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the evaluation to settings with explicit carryover and spillover dynamics. They also suggest evaluating washout periods, staggered switching, and estimators that account for lagged treatment exposure.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further research could test these designs prospectively across multiple airlines, route networks, and product types, including practical constraints on when pricing can be changed. It could also compare how well the designs estimate treatment effects that vary across routes, rather than assuming one common effect.

narrate.summary: The paper presents R-Design, a method for adaptively designing experiments when a large observational dataset is available but may be confounded. It focuses on estimating the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) or choosing a treatment policy in a setting with binary treatment. The method first fits an outcome model to observational data, then treats that model as a fixed starting point and uses experimental observations to learn the residual correction. Its R-EPIG criterion selects covariate-treatment queries for their expected information about the target, while a two-stage regression (TSR) strategy models residual uncertainty. The authors report theoretical and benchmark results indicating that residual learning can use limited experimental data more efficiently than learning the outcome surfaces from scratch, provided the observational prior is informative.
narrate.key_results: In synthetic treatment-effect estimation tests, R-EPIG with TSR had the best average rank of 3.00, and its direct residual-contrast variant ranked second at 3.60; the paper reports win rates of 84.5% and 80.5% against the compared baselines, respectively. In a six-covariate synthetic benchmark, the best reported PEHE was 0.319, compared with 1.220 for random acquisition using only experimental data and 0.493 for the random Kallus baseline; under heavy covariate shift, a residual-contrast version reached 0.376, compared with 1.497 and 0.538 for those baselines. For policy learning in a synthetic benchmark, the policy-aware criterion achieved average policy error of 0.105 and average regret of 0.042, with regret reductions of 72% versus random experimental-data-only acquisition and 61% versus the random Kallus baseline. On the Infant Health and Development Program benchmark, the best reported treatment-effect error was 0.980 versus 1.297 for random experimental-data-only acquisition; on the AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175 benchmark, it was 1.647 versus 1.908. The theoretical analysis gives a residual-based convergence bound and shows that the experimental-model fitting cost in TSR scales with the experimental sample size rather than the observational sample size.

key_equations.name: Treatment-effect residual decomposition
key_equations.explanation: The treatment effect is the observational treatment-effect estimate plus a correction, and that correction is the difference between the treatment-arm and control-arm outcome residuals.

key_equations.name: Residual Gaussian-process model
key_equations.explanation: The outcome residual function has a zero-mean Gaussian-process prior with covariance kernel K, and the observed residual outcome has a normal distribution centered on that function with noise variance sigma squared.

key_equations.name: R-EPIG acquisition criterion
key_equations.explanation: The acquisition score averages, over the target covariate distribution, the mutual information between a candidate residual outcome and the target quantity after conditioning on the candidate and current history.

key_equations.name: Sequential query and residual update
key_equations.explanation: At each step, the design selects the candidate covariate and treatment with the greatest utility from the available pool, then subtracts the fixed observational outcome estimate from the observed outcome to form the residual.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the current framework is limited to binary interventions and a single observational prior. They also report that targeted acquisition can be less effective when the observational dataset is very small or model uncertainty is poorly calibrated, and that its gains diminish with large acquisition batches.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The approach depends on transportability, adequate experimental support across the target population, and a useful observational model; if these conditions fail, the fixed prior can leave a complex or systematically wrong residual for the experimental learner. Evaluation is on synthetic and semi-synthetic data rather than prospective real experiments, and the finite candidate pool and repeated information scoring may constrain practical use at larger scales.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework from binary interventions to continuous treatment regimes, such as dosage, where the objective would be to learn residual dose-response surfaces.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method prospectively in real experiments and assess sensitivity to violations of transportability and limited overlap. Further work could also let experimental observations update the observational model when that prior is weak, and incorporate practical assignment, recruitment, or safety constraints into the design.

narrate.summary: This paper develops design-based methods for estimating treatment effects in sequential experiments, including adaptive assignments and assignments made in blocks. It targets treatment averages and prespecified contrasts in a finite population, so units need not be exchangeable or independently sampled from a common population. The authors use inverse-propensity weighting and augment it with outcome estimates based only on information available before each unit’s assignment. They also construct a more precise covariance estimator and apply the same adaptive estimation approach to covariate adjustment in nonadaptive experiments. The theory gives conditions for unbiased estimates and valid large-sample confidence sets, while simulations show improved precision and, in one comparison, more reliable coverage than standard adjustment using all units.
narrate.key_results: In simulations of adaptive covariate adjustment, the improved AIPW variance estimate with random forest outcome regression had 0.965 coverage, compared with 0.687 for nonadaptive adjustment using all units; their average confidence-interval lengths were 0.214 and 0.099, respectively. With ordinary least squares, the improved AIPW approach had mean squared error 0.002 and coverage 0.945, comparable to the all-unit approach, which had mean squared error 0.002 and coverage 0.946. In a sequential rerandomization simulation with 200 blocks of 8 units, the treatment-effect estimator’s root mean squared error was 0.077, versus 0.262 under complete randomization, a 70.6% reduction. The sequential rerandomization confidence interval had 94.8% coverage and average length 0.296, compared with 95.5% coverage and length 1.03 under complete randomization.

narrate.summary: The paper presents Experimentation Accelerator, a system for helping marketers choose and understand creative variants in randomized experiments. It predicts the relative click-through rate (CTR) ranking of text treatments using embeddings from historical experiments, dimension reduction, and a regression model with experiment-level fixed effects. For interpretation, it maps the model into a set of 122 curated marketing attributes using a sparse, sign-constrained Lasso procedure. It combines attribute importance with how little an attribute appears in the current variants to find opportunities, then uses large language models (LLMs) to generate explanations and creative suggestions. The authors report ranking results on 65 customer experiments and human assessments of the generated insights and suggestions.
narrate.key_results: On 65 customer experiments with statistically significant differences among treatment arms, the transfer-learning ranker achieved mean Spearman rank correlation of 0.5144 ± 0.1658 and top-1 accuracy of 0.7021 ± 0.1180; the random-guess baseline had correlation 0 and top-1 accuracy 0.4293. In a separate leave-one-out embedding comparison, the Llama embedding model had the highest mean rank correlation, 0.727 ± 0.116, compared with 0.454 ± 0.155 for MiniLM and 0.576 ± 0.142 for attribute scores. In human review of insight generation, GPT-4o had 46 high-quality insights out of 52 generated, an 88.46% acceptance rate; LLaMA-70B had 23 out of 26, also 88.46%. For opportunity generation, GPT-4o had 168 high-quality suggestions out of 195, an 86.15% acceptance rate, while GPT-4o-mini had 164 out of 195, an 84.10% acceptance rate.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a stratified survey experiment to estimate the average treatment effect in a finite target population. It combines stratification with rejective sampling to select a representative sample and rerandomization to balance treatment and control groups. At each stage, candidate samples or assignments are accepted only when their covariate imbalance falls below a prespecified threshold. The authors derive design-based results for the stratified difference-in-means estimator and propose a covariate-adjusted estimator for analysis. They find that the combined design can improve estimation precision, with further gains possible from covariate adjustment.

Relative to stratified random sampling and assignment, rejective sampling reduced the standard deviation by a further 2.2%, rerandomization by 13.1%, and their combination by 19.0%; the combined design was 30.6% below the complete-randomization baseline. Regression adjustment reduced standard deviations by about 21% to 49% across the compared designs, and reported confidence-interval coverage was close to or slightly above the nominal 95%. In the Cooperative Congressional Election Study illustration, which used a target population of 49,452 people and a sample of 1,000, the adjusted estimator reduced root mean squared error by 17.0% to 54.5% across the three constructed datasets; the unobserved potential outcomes were imputed for this comparison.

narrate.summary: This paper develops sequential designs for fitting Kriging models to computer experiments, with global prediction accuracy as the objective. It introduces a gradient-based criterion that uses estimated gradient magnitude, distance from existing points, and predicted response differences, plus a variance-based criterion that considers prediction and gradient uncertainty. The authors also propose a batch-selection framework that sorts candidate points by a chosen criterion, clusters nearby high-ranking candidates, and selects a representative from each cluster. They assess the methods on seven smooth test functions and compare them with existing sequential criteria and a space-filling benchmark. In the reported simulations, the gradient-based criterion tends to give better root mean square error, while the variance-based criterion tends to give better maximum absolute error; the batch framework often performs competitively with one-point selection.
narrate.key_results: The one-point comparisons used 20 added points, an initial design of 5 times the input dimension, and a test matrix of 10 to the fifth points; seven test functions were studied, including variable-dimension cases at dimensions 3, 5, and 8. On the two-dimensional Branin function, the gradient-based design had root mean square error 0.52, compared with 0.72 for each of two existing improvement criteria and 0.65 for the variance-based design; the variance-based design had maximum absolute error 2.05, compared with 3.07 for the best of those existing criteria. For batch comparisons, the authors tested batch sizes 2, 3, and 5 over 10 iterations, and report that the proposed gradient-based or variance-based batch designs outperform other comparisons in most tested cases. With batch size 2 on the Branin function, the gradient-based batch design had root mean square error 0.40 and the variance-based batch design 0.43; the authors report that batch and one-point designs sometimes have similar accuracy and sometimes the batch design performs better.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an open-loop calibration and posture-selection method for a three-degree-of-freedom ankle rehabilitation robot. Its calibration model represents the relationship between commanded and measured postures as a linear model with axis coupling and bias, and estimates 12 parameters from posture measurements. The authors frame selecting postures as a design of experiments problem and use a D-optimality criterion to favor subsets with high information content. A Proximal Policy Optimization agent is trained in simulation to choose 4 postures from 50 candidates, then applied to simulated and physical-robot data. The learned policy produces much more informative selections than random selection and supports more consistent parameter estimates and output predictions.
narrate.key_results: The policy was trained for 200,000 episodes and evaluated by selecting 4 of 50 postures. In simulation, the mean information-matrix determinant was 5.58 × 10^34 for the learned policy and 9.50 × 10^31 for random selection. On the independent real-time dataset, the corresponding means were 7.32 × 10^34 and 1.31 × 10^32. The reported average variance across estimated parameters was 2.50 × 10^-3 for the policy and 1.71 for random selection in simulation, and 2.55 versus 36.2 in real-world data. The authors also report that predictions from a parameter estimate based on four carefully selected postures agree more closely across episodes than predictions from an unstructured posture combination.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an enumeration method for two-level D-optimal and A-optimal designs for a main-effects model with an intercept, focusing on run sizes that are three more than a multiple of four. The method constructs designs column by column whose information matrices have an Ehlich structure, then removes duplicates by retaining one representative from each class of equivalent designs. The authors use it to enumerate designs for run sizes 7, 11, and 15, and examine promising optimal information-matrix forms for run size 19. They also rank designs by how much main-effect estimates are affected by omitted interactions. The work expands the catalog of available designs, while identifying cases where candidate information matrices cannot be realized by a design.
narrate.key_results: For 15 runs, the authors enumerate designs for the Ehlich-type information-matrix forms considered, but report exceptions at 13 and 14 model parameters where the candidate optimal forms have no corresponding designs. For 13 parameters, the best feasible form they found has 99.90% relative D-efficiency against the infeasible candidate forms; for 14 parameters, the identified A-optimal form has 99.53% relative D-efficiency against its infeasible D-optimal candidate. For 15 parameters, the feasible form they identify is both D-optimal and A-optimal. Their results also show that, for some parameter counts, an optimal design can have more aliasing between main effects and interactions than a non-optimal design.

narrate.summary: This paper extends the physics-informed polynomial chaos expansion framework for surrogate modeling and uncertainty quantification of systems governed by ordinary and partial differential equations. It replaces the standard Karush-Kuhn-Tucker constrained least-squares solver with a solver that updates Lagrange multipliers, and adds D-optimal selection of virtual points that enforce physical constraints. The sampling procedure draws an oversized candidate pool, then uses singular value decomposition and QR factorization with column pivoting to select informative points. The authors compare the original solver and the new solver, with and without D-optimal sampling, in simulated engineering examples. They find that the multiplier-update solver often reduces computation time, while combining it with D-optimal sampling can improve accuracy and stability in more complex cases.
narrate.key_results: In the two-dimensional heat equation with Dirichlet boundaries, all four configurations reached an error of about 10^-4; the multiplier-update solver was faster than the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker solver, although D-optimal sampling increased cost as the number of virtual points grew. In the Neumann-boundary heat example, the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker result reached mean squared error on the order of 10^-3 at 1,200 virtual points, then rebounded and stabilized near 10^-2; the multiplier-update method continued improving, and D-optimal selection reduced run-to-run outliers. For the stochastic-source heat example, minimum mean squared errors were 8.45×10^-4 for the standard solver, 6.79×10^-4 for the multiplier-update solver, and 6.45×10^-4 for the multiplier-update solver with D-optimal sampling. In that example, the multiplier-update solver was faster, while the D-optimal combination provided the lowest reported error and performed best over 100 stochastic fields. In the five-dimensional random-stiffness beam example, the authors report that the best accuracy settings for the mean and standard deviation were also less costly with the D-optimal multiplier-update method than with the standard solver.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a local empirical Bayes method to estimate treatment effects in online controlled experiments when effects vary over time and across experiments. It constructs a tailored comparison group for each experiment, first comparing traffic patterns and scale, then refining the group using cross-fitted pilot outcomes. The proposed Cross-Fitted Stratified Hybrid Neighbors procedure uses that group to shrink noisy estimates toward a local mean rather than a single global mean. The authors analyze mean squared error theoretically and evaluate the method in a semi-synthetic study based on operational data from 78 ASOS experiments. The method improves estimates in that study, while the evaluation does not test a live deployment.
narrate.key_results: On the semi-synthetic ASOS study, which covers 78 experiments and 24,153 snapshots, the proposed method at a neighborhood size of 10 reduced mean squared error by 27.2% relative to the raw estimator; its mean error was 3.53 × 10⁻⁵, compared with 4.85 × 10⁻⁵ for the raw estimator. Classical global empirical Bayes reduced error by 1.2% and had a 52.7% win rate, while the proposed method had an 82.4% win rate. At the same neighborhood size, the outcome-only and process-only local methods reduced error by 11.8% and 17.9%, respectively. The proposed method maintained more than 23% error reduction across the tested neighborhood sizes from 6 to 20.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a Bayesian method for choosing input signals to identify quasi-linear stochastic dynamical systems, which are linear in their states but may depend nonlinearly on the control input. Its objective is to gain information about uncertain model parameters, rather than relying only on local Fisher-information criteria. The method approximates mutual information with a tractable lower bound based on pairwise distances between parameter-dependent Gaussian observation distributions, using a discretized prior when needed. A Kalman-filter-based computation avoids large observation-covariance matrix inversions, reducing the matrices to be inverted to the size of the output at each time step. In simulations, the designed inputs performed as well as or better than the comparison designs, including a substantial improvement over a harmonic input in the magnetometer example.
narrate.key_results: The authors report four examples and conclude that their Bayesian designs were no worse than the classical comparison methods in the examples; they were better in some cases, while the methods gave nearly identical results for the narrow-prior atomic sensor example. For the pump-control magnetometer with a 5 ms experiment and maximum input amplitude 200, the optimal signal gave a reported frequency-estimation error of 0.48 mHz, compared with 7 mHz for the harmonic signal, approximately a 14-fold reduction. In that example, the maximum a posteriori estimator attained the information-theoretic lower bound. The reported Monte Carlo evaluations used 3,000 repetitions in examples 1 and 3, 6,000 in example 2, and 2,000 in example 4; the comparison designs included average D-optimal, spectral, constant or step, pseudorandom binary, and harmonic inputs where applicable.

key_equations.name: Approximate information objective
key_equations.latex: I_l(U)=-\sum_i p_i\ln\left(\sum_j p_j\exp[-d_{ij}(U)]\right),\qquad U^*=\arg\max_{U\in U_{ad}} I_l(U)
key_equations.explanation: I_l is the lower bound on mutual information, p_i and p_j are prior weights for parameter candidates, d_ij is their pairwise distance, U is the input design, U* is the maximizing design, U_ad is the admissible design set, and the sums run over candidates.

key_equations.name: Pairwise Gaussian distance
key_equations.explanation: d_ij is the pairwise distance for candidates i and j, Delta_ij is the difference between their predicted means, the superscript T denotes transpose, S_i and S_j are their observation covariance matrices, vertical bars denote determinants, and ln denotes the natural logarithm.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that exponential terms in the information lower bound can become numerically problematic when pairwise distances are large, and that discretizing the prior can introduce approximation error if the quadrature nodes and weights are not selected carefully. They also state that the lower bound is not generally tight, so maximizing it can produce a design that is not close to the mutual-information optimum.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence comes from simulated examples rather than validation in physical experiments, including the magnetometer case. The approach also depends on the assumed system and noise models and on approximating continuous parameter priors with a finite set of points; the reported designs do not establish performance when those assumptions are inaccurate or when practical constraints beyond the stated input limits apply.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose converting the method into a sequential Bayesian adaptive design that updates the input using the current posterior distribution. They also describe checking the Markovian-noise assumption in experiments and using an extended Kalman filter rather than the slower maximum a posteriori estimator for real-time implementation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method in real system-identification experiments and compare predicted information gains with observed estimation errors. Further work could also incorporate practical limits such as input slew rates, actuator dynamics, and safety constraints, and evaluate robustness when the assumed model or noise distribution is misspecified.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for choosing which experiments to run and how to allocate the sample when experimental results will be combined with potentially biased external evidence. It targets a policy outcome defined by unknown parameters, some of which may be learned experimentally and others from observational or prior-study estimates. The design balances sampling variance against sensitivity to unknown bias, using proportional regret relative to an oracle that knows the bias magnitude. The authors derive solutions for researchers using linear estimators and for audiences that update their own beliefs after seeing the reported evidence. In a cash-transfer illustration using Kenya and external estimates from Mexico, the proposed design balances bias and variance and can achieve comparable precision with substantially fewer participants than variance-only designs when external estimates may be biased.
narrate.key_results: In the illustration, the regret-optimal design combines unconditional and conditional cash-transfer experiments, while both variance-based Neyman designs put the sample entirely into the employment experiment. At the benchmark sample size of 3,700, the linear-regret design has overall regret of about 3; the Neyman design with variance-optimal weights has regret of about 13, and the classical Neyman design has regret above 11. The proposed design equalizes bias and variance regret, whereas the Neyman designs attain low variance regret at the cost of much greater sensitivity to misspecification. For bias above 2% of the outcome standard deviation, the proposed design can achieve the same audience mean-squared error with more than 60% fewer participants than the Neyman design; the paper also reports that the proposed design's audience regret remains close to one as bias increases, while Neyman regret exceeds 7 at a normalized bias of 8%.

key_equations.explanation: Regret is the larger of the variance ratio and bias-sensitivity ratio; α is variance, β is sensitivity to bias, and α* and β* are the smallest feasible variance and sensitivity.

key_equations.name: Optimal sample allocation

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that their main regret characterization applies most directly when no feasible design can eliminate worst-case bias in the target. Their linear-estimator class excludes more general adaptive nonlinear rules, and they describe design optimization with nonlinear estimators as computationally demanding. The analysis also relies on a first-order approximation for smooth targets under local misspecification.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical illustration is a calibrated example built from estimates in existing studies, not a new experiment that tests the proposed allocation in practice. Its recommendations depend on the chosen bias-shape restrictions and variance inputs, so results could change if those assumptions or the candidate experiment menu differ from the illustration.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying sequential or adaptive experimental decisions, cases where experimental precision is learned during the study, and combining their approach with algorithmic site selection. They also identify informing funding agencies as a possible application.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method prospectively in real studies and compare planned allocations with realized costs, precision, and external-validity errors. Further work could examine how design recommendations change under misspecification shapes elicited from practitioners and under operational constraints not represented in the example.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a way to combine CUPED with Yuen’s t-test for treatment effect analysis in online controlled experiments. The method targets the difference in trimmed means, making it more robust to outliers and skewed data than tests based on ordinary means. It first trims the outcome and pre-experiment covariate separately, then uses their trimmed means, variances, and covariance to calculate the adjustment. The authors evaluate the method with simulations of normal, lognormal, and zero-inflated lognormal data. In the skewed scenarios, the combined method achieved much higher power than Welch’s t-test, especially when pre-experiment and experiment data were highly correlated.
narrate.key_results: Each simulation was repeated 50,000 times with 100,000 subjects in each group, and the tests used a 1 percent trim for Yuen’s method. With a 5 percent treatment effect and a Spearman correlation of 0.95, CUPED-adjusted Yuen power was 99.34 percent for lognormal data and 66.39 percent for zero-inflated lognormal data; the corresponding Welch power was 6.47 percent and 5.24 percent. At a Spearman correlation of 0.25, CUPED provided little improvement: Yuen power was 64.66 percent without CUPED and 64.94 percent with it for lognormal data, and 28.58 percent and 28.62 percent for zero-inflated lognormal data. Under the null, Yuen’s false positive rates were close to the nominal 5 percent across the reported scenarios, while Welch’s rates were lower for the skewed scenarios.

key_equations.name: CUPED-adjusted trimmed treatment effect
key_equations.explanation: The estimated adjusted trimmed effect is the adjusted treatment-group trimmed outcome mean minus the adjusted control-group trimmed outcome mean; theta is the adjustment coefficient, Y_tj and X_tj are the trimmed outcome and covariate means for group j, and X_t is the pooled trimmed covariate mean.

key_equations.name: Variance-minimizing adjustment coefficient
key_equations.explanation: Theta is the adjustment coefficient; Cov denotes covariance, Var denotes variance, and X_tj and Y_tj are the trimmed covariate and outcome means for group j.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the trimmed effect can differ from the overall treatment effect, so trimming may conceal effects in the tails or lead to decisions that do not benefit the most valuable subjects. CUPED provides little benefit when suitable pre-experiment data are unavailable or weakly correlated with the outcome, and the authors say there is no universally suitable trim percentage because the choice depends on power, generalization, and repeated values in the tails.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to three simulated distributions, one treatment shift, a 1 percent trim, and the reported sample size; it does not establish how the method performs across a broader range of practical experiment conditions. The construction also depends on comparable pre-experiment covariate distributions between groups, and the paper does not report validation on real experiments or the effects of alternative allocation and missing-data patterns.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors describe the method as a foundation for more adaptive methodologies in data-driven decision-making. They do not give a specific implementation or evaluation plan for that future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future research could evaluate the method on real controlled experiments and across different sample sizes, trim percentages, treatment effects, and missing-data patterns. It could also compare alternative covariates and adjustment or inference procedures, and assess how the method can be incorporated into sequential experiment monitoring.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a sequential placement method for free-floating drifters that measure time-dependent, two-dimensional ocean vector fields. It introduces Bayesian Active Learning with Look-ahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories (BALLAST), using a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate and an information-gain objective. Unlike a standard information-gain design, BALLAST simulates likely future drifter paths under sampled vector fields and counts the observations those paths would produce. The authors also develop Vanilla SPDE Exchange (VaSE) to make the large posterior field samples needed by the method more efficient. Simulations using synthetic fields and a high-fidelity ocean-current simulator show that BALLAST generally improves field estimation over the tested placement strategies.
narrate.key_results: With synthetic temporal Helmholtz ground truth, BALLAST saved about 3 drifters, or about 16% of deployment cost, compared with uniform placement at the reported final performance. With SUNTANS ground truth, it saved around 2 drifters, or about 22%, compared with the same benchmark. In the sample-size study, using 20 posterior field samples brought BALLAST’s estimated utility gap below 1% consistently in the tested decisions. For the reported sampling setup, the estimated computational cost was of order 10^8 for VaSE, compared with 10^11 for the SPDE method and 10^17 for standard GP sampling; one VaSE sample took under 4 seconds in the reported laptop tests, while SPDE sampling took about 4.5 minutes. BALLAST generally ranked better than uniform, expected-information-gain, and distance-separation policies; the Sobol sequence was comparable to the optimized BALLAST policy in one synthetic setting, and BALLAST’s advantage diminished for slowly evolving flows.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that BALLAST’s advantage diminishes as the flow becomes slow and nearly stationary, where a space-filling design can be more desirable. The VaSE implementation is developed for a separable spatio-temporal model with a Matérn temporal kernel, although the authors note that broader kernels may be accommodated using other SPDE formulations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated fields, including fields from a high-fidelity simulator, rather than a reported real-world deployment, so operational performance is not established. The method also relies on assumed vector-field dynamics and simulated trajectories on a discretized spatial grid; errors in the surrogate or trajectory projection could affect the selected locations. The reported computation and design comparisons do not establish performance under practical deployment constraints such as limited launch sites or restricted access areas.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose applying BALLAST with other surrogate models, including other physics-informed Gaussian process models and deep adaptive designs that could speed acquisition optimization. They also identify collar sensors for animal movement and balloon sensors for meteorological data as possible applications.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method in field deployments and assess whether its estimated gains persist with real measurements, operational launch constraints, and imperfect trajectory information. Further work could also evaluate sequential use when observations arrive with delays or when deployment times and available drifters are constrained.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes Generative Stratification, a way to improve randomized experiments by using a large language model (LLM) to combine varied pre-treatment information into a score for forming strata. It targets more precise estimation of the average treatment effect, particularly when researchers have many covariates but do not know which ones are most useful for stratification. The LLM predicts outcomes under both treatment and control for each unit, and the predictions are added to create a score used to sort and pair units before random assignment within pairs. Across four empirical applications, the authors report lower estimation error than with simple randomization, with further gains when the score is combined with standard matching methods.
narrate.key_results: In simulations based on four experimental datasets, the method reduced mean squared error by 34.3%, 11.2%, 51.6%, and 14.8% relative to simple randomization, respectively. The average standard error was 15.3% lower than under simple randomization and 12.6% lower than under the original studies’ stratification methods. In comparisons using a hybrid of the generated score and Mahalanobis matching, mean squared error was 2.8% to 12.6% lower than with Mahalanobis matching alone, and about 50% lower than with regression following simple randomization. The evaluation used 3,000 replications per study, based on samples of 1,000 observations, except for one study that used 400.

key_equations.name: Optimal stratification score

key_equations.name: LLM-generated score
key_equations.explanation: Here X is the observed pre-treatment covariates, Yhat(1) and Yhat(0) are the LLM’s predicted outcomes under treatment and control, and g_LLM(X) is their sum, used to form strata.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their empirical applications are constrained by the limited pre-treatment data available in existing experimental datasets. They note that the method’s value may be greater when researchers have richer unstructured pre-treatment information.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers only four datasets and relies on imputed unobserved potential outcomes as the ground truth, so the reported gains may depend on the imputation procedure. The experiments also use one specified language model and prompt setup; the paper does not establish how results vary across models, prompts, or prospective real-world deployments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors anticipate that the method may become more valuable as richer pre-treatment data, including text and behavioral histories, become available and language models improve. They do not specify a separate study or implementation plan for pursuing this work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method prospectively in new experiments and assess whether its predicted scores improve precision across domains and populations. Researchers could also compare models and prompt designs and develop practical guidance for choosing how much weight to give the generated score when combining it with existing matching methods.

narrate.summary: The paper applies Taguchi design of experiments to choose hyperparameters for a convolutional neural network that classifies professional boxing frames as gameplay or break periods. It studies eight two-level factors, including image size, activation function, learning rate, preprocessing, and image augmentation, using a twelve-run orthogonal array. The authors compare five ways of combining training and validation accuracy and loss, including a logarithmic transformation that makes lower loss contribute positively to a larger-is-better objective. The third approach was the most balanced in the reported validation results, and the analysis ranked learning rate as the leading factor. The experiments used a boxing-video dataset and a fixed network trained for ten epochs per configuration.
narrate.key_results: The twelve-run design reduced the stated full-factorial search from 256 combinations to 12, which the paper describes as 95% fewer trials; it did not report a head-to-head grid-search experiment. In validation of the third approach's selected configuration, training accuracy was 98.84%, validation accuracy was 86.25%, training loss was 0.0442, and validation loss was 0.5784. Across the five selected configurations, the third approach had the highest validation accuracy and lowest validation loss; the first had 79.31% validation accuracy, the second had 0% validation accuracy, and the fourth and fifth each had 77.71%. The authors ranked learning rate among the most influential factors across approaches, while their analysis of variance found no factor statistically significant at the 0.05 level across all approaches.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the study tested only two levels for each of eight factors, used one fixed network architecture, and focused on boxing action recognition, limiting the range and transferability of the findings. narrate.limitations_unstated: Each configuration appears to have been run once, with random initialization, so the reported results do not establish how much performance varies across training seeds. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using three-level or mixed-level arrays to examine hyperparameter values between the tested levels, adding architectural and training-method factors, and testing the method on other tasks and datasets. narrate.future_work_unstated: A follow-up study could repeat selected configurations with multiple random seeds and evaluate the chosen setting on matches held out from both tuning and validation. It could also test a sequential refinement procedure after the initial array and assess video-level segmentation performance alongside frame-level accuracy and loss.

narrate.summary: The paper develops adaptive designs for online randomized experiments with two treatments and heterogeneous effects. Its objectives are to limit welfare loss during the experiment while estimating conditional average treatment effects accurately, and to provide privacy protection. The proposed ConSE method recursively segments the covariate space, eliminates treatments that appear inferior in a segment, and then uses controlled randomization to meet a chosen estimation target. A private extension, DP-ConSE, adds noise to the design’s statistics and final estimates. The authors establish theoretical regret-estimation trade-offs and show that the resulting treatment policy has a strong post-experiment performance guarantee.
narrate.key_results: The authors derive a lower bound linking cumulative regret and estimation error through an instance-complexity measure, and show that ConSE attains the corresponding trade-off up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, regret scales with the target estimation error raised to the negative of one half of two plus the covariate dimension, multiplied by instance complexity, or with the minimum-regret floor, whichever is larger. The paper reports that DP-ConSE achieves the same asymptotic regret and estimation-error bounds as ConSE while providing privacy guarantees for the allocation process and final estimate. Its post-experiment policy has a simple-regret bound that matches, up to logarithmic factors, the cited instance-optimal rate for the stated margin-condition class; the paper presents theoretical results rather than empirical comparisons.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the full instance-specific Pareto frontier may not be learnable or achievable because statistically indistinguishable instances can have different frontiers. Their data-driven procedure therefore guarantees a robust trade-off over the range that remains optimal across such indistinguishable alternatives.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results rely on a stationary covariate distribution, bounded rewards, and Lipschitz outcome functions, so their practical performance under drift or violations of smoothness is not established. The paper gives theoretical guarantees but no empirical validation of the algorithms, their run-size requirements, or the practical effect of privacy noise.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to settings with network interference and non-stationary environments.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the designs in simulated and real experiments, including their sample-size demands and sensitivity to model violations. Further work could also develop practical guidance for choosing the exploration target and privacy level under operational constraints.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a neural stencil emulator (NSE) for identifying and forecasting the dynamics of computer models expressed as partial differential equations (PDEs). Instead of training on long solution trajectories, the method learns a local stencil-to-time-derivative mapping from samples chosen to cover the stencil state space. Its space-filling designs include random sampling and principal component analysis (PCA)-guided sampling, with mixed versions that combine synthetic samples and downsampled trajectory data. The authors test the method on Allen-Cahn, advection-diffusion, and scalar Burgers’ systems, comparing its forecasts with trajectory-based sampling and established machine-learning emulators. Their results show that the stencil sampling strategies can produce accurate long-horizon forecasts using a small solver budget, although the best sampling strategy varies across systems.
narrate.key_results: For the pure designs, the paper uses 10 simulation timesteps to create 10,240 stencil examples; mixed designs use a 1,000-timestep trajectory plus a supplemental budget equivalent to 10 timesteps, producing 20,480 examples. Table 1 reports scores as 1,000 times normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE): for Allen-Cahn at diffusion coefficient 0.001, the mixed downsampled-plus-PCA uniform design scores 0.4, compared with 106.7 for the Fourier neural operator (FNO) trained with a 2,000,000-timestep budget. narrate.summary: This paper develops analytical optimal designs for degradation tests whose measurements follow a gamma process, with the goal of efficiently estimating model parameters or a product lifetime quantile. It considers designs with equal inspection intervals and designs in which inspection intervals can differ, under constraints on test duration, test-unit and inspection costs, and a minimum inspection interval. The authors derive results for determinant-based, trace-based, and lifetime-quantile variance criteria using properties of the trigamma function and majorization. For fixed duration and inspection count, equal intervals give the least information among the feasible interval schedules; the most informative schedule uses one long interval and the other intervals at the minimum allowed length. Two light-emitting diode examples show that the benefit of unequal intervals depends on the setting.
narrate.key_results: In the first example, the relative efficiencies of the equal-interval designs compared with the optimized unequal-interval designs are 0.99 for determinant-based optimality, 0.99 for trace-based optimality, and 0.98 for lifetime-quantile variance optimality. In the second example, the corresponding equal-interval design efficiencies are 0.75, 0.98, and 0.89, so the advantage of unequal intervals is larger for the determinant and lifetime-quantile criteria. The second example's optimal integer unequal-interval designs use 4 units, 82 inspections, and a test duration of 2991 for the determinant criterion; 6 units, 4 inspections, and 4453 for the trace criterion; and 6 units, 20 inspections, and 3583 for the lifetime-quantile criterion. For those integer designs, the reported relative efficiencies are 0.99, 0.99, and 1, respectively, and their objective values are close to those of the corresponding approximate designs.

narrate.summary: This paper designs a sequential exploration and elimination method for stochastic linear bandits when a learner has both prior offline observations and a limited online horizon. Its objective is to minimize cumulative regret while exploiting the information in the offline observations. The Offline-Online Phased Elimination (OOPE) method allocates exploration using a D-optimal design that combines the offline information matrix with a design for the current set of live actions, then eliminates actions that appear substantially worse. The analysis introduces an effective dimension determined by the offline information and proves regret guarantees and lower bounds for different offline-data quality regimes. A Frank-Wolfe approximation, called OOPE-FW, reduces the design's support and can improve regret when the action set is large and the effective dimension is moderate.
narrate.key_results: The paper bounds OOPE regret, with probability at least 1 minus the reciprocal of the online horizon, by a rate of order the square root of effective dimension times online horizon and a logarithmic factor, plus a dimension-squared term. The lower bounds show that OOPE is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors and additive dimension terms when the offline data is well explored or when many directions remain poorly explored; the authors report a gap between bounds when only a small number of directions are poorly explored. OOPE-FW reduces the support-related term and is shown to improve the bound when the effective dimension is at least constant, although its leading regret term has a larger constant. In simulations, run 50 times per horizon, OOPE had lower regret than purely online phased elimination and the warm-started linear UCB and Thompson-sampling baselines; OOPE-FW performed better in the tested setting with 30 dimensions and 900 actions, while comparisons across other settings showed its advantage depended on horizon and effective dimension.

key_equations.name: OOPE regret rate

narrate.limitations_unstated: The guarantees rely on a correctly specified linear reward model and the stated noise assumptions, so they do not establish performance under nonlinear responses, heavy-tailed noise, or unmodeled changes during deployment. Further work could also develop robust designs for model misspecification and changing rewards, and benchmark the computational cost of exact and approximate design construction.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for efficient Bayesian design of fixed and adaptive studies when the analysis model includes nuisance parameters. Its objective is to estimate operating characteristics, such as power and expected cost, while incorporating uncertainty about both the target effect and nuisance parameters. The method uses the Bernstein-von Mises large-sample approximation and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) trained on simulated estimates of a variance parameter. It applies the resulting predictions to fixed designs and group sequential designs, integrating operating characteristics over a design prior. In the examples, the method produced estimates close to Monte Carlo results and enabled comparison of two hypothetical clinical trial designs with similar overall assurance.
narrate.key_results: In the logistic regression example, the authors trained the BART model using 40 parameter settings; its estimated power was reported to compare satisfactorily with Monte Carlo estimates. For the clinical-trial example, the method used 60 training settings and 100,000 draws from the design prior for integration. Design D1, with analyses at sample sizes 350, 500, and 700, had cumulative Bayesian assurance of 0.44, 0.67, and 0.81, an integrated expected sample size of 365, and an integrated expected cost of 394. Design D2, with analyses at 300, 400, 500, and 600, had cumulative assurance of 0.38, 0.52, 0.61, and 0.82, an integrated expected sample size of 341, and an integrated expected cost of 384; the authors describe the overall assurance as about 80% for both designs. In the clinical example, the maximum reported difference between the method’s cumulative power estimates and Monte Carlo estimates was under 0.04.

key_equations.explanation: Pi of theta is the estimated probability of meeting the posterior decision threshold, Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, u is that threshold, n is the sample size, lambda hat of theta is the predicted variance parameter, psi of theta is the target quantity, and psi zero is its null value.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the normal approximation may be poor at small sample sizes and in more complex models, and that BART predictions may depend on the size and distribution of the training set. They caution that the satisfactory results in the paper are not broadly generalizable and suggest using the method for exploration followed by Monte Carlo evaluation of a few final design options.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence comes from a stylized example and one hypothetical clinical-trial application, so the paper provides limited evidence about performance across other data models, design priors, or practical constraints. The clinical application is hypothetical rather than an evaluation using trial outcomes, and the paper does not report numerical runtime comparisons that quantify the computational savings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest small-sample corrections or linear approximations as alternatives to the normal approximation. They also note that the method can be extended to interval hypotheses and can accommodate other loss functions, including functions that account for estimation accuracy and precision.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the method on a broader set of models and real experiments, including cases with more complex censoring, missingness, or operational constraints. It would also be useful to test sequential updating of the design as information accumulates and to quantify runtime and accuracy against full simulation across a wider range of design choices.

narrate.summary: This paper designs current-input experiments to estimate the anode and cathode reaction-rate constants of a lithium-ion battery cell. It uses a simulated 30 amp-hour nickel-manganese-cobalt and graphite cell represented by an electrochemical equivalent-circuit model. A deep reinforcement learning policy, trained with the twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm, selects current inputs to increase Fisher information while accounting for voltage constraint violations. The authors compare the resulting design with nonlinear model predictive control and conventional battery tests. In the simulations, the learned design provides the highest information values and lowest median estimation errors among the compared profiles.
narrate.key_results: For the learned design, average Fisher information was 2.90e+12 for the cathode rate constant and 4.86e+12 for the anode rate constant, compared with 1.33e+12 and 1.65e+12, respectively, for nonlinear model predictive control. Median parameter estimation errors were 0.244% for the cathode and 0.233% for the anode with the learned design, compared with 0.340% and 0.304% for nonlinear model predictive control. Both optimized profiles used an 1800-second test, while the relaxation current interrupt discharge test lasted 102212 seconds; the authors report that nonlinear model predictive control took an average of 5 seconds per input step, compared with 5.2 milliseconds for the learned policy, which itself required about 24 hours of training. The learned design also had lower median errors than the reported conventional tests, including constant-current discharge, relaxation current interrupt discharge, and a drive cycle.

narrate.summary: This paper develops experimental-design methods for finite-armed semiparametric bandits, where rewards include both a linear feature-based component and a bounded, potentially adversarial shift. Its objective is to estimate arm-value differences well enough to support low-regret learning, probably approximately correct (PAC) guarantees, and best-arm identification (BAI). The authors design a policy for orthogonalized regression by applying a standard G-optimal design to feature differences from a reference arm, then mixing that design with the reference arm. They use this design and a sharper estimation-error analysis to construct an adaptive phase-elimination algorithm. The paper’s theoretical results establish regret and exploration guarantees, and simulations compare its regret with two existing semiparametric bandit methods.
narrate.key_results: The adaptive method achieves regret of order the square root of dimension times horizon times the logarithm of the number of arms, up to logarithmic factors, matching the stated minimax rate for finite-arm linear bandits. With a positive suboptimality gap, its regret is logarithmic in the horizon; the paper gives a gap-dependent bound of order dimension times logarithm of the number of arms divided by the gap, up to logarithmic factors. Its best-arm identification sample complexity is of order dimension times logarithm of the number of arms divided by the squared gap, up to logarithmic factors, and its PAC sample complexity is of order dimension times logarithm of the number of arms divided by the squared accuracy, up to logarithmic factors. Simulations compared the proposed method with BOSE and semiparametric Thompson sampling for dimension and arm-count settings of 5 and 10, and 20 and 30; the proposed method had lower plotted cumulative regret in those cases. In ten repeated estimation experiments with 30 arms and dimensions 5 and 30, the paper reports that the scaled estimation error stayed below ten times the square root of dimension times the logarithm of the number of arms.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The guarantees rely on bounded features, a bounded parameter and bounded shifts, with each shift determined before the action is selected; this may not cover settings with unbounded disturbances or shifts that respond to the selected arm. The empirical evaluation uses simulated rewards, two shift patterns and a small number of dimension and arm-count settings, so it does not establish performance in deployed experiments or under practical randomization constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose refining pure-exploration algorithms to achieve optimal sample complexities, even if that does not simultaneously achieve optimal regret. They also propose studying the fixed-budget setting.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the design in real experiments and study its performance when arms have unequal costs, availability limits or other restrictions on randomization. It could also develop and test methods for shifts that violate the paper’s boundedness or pre-action timing assumptions.

narrate.summary: This paper develops optimal experimental design criteria for data-consistent inversion, which updates uncertainty in model inputs so that predicted quantities of interest match observed data. The criteria are intended to select measurements that reduce uncertainty about variable properties in a population, rather than to estimate one fixed set of unknown parameters. The authors construct the criteria from singular values of Jacobians: the expected scaling effect measures how tightly data values restrict possible inputs, while the expected skewness effect measures geometric redundancy among measurements. They use the scaling effect to choose an initial measurement and the skewness effect to add measurements sequentially. In simulations of heat flow through a metal rod and a welded metal plate, the selected sensor arrangements were informative and the sequential arrangement was intuitive, without requiring an inverse problem to be solved during design selection.
narrate.key_results: For the thin-rod example, the authors evaluated 820 candidate two-sensor maps using 10,000 parameter samples. The largest reported inverse expected scaling effect was 906.9 for sensors at positions (1.0, 0.45); the inverse expected scaling effect at the two rod ends was 890.5, while the inverse expected skewness effect was highest at the two ends, at 0.995. The preferred end-sensor design produced an updated input density concentrated near the chosen midpoint observation, whereas suboptimal designs produced broad or multimodal updated densities. In the plate example, the design space contained 10,201 possible sensor locations and about 10^30 combinations of nine locations; the greedy procedure selected an interpretable arrangement with sensors distributed across the nine plates, but the paper does not report a numerical head-to-head performance comparison with exhaustive search or other design criteria.

key_equations.name: Data-consistent density update
key_equations.explanation: The updated density pi-up on the parameter domain is the initial density pi-init multiplied by r, the ratio of observed density pi-obs to predicted density pi-pred evaluated at the quantity-of-interest map Q of input lambda.

key_equations.name: Expected scaling effect
key_equations.explanation: The expected scaling effect of map Q is the reciprocal of the average product of its Jacobian J_Q singular values sigma-k over parameter domain Lambda, using measure mu, output dimension m, and index k.

key_equations.name: Expected skewness effect
key_equations.explanation: The expected skewness effect is the harmonic mean of local skewness SK; local skewness uses row j-k of the Jacobian, singular values sigma-i of the full Jacobian, singular values sigma-k,i after removing row k, and the same measure and output dimension.

key_equations.name: Design objective
key_equations.explanation: The optimal map Q-opt is selected from candidate design space Q to maximize utility U, defined as the reciprocal of either the expected scaling effect or the expected skewness effect.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors restrict their optimization experiments to finite, discretized candidate design spaces and leave continuous optimization over the design space for future work. They also note that the simultaneous-design results apply when the entire quantity-of-interest map can be optimized at once, and present a greedy approach for larger problems.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstrations use simulated heat-transfer models and do not validate the criteria on real manufacturing measurements. The criteria are based on sampled Jacobians and do not explicitly incorporate measurement noise or practical sensor constraints such as cost and accessibility; the plate example also avoids exhaustive comparison across its very large design space.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying continuous optimization over the design space. They also identify a future study of using these criteria to optimize data acquisition that produces data-derived or data-learned quantities of interest.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the selected designs with real manufacturing data and assess whether the predicted uncertainty reduction persists under model error and measurement noise. Further work could incorporate sensor cost, access restrictions, and other operational constraints, and compare sequential selections with alternative designs on the same problems.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an estimator for measuring improvement between a new decision policy and a baseline in a standard A/B test. It targets lower estimation error by using the policies' action probabilities to exploit similarities between them, while leaving the user-allocation protocol unchanged. The estimator combines weighted rewards from both policy groups and includes a correction term to retain unbiasedness when the probabilities are known. Its weight-transform function can be chosen to account for unequal group sizes or for errors in estimated probabilities. Theoretical analysis and simulations find the largest gains when policies overlap, while the method returns to the difference-in-means estimator when overlap is absent.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with close policies, the reported variance-reduction ratios over the difference-in-means estimator reached 27.52 when the policy-distance measure was approximately 1 and the target-to-baseline user ratio was 1/4; the corresponding ratio was 19.05 at a ratio of 1. At a policy distance of approximately 10, reported ratios were about 2.6 to 3.05, while at approximately 10 squared they were about 1.08 to 1.20. In a recommendation simulation, the authors used 1,000 interactions under each policy and repeated each horizon configuration 500 times; the horizons ranged from 1 to 32. Their misspecification-aware estimator had lower mean squared error than the difference-in-means baseline across the tested horizons, whereas the estimator optimized for known probabilities degraded at longer horizons.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a fixed-budget adaptive experiment for choosing among treatments that will later be compared with a control in an A/B validation test. The authors characterize each treatment using a validation z value, which reflects both its mean improvement and the uncertainty relevant to validation. narrate.summary: The paper proposes an adaptive A/B testing framework for personalized marketing that combines a large language model (LLM) with reinforcement learning (RL). The LLM generates two content versions from a user portrait and current context, and the framework combines those inputs and content representations into a state for decision-making. The authors evaluate the method using advertising interaction data from the Criteo dataset and compare it with static A/B testing, a contextual bandit, a recommendation model, and a language-model-plus-rules approach. They report higher click-through rates and narrower confidence intervals for their framework than for the compared methods.

They report that dynamically optimized prompts increased CTR by 7.3% on average relative to static-template prompts. The evaluation used a sampled 5% subset of about 14 million entries from a dataset described as containing over 283 million training interactions, with 6 million interactions used for evaluation. The comparisons included static A/B testing, LinUCB, DeepFM, and a language-model approach with a rule-based delivery policy; the paper does not give precise numerical CTR differences between the full framework and each of these methods in the text.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) method accelerated by local radial basis functions (RBFs). The method targets expected information gain (EIG) for laser-induced cavitation (LIC) experiments that use inertial microcavitation rheometry (IMR) to characterize hydrogel viscoelastic properties. It runs expensive bubble-dynamics simulations for a small batch of prior parameter values, then uses nearby simulations to approximate responses for the larger sample needed to estimate information gain. The authors test both designs assuming one constitutive model and designs accounting for five candidate models. They report that the approach substantially reduces forward-simulation cost while retaining useful EIG estimates and design recommendations.
narrate.key_results: In a separate three-parameter benchmark, using 500 batch simulations produced estimates converging to the reference based on 20,000 samples at 2.5% of the forward-simulation cost; with 200 batch simulations, the estimated marginal posteriors closely matched the Markov chain Monte Carlo benchmark based on 20,000 simulations. In the single-model LIC tests, the two-parameter cases required about 4% of the baseline simulation cost, while the tested three-parameter cases required about 10%; a batch of about 500 was reported to give reasonably accurate EIG estimates for the more complex cases. For the five-model LIC problem, the reference sample size was 25,000, and the authors report comparable EIG accuracy with 2,000 or fewer batch simulations and an 8% computational cost in the design comparison. They identify a high-information region at Weber numbers above about 500 and equilibrium radii below about 0.2; the reported search used 900 core-hours compared with 11,250 core-hours for the high-fidelity comparison, a 12.5-fold acceleration.

The multi-model study assigns equal prior probabilities to five candidate models and assumes those models can represent the experiment; performance could differ with other models, unequal prior probabilities, or model misspecification.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces PLanet, a tool for specifying and comparing experimental assignment procedures, especially those used in human-subjects research. It represents plans as matrices and lets researchers combine design elements, such as counterbalancing, nesting, and crossing, using composable operations. A constraint solver generates assignments that meet the specified requirements, while static checks identify causal effects that the design can test and assumptions that differ between designs. The authors evaluate PLanet against existing design tools and report that it expressed more of the sampled experiments. Think-aloud studies also indicate that it helped researchers explore alternatives and make design assumptions easier to articulate.
narrate.key_results: In a purposive sample of 15 experiments from human-computer interaction publications, PLanet expressed 14, compared with 12 for edibble and 8 for Touchstone 2; the one experiment PLanet could not express was also inexpressible in both comparison tools. All 15 PLanet programs ran in under 33 seconds, and 14 ran in under 1 second; the slowest reported run took 32.297 seconds. In six think-aloud studies, all participants successfully specified the presented design and constructed between two and six designs. The evaluations suggest that PLanet supports design exploration and helps users describe assumptions, but they do not establish improved outcomes in real experiments.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test whether PLanet’s recommendations and warnings lead to more valid or informative assignments in independently conducted experiments, including settings outside the sampled human-subjects studies. narrate.summary: The paper studies whether rerandomization can reduce false discoveries when researchers search over covariate combinations in regression adjustment and report the most significant result. It considers randomized treatment-control experiments and regression models that include covariates and treatment-by-covariate interactions when estimating the average treatment effect. The design accepts only treatment allocations with sufficiently balanced covariates, using either a Mahalanobis-distance rule or covariate balance-test p-values. The authors derive conditions for these designs to reduce or control the type I error caused by this form of p-hacking, including threshold guidance when outcome-prediction information is available. Their theoretical results, simulations, and a real-data illustration show that more stringent balance requirements generally reduce the inflation, although some settings require impractically stringent thresholds for complete control.
narrate.key_results: The theory shows that both ReM and ReP reduce the asymptotic type I error of the hacked p-value relative to complete randomization, and can control it when their thresholds are sufficiently stringent. Under the paper's assumption of five orthogonal, equally important covariates, a significance level of 0.05 and outcome-prediction R-squared of 0.6 require a ReM acceptance probability of about 0.15% for uniform control. In simulations with 1,000 units, five covariates, and 100,000 allocations, an acceptance probability of 0.01 resolved the inflation when covariates were independent and equally important with outcome-prediction R-squared at least 0.7; with unequal importance, the reported requirement was at least 0.9, while correlation of 0.8 prevented resolution in the settings studied. The simulation results also show that inflation increases with the number of covariates searched and tends to decrease as rerandomization becomes more stringent. In the real-data illustration, the analysis used 368 students, five covariates, four strata, and 100,000 assignments; rerandomization reduced the hacked-p-value error rates relative to the randomized-design baselines, but did not always eliminate inflation.

The methods choose observation times to maximize determinant-based information criteria, subject to practical timing constraints. narrate.summary: The paper designs a geometry-aware spatiotemporal Gaussian process (G-ST-GP) for predicting dynamic signals over complex three-dimensional geometries. Its spatial covariance uses eigenfunctions of the geometry’s Laplacian, while a temporal covariance models change over time. In the active-learning comparison, after 45 added locations, the adaptive strategy reached relative error 0.2436, versus 0.2495 for the fixed-weight combined strategy, 0.2482 for space-filling, 0.2527 for uncertainty sampling, and 0.2904 for random sampling. narrate.summary: This paper compares three methods for choosing parameter settings for the Firefly Algorithm: standard Monte Carlo sampling, quasi-Monte Carlo sampling, and Latin Hypercube Sampling. It applies the methods to the algorithm’s attractiveness, scaling, and perturbation-decay parameters, then tests performance on six optimization benchmarks, including constrained engineering design problems. They report that the methods generally produce similar solution quality and parameter values, although some objective-value variances differ by benchmark and sampling method.
narrate.key_results: The main experiments used a population of 20, 1,000 iterations, and 10 independent parameter settings per sampling method; each setting was used for 50 algorithm calls, and the paper reports 500 simulation realizations.
