narrate.summary: This paper extends a regret-minimization method for selecting a one-shot subset of unlabeled examples to label, with downstream multiclass logistic regression as a key application. It treats selection as optimal experimental design, aiming to improve prediction or parameter estimation through commonly used design criteria. The method first solves a continuous, weighted design problem and then rounds that solution into selected samples using follow-the-regularized-leader actions and either an entropy or square-root regularizer. The authors also extend the method to ridge-regression design and relate a prediction-error design objective to excess risk under stated statistical assumptions. On synthetic data and image benchmarks, the method generally performs well against the tested alternatives, while the entropy version more reliably aligns its design-objective choice of learning rate with classification accuracy.
narrate.key_results: For unregularized design, the paper proves that the entropy method can achieve a one-plus-epsilon approximation with a deterministic budget of at least 16 times the feature dimension times its logarithm divided by epsilon squared; a data-dependent bound scales linearly rather than quadratically with inverse epsilon. The square-root-regularized method has a stated budget bound of 32 times the feature dimension divided by epsilon squared, and the ridge-design extension also has near-optimality guarantees. In the experiments, the method was usually best or near-best: on MNIST with 20 selected samples it reached 92.02% accuracy, compared with 91.76% for the next-best listed method, and on balanced ImageNet-50 with 50 selected samples it reached 77.18%, compared with 73.84% for the next-best method. On class-imbalanced ImageNet-50, it reached 77.18%, 81.88%, and 82.81% accuracy for budgets of 50, 100, and 150 samples, respectively, exceeding all listed baselines at each budget. On synthetic data with 2,000 points and 100 features, both regularizers consistently had smaller relative design-objective gaps than uniform sampling and the swapping baseline; their observed performance was nearly identical.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes Physics-Informed Experimental Design (PIED), a method for choosing observations to estimate unknown parameters in systems governed by partial differential equations. It targets one-shot designs, where observation locations must be selected before data collection and cannot be adjusted between trials. PIED uses physics-informed neural networks both to simulate possible system responses and to estimate parameters from simulated observations, then optimizes a design using gradients. The method adds a shared, meta-learned network initialization and two criteria that approximate how well a partially trained or estimated inverse solver will recover parameters. Across simulated cases and two real datasets, its proposed criteria generally produce lower parameter-estimation error than the tested design benchmarks.
narrate.key_results: The paper reports median expected parameter-estimation losses, with the parenthetical values giving the semi-interquartile range; lower losses indicate better results. For the wave case, Few-step Inverse Solver Training (FIST) gives 3.87 times 10 to the minus one (0.76) and Model Training Estimate (MoTE) gives 3.81 times 10 to the minus one (2.34), compared with 4.46 times 10 to the minus one for the mutual-information benchmark and 4.63 times 10 to the minus one for variational Bayesian optimal design. For Navier-Stokes, MoTE gives 1.18 times 10 to the minus two (0.11), versus 4.33 times 10 to the minus two for the best listed benchmark; for the function-valued Eikonal case, FIST gives 0.74 times 10 (0.02), versus 1.56 times 10 for the grid benchmark. On the groundwater dataset, FIST gives 1.93 times 10 (0.08), versus 2.10 times 10 for the mutual-information benchmark; on cell-growth data, FIST gives 2.62 (0.11), versus 2.82 for variational Bayesian optimal design. The paper also reports that meta-learned initialization speeds network training and that, in its Eikonal comparison, using neural-network simulators was more accurate and faster overall than using the tested numerical simulator, although no exact timing values are given in the text.

narrate.summary: This paper compares reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms for training policies that select experiments sequentially in Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED). The goal is to choose designs that maximize expected information gain (EIG), using sequential prior contrastive estimation (sPCE) as a tractable training objective. The authors compare five algorithms in simulations of finding object locations and inferring preferences between baskets of goods, including tests where the deployment model differs from the training model. Their results show that the best-performing algorithm depends on the problem: DroQ performs especially well in the preference experiment, while SUNRISE and the combined SUNRISE-DroQ approach perform well in location finding. The combined approach can improve performance in some cases, but requires more training time.
narrate.key_results: In location finding, with a 30-experiment horizon and two objects, SUNRISE achieved an sPCE of 11.837 plus or minus 0.012; the random-design baseline achieved 7.443 plus or minus 0.016. When testing different numbers of objects, SUNRISE-DroQ reached 12.143 plus or minus 0.013 for three objects, compared with 12.133 plus or minus 0.013 for SUNRISE; for one object, the combination scored 6.433 plus or minus 0.012. In the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) experiment, with a 10-experiment horizon, DroQ achieved the highest reported sPCE at both tested noise settings: 14.090 plus or minus 0.020 at nu equal to 0.005 and 12.683 plus or minus 0.022 at nu equal to 0.01; random designs scored 11.145 plus or minus 0.035 and 9.692 plus or minus 0.030, respectively. Average training times in the CES experiment were 8.95 hours for REDQ, 13.18 hours for DroQ, and 18.16 hours for SUNRISE-DroQ; the authors report that the most informative algorithms can also be more computationally expensive.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes LeGIT, a sequential approach to choosing interventions while learning a causal graph. It combines an LLM’s suggestions, based on variable descriptions and domain knowledge, with numerical intervention targeting. The LLM guides early experiments, including a bootstrap stage that focuses on variables not yet represented in the learned graph; later experiments use a numerical method. The approach is evaluated with four established benchmark networks and compared with other intervention strategies and human choices. The authors report that the hybrid approach generally improves graph recovery, particularly on the more complex benchmarks.
narrate.key_results: In the standard setting, each method used 33 intervention rounds with 32 samples per round, for 1,056 interventional samples. LeGIT’s average structural Hamming distance was 17.40 for Alarm, 12.60 for Insurance, 2.20 for Child, and 0.80 for Asia; the corresponding values for gradient-based intervention targeting were 19.60, 16.40, 2.80, and 1.00. LeGIT also had lower structural intervention distance and higher balanced scoring function than gradient-based targeting on Alarm, Insurance, and Asia, but not on Child; it was not best on every metric against every baseline. In the 16-sample-per-round setting, with 528 interventional samples total, LeGIT had lower structural Hamming distance than gradient-based targeting on Alarm, Insurance, and Child, while gradient-based targeting had a lower value on Asia. Compared with the human baseline, LeGIT had lower structural Hamming distance on Alarm and Insurance, while the human baseline had lower values on Child and Asia.

narrate.summary: The paper develops active selection of preference data for direct preference optimization, a form of reinforcement learning from human feedback used to train language-model policies. narrate.summary: The paper develops economical designs for experiments that vary both component quantities and the order in which components are arranged. The designs are intended for the mapping-based additive Gaussian process model and can also support linear models and active learning. The authors construct designs from transformed and combined good lattice point sets, using Latin hypercubes for the quantitative settings and balanced Latin squares for sequences. The resulting designs target space filling, balanced coverage of adjacent component pairs, low correlation among sequence columns, and coupling between the quantitative and sequence portions. The authors prove these properties for specified design sizes and demonstrate improved active-learning results in a simulated traveling-salesman problem.
narrate.key_results: For designs with the number of runs equal to the number of components, the sequence design has maximum possible minimum Hamming distance and each ordered adjacent pair occurs once; the quantitative design approaches the Manhattan-distance upper bound as the number of components grows. For larger designs, the construction supports run sizes that are multiples of the number of components; its sequence design is pair-balanced, and its distance and correlation properties approach the stated asymptotic bounds. In the six-city simulation, the proposed initial design had minimum Manhattan and Euclidean distances of 14 and the square root of 40, compared with 12 and the square root of 28 for the competing initial design; average absolute correlation was 0.2 versus 0.36. With 24 additional sequential experiments, the proposed initialization exceeded the competitor’s profit of 207.37 by the ninth sequential point and reached 222.84 by the 24th; the competitor reached 207.37 at its 17th point. A random design with 300 runs had a maximum profit of 204.93.

narrate.summary: This paper studies randomized experiments for comparing inventory policies in a multi-item, multi-period system with lost sales and a shared warehouse capacity. It focuses on policies that use different demand forecasts and estimates the global treatment effect, meaning the outcome difference if all item-periods used treatment rather than control. The authors compare switchback randomization across periods, item-level randomization fixed over time, and pairwise randomization independently across item-periods, using an inverse-probability-weighted estimator. Their analysis identifies different sources of bias: inventory carried between periods and competition between items for capacity. The results show that which design is preferable depends on whether the forecasting improvement mainly corrects a biased mean or reduces forecast-error dispersion.
narrate.key_results: For forecasts that reduce downward mean bias, the theoretical analysis finds that switchback estimates tend to be biased downward and item-level estimates are nonnegative-biased; pairwise bias is bounded above by item-level bias. For forecasts that reduce error dispersion without changing the mean, switchback and pairwise estimates have nonnegative asymptotic bias, while item-level randomization is asymptotically unbiased. Controlled simulations used 3,000 items, 60 periods, and 300 randomizations per design; their observed directions matched the theory. Trace-driven tests used 50,000 store-product series from 898 stores in 18 cities, with a 7-day evaluation horizon; they showed similar mechanisms, including with simulated stockout substitution. The paper reports qualitative directions and plotted comparisons rather than precise numerical bias or effect-size estimates.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors assume zero replenishment lead time for tractability and use uniform demand distributions to obtain analytical results. They note that their assumptions may not always hold in the trace-driven experiments, and that the 7-day evaluation horizon provides limited temporal replication for switchback randomization.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data evaluation is trace-driven simulation rather than a live randomized inventory deployment, and its latent-demand recovery, substitution mechanism, and economic parameters depend on modeling choices. The comparisons cover three designs and two forecast-improvement scenarios; the paper does not report precise numerical bias estimates or uncertainty intervals that would quantify performance across other settings.

Extend the analysis to positive lead times, alternative demand distributions, operational constraints on randomization, and estimators or designs that explicitly correct for interference.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes plug into closed-form solution (PICS), a sequential design method for estimating parameters in nonlinear models using the determinant-based D-optimality criterion. It is intended for models whose locally optimal designs have known closed-form probability distributions that depend on unknown parameters. After an initial set of runs, PICS substitutes current parameter estimates into the closed-form design and draws subsequent design points from it, avoiding repeated optimization of the design criterion. The authors also describe a balanced version that allocates runs in batches across the design’s support points. Theoretical results establish convergence of the design information and asymptotic normality of the parameter estimates, while simulations report better estimation efficiency and shorter computing times than the Chaudhuri–Mykland (C-M) approach in the examples studied.
narrate.key_results: In nonlinear regression simulations, PICS had lower median computing times than C-M in every reported setting; for example, for model M1 with an initial design of 40 runs and a total of 100 runs, the median times were 0.039 seconds for PICS and 0.262 seconds for C-M. For model M3 with an initial design of 60 runs and a total of 200 runs, the reported median times were 0.425 seconds and 7.118 seconds, respectively. For model M2 with an initial design of 60 runs, PICS reached about 60% efficiency at approximately 135 total runs with the three-point initial design, compared with approximately 185 for C-M; with a uniform initial design, the corresponding figures were approximately 120 and 160. In the logistic-regression simulations with an initial design of 100 runs, median computing times were 3.904 seconds for PICS and 5.267 seconds for C-M in one case, and 4.516 and 5.922 seconds in the other; the paper reports higher relative efficiency for PICS overall in these comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper develops methods for choosing simulation-model parameter settings efficiently when calibrating an expensive model to observed data. It considers Bayesian calibration with a Gaussian process emulator for scalar simulation outputs, seeking both close matches to the observations and improved estimates of the parameter posterior. The proposed HYBRID procedure alternates expected improvement, which exploits promising settings, with expected integrated variance, which encourages exploration of uncertain high-posterior regions. The paper also presents a Monte Carlo performance model that compares sequential-design configurations using batch size, worker count, acquisition time, and simulation run time. In the synthetic examples, HYBRID generally found closer matches than the other tested acquisition methods, while the performance model showed that the best batch size depends on computational conditions.
narrate.key_results: The authors tested the methods on six synthetic functions, using 30 replications per setting, an initial design of 10 points, and experiments that acquired up to 1,000 parameter settings. HYBRID consistently achieved lower calibration error than expected improvement, expected integrated variance, and uniform random sampling in the three examples highlighted in the main comparison; it also improved posterior estimation relative to expected improvement in those examples. In the performance-model analysis, the reported evaluation counts to reach an error level of 0.1 were 447, 767, and 895 for batch sizes 1, 4, and 128, respectively. The fastest configuration depended on the balance of acquisition time, simulation time, and run-time variability: large batches could be favorable when acquisition time dominated, whereas small batches were generally favored when simulations were long or highly variable.

narrate.summary: This paper develops theoretical results about orthogonal arrays, including arrays whose factors have different numbers of levels. It represents these arrays as algebraic designs in a specially weighted graph and uses that representation to derive a mixed-level Bierbrauer–Friedman lower bound on run size. The authors characterize equality cases through completely regular codes and, when the level counts are powers of the same prime, relate additive equality cases to multispreads. They also generalize the bound using distance-based graph polynomials for pure-level arrays. The mixed-level bound is tighter than an earlier mixed-level bound, and the polynomial approach gives positive lower bounds in some cases where the original bound is trivial.
narrate.key_results: The mixed-level lower bound is proved to be at least as strong as the earlier bound for mixed-level arrays. A worked example gives a 64-run array with one two-level factor and four four-level factors at strength 3 that attains the new bound. For binary arrays with an even number of factors and strength one less than half that number, the polynomial method gives a run-size fraction greater than 0.2046 divided by half the number of factors. The paper also shows that equality in the mixed-level bound corresponds to a simple set that is a completely regular code with covering radius 1.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an experimental-design framework for estimating uncertain travel costs and finding low-cost delivery routes. It models route costs as sums of edge costs for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with Bayesian priors that can incorporate existing distance or historical information. It selects a small set of Hamiltonian circuits using Bayesian D-optimality and gives a recursive construction for optimal fractional designs, along with heuristic algorithms for affordable designs. After collecting costs for the selected routes, the method estimates edge costs and uses routing heuristics to find a promising route. The simulations show that the design heuristics can achieve high relative efficiency with a small fraction of all possible routes, and that data-based cost estimates generally improve the routes found over using prior costs alone.
narrate.key_results: In design comparisons for 6, 8, and 10 locations, bubble sort had higher median relative D-efficiency than simulated annealing at every reported run size. For 10 locations and 136 runs, bubble sort achieved 0.985 relative efficiency while using less than 0.1% of all possible circuits; for 8 locations and 85 runs, it achieved 0.992. In the 20-location route simulations, there were 100 simulation iterations, with designs of 49, 96, 191, and 381 runs. Across the two simulated noise scenarios, frequentist or Bayesian estimates generally produced lower median route costs than prior-only costs; Bayesian estimates often performed better at smaller run sizes, while frequentist performance became similar or marginally better in some large-run comparisons.

narrate.summary: This study investigates Japanese consumers’ preferences for vegetable baskets and their intentions to participate in community-supported agriculture (CSA). The authors surveyed 2,484 consumers using a stated-choice experiment in which basket source, organic labeling, pickup distance, and price varied. They used latent class analysis (LCA) to identify consumer groups and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine factors associated with participation intention. The choice tasks were generated using an orthogonal array, with two basket options and an opt-out option in each task. The authors identified five consumer segments and found that educational opportunities and environmental and social contribution were more closely associated with participation intention than ingredient variety.
narrate.key_results: The analysis identified five segments: Conventional Shoppers (18.5%), Organic Enthusiasts (33.8%), Farmers’ Market Advocates (11.3%), Home Delivery Preferers (10.0%), and Sustainable Food Seekers (26.4%). Only Sustainable Food Seekers had positive estimated utility for the CSA basket option, with a reported marginal willingness to pay (MWTP) of Japanese yen 286.21; the estimate was negative for Conventional Shoppers, Organic Enthusiasts, and Home Delivery Preferers. In the structural model, food education and learning opportunities were positively associated with participation intention in the full sample and all five segments, with path coefficients from 0.329 to 0.439; environmental and social contribution had a full-sample coefficient of 0.233 and a coefficient of 0.305 among Sustainable Food Seekers. narrate.summary: This paper designs an adaptive experiment for estimating the average treatment effect (ATE) between treatment and control, both with and without subject covariates. It uses a doubly robust estimator, specifically an augmented inverse probability weighted (AIPW) estimator, and updates treatment probabilities in batches as outcome variances are learned. Its low-switching adaptive experiment (LSAE) estimates variance functions, uses them to approach Neyman-style allocations, and, with covariates, uses data splitting and cross-fitting. The authors derive non-asymptotic guarantees and lower bounds, establishing that the target allocation achieves the best possible variance among the considered unbiased estimators and adaptive designs. Simulations show that the design substantially improves estimation over non-adaptive allocation without covariates, while the covariate design improves on an allocation that ignores covariates but does not match the oracle result in the reported simulation.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation without covariates, with 2,000 subjects and one million simulations, the reported squared estimation loss was 0.037 for non-adaptive allocation, 0.023 for the LSAE with two batches, and 0.022 for optimal Neyman allocation; the authors report a reduction of more than 30% against the non-adaptive design. The LSAE’s reported bias was very small, and the authors describe it as more than ten times smaller than the adaptive Neyman allocation’s bias in the comparison. With covariates, the reported loss was 0.14 for the oracle Neyman allocation ignoring covariates, 0.12 for the LSAE with two or three batches, and 0.10 for optimal generalized Neyman allocation (OGNA); the LSAE’s reported bias was negligible. Theorems establish an unbiased estimator and a variance approaching the oracle bound, with the covariate result depending on the assumed regression-oracle rates; the paper also proves a lower bound for unbiased estimation under adaptive allocation.

They also state that, although they believe the covariate design’s convergence rate is optimal, they do not have a matching lower bound for that rate.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying Bayesian adaptive experiments, using offline experiment data to improve allocation, and designing experiments under limited resources. They also suggest extending the learning-to-design framework to non-stationary outcomes, learned interference structures, and dynamic treatment effects.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on real experiments and in larger simulation studies that vary covariate dimension, model misspecification, and outcome-tail behavior. The design could also be extended and validated under operational restrictions such as cluster randomization, minimum arm sizes, and allowable allocation changes.

narrate.summary: The paper develops order-of-addition (OofA) mixture-amount and component-amount designs for experiments where both the component quantities and the sequence in which they are added may affect the response. The models incorporate pair-wise ordering (PWO) effects, and the authors construct full designs from standard mixture designs. To reduce the number of experimental runs, they use the threshold accepting (TA) algorithm to select subsets that minimize the worst prediction variance under the G-optimality criterion. Two three-component examples illustrate the designs: a hormone mixture and a placebo tablet formulation. The authors report that the selected designs substantially reduce runs while retaining useful prediction performance, based mainly on simulated responses and simulation comparisons.
narrate.key_results: In the hormone example, the TA-selected design used 36 runs rather than the full design's 63; the paper reports mean G-efficiency values of 2451.3 for the reduced design and 4520.3 for the full design, with normalized G-efficiency of 51.3% for the reduced design. For that example, a separate analysis reports 89% G-efficiency, and the 10,000-dataset simulation reports a lower median mean squared error for the reduced design but a slightly wider spread than the full design. In the placebo example, the main application reports an 18-run design and 89% G-efficiency; the separate simulation comparison reports a 16-run design versus a 31-run full design, mean G-efficiency values of 934 versus 1485, and normalized G-efficiency of 63%. The paper reports that component amounts and order effects were significant at the 0.05 level in both examples.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate these designs in real experiments and across more component counts, checking whether prediction and estimation performance persists under model misspecification and practical manufacturing constraints. narrate.summary: The paper develops response surface methodology (RSM) for tuning a combined actuarial neural network (CANN) that predicts insurance claim frequency. It uses a design of experiments (DOE) strategy to sample hyperparameter settings, first screening factors and then fitting a quadratic response surface using a central composite design (CCD). The response being minimized is out-of-sample Poisson deviance loss on a public French motor insurance dataset. The authors compare tuning all selected hyperparameters with a reduced approach that omits two factors found statistically insignificant during screening. They report that the reduced approach gives near-minimum loss with fewer runs, and compare the run count with grid search (GS).
narrate.key_results: Tuning all hyperparameters reached an out-of-sample Poisson deviance loss of 0.245823 in 288 runs. Omitting two statistically insignificant neuron-count factors reached a near-minimum loss of 0.245976 in 188 runs. For seven hyperparameters, the paper reports 288 response-surface runs, compared with 2,187 runs for three-level grid search and 16,384 for four-level grid search; it reports run reductions from 86.8 percent to 98.2 percent against grid search. Confirmatory tests showed that some quadratic-surface predictions were suboptimal, while the all-factor setting with optimizer values rotated into range produced the best observed loss reported in the paper.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that some predicted settings were suboptimal in confirmatory experiments. They recommend repeating the process in such cases or selecting the best hyperparameters observed during the experiments.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses one public insurance dataset and one random training and test split, so the results do not establish that the method performs similarly on other data or splits. A quadratic response surface may poorly represent effects for a nominal optimizer choice, especially when out-of-range values are wrapped to an in-range value; this treatment can change the meaning of nearby points.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose combining response surface methodology with surrogate models or homotopy-based optimization, and extending the approach to other machine-learning methods. They also suggest hybrid approaches that use these techniques together to improve search efficiency and robustness.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could repeat the comparison across multiple data splits and insurance portfolios, and report uncertainty in both loss and the selected hyperparameters. They could also test designs that handle nominal optimizer choices directly and assess practical constraints such as training budgets and reproducibility.

narrate.summary: The paper develops tests for comparing restricted mean time lost (RMTL) across groups when there are competing event types and right-censored observations. It covers general group contrasts in factorial designs and allows event times to have ties. The authors estimate each RMTL from the area under an estimated cumulative incidence curve, then use Wald-type tests and a studentized permutation approach. For simultaneous testing, they use the dependence among the local test statistics rather than relying only on a Bonferroni adjustment. Simulations show that the asymptotic tests can be seriously liberal in small, unbalanced designs, while the permutation approach is more reliable in those settings; a leukemia transplant dataset illustrates the methods.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used 5,000 runs, 1,999 resampling iterations, and a 5% significance level; sample sizes included balanced groups of 60 per group at the smallest scale and unbalanced groups with one group of 16. In unbalanced small samples, the asymptotic approaches had family-wise error rates that exceeded 50% in some scenarios, whereas the Bonferroni-corrected permutation approach reached at most 10% in the reported scenarios. For balanced designs or large samples, the methods had comparable power; the dependence-aware asymptotic multiple tests were slightly more powerful than Bonferroni-corrected asymptotic tests, but their error inflation makes them unsuitable in small to medium unbalanced designs. In the transplant example, 6,110 patients remained after records with unknown treatment status were removed, and all methods identified effects of treatment depletion on relapse and other causes and of gender match on graft-versus-host disease.

narrate.limitations_stated: The proposed comparisons address event-specific RMTLs across groups, not comparisons between event types within a group. The authors also caution that the transplant analysis was simplified and does not support clinical conclusions because factors relevant to causal interpretation were not considered.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The tests rely on independent right censoring within each group and on adequate survival and censoring follow-up through the chosen terminal time; violations could affect the estimates and tests. The permutation tests require repeated recalculation and the reported implementation uses thousands of resampling iterations, which may be burdensome when many contrasts or large datasets are analyzed.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further research on within-group comparisons of different event types, including the validity of a randomization approach. They also suggest developing multiple tests for other effect measures, including cumulative incidence quantiles, probabilistic-index extensions, and area-between-curves statistics.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the procedures under departures from independent censoring and in settings with covariate adjustment or stratified randomization. Developing accessible software and testing the methods prospectively in real operational or clinical studies would also help establish practical performance.

narrate.summary: This paper develops optimal experimental design for universal differential equations, which combine mechanistic differential equations with an artificial neural network that represents unknown behavior. The objective is to choose measurement times and, where appropriate, experimental controls to improve estimation of mechanistic parameters and training of network weights. The authors formulate the design problem using parameter sensitivities and an information matrix, then reduce the number of sensitivities using truncated singular value decomposition or by lumping network weights into shared scaling parameters. They test the methods on simulated Lotka–Volterra and urethane-reaction examples. The results show that optimized measurements and controls can reduce estimation uncertainty and improve network accuracy, including predictions outside the training region.
narrate.key_results: In the Lotka–Volterra parameter-estimation example, equidistant sampling with no control gave estimates of 0.998 ± 0.057 and 0.980 ± 0.082 for the two parameters; optimized sampling and controls gave 0.995 ± 0.017 and 1.004 ± 0.006. For network training, the reported D-objective for weight lumping fell from 5.25e-3 with equidistant sampling and no control to 2.34e-3 with optimized sampling and no control, and to 1.59e-4 with both optimized sampling and controls. With ten measurements per state, the reported average absolute network error on the domain [0, 4] squared was 0.52 for the equidistant, no-control weight-lumping setting and 0.18 for optimized sampling and controls with the two-direction truncated decomposition. In the urethane example, the reported D-objective was 1.704e-4 for the one-direction truncated decomposition and 1.201e-2 for the outer scaling-parameter approach; the authors note that results across truncation sizes were not monotonic, in part because of noise and local optima.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that a global error analysis for the dimension-reduction approaches is difficult because the design problem is nonlinear. They also describe concurrent parameter estimation and network training as an open research topic, and use an alternating heuristic for their small-scale examples; the discretized nonconvex problems can produce only locally optimal candidates.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated benchmark problems rather than experiments on real processes, so performance under real measurement noise, operational restrictions, and model mismatch is not demonstrated. The design is based on sensitivities at a fixed parameter estimate, and its usefulness may depend on that estimate and on the assumed model structure. The examples also allow controls and measurement schedules to be optimized under simplified setups, so the practical cost and feasibility of implementing those schedules are not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using global information gain to select the decomposition truncation point and to decide when to recompute the decomposition during optimization. They also suggest using information-gain functions to regularize network training in sequential or online design, and note that weight lumping could be useful for sparse networks.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the approach in real industrial experiments and quantify sensitivity to measurement noise, model misspecification, and uncertain initial parameter estimates. It would also be useful to include practical limits on control moves, measurement cost, and sensor availability, and to assess how sequential redesign performs after each new batch of data.

narrate.summary: The paper develops approximate algorithms for choosing a useful subset of polymers from a larger set of permissible designs, with applications motivated by nucleic-acid therapeutics. Its goal is to select experiments that efficiently reveal how individual and interacting polymer components affect measured properties, or that maximize information for general numerical features. For composition-based designs, it represents permissible polymers as a graph and searches for a dense subset using two algorithms based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). For general feature matrices, it gives an approximate method for selecting a subset by D-optimality. In simulations, the graph methods often recovered planted designs, while the general-feature method found designs close to the planted D-optimal design.
narrate.key_results: For polymers of lengths from 10 to 70, the sparse ADMM method recovered the planted clique in 100% of 500 runs at each tested length; the approximate integer programming method reached 100% recovery at lengths of 20 and above. For polymer length 50, both graph algorithms achieved 100% recovery with graph sizes from 1,000 to 4,000 and a planted clique of 100 nodes, including a clique-to-graph size ratio of 1/40. For length 10, the planted clique was often missed, but the methods still found subgraphs with density about 0.98, compared with random subgraphs around 0.92. In the D-optimal simulation, the best result over 100 runs had a sum of log eigenvalues of 53, compared with 57 for the planted design; random subsets were typically rank deficient.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated polymers with planted cliques or planted designs, rather than measurements from real experiments, so it does not establish that the selected designs improve learning in an applied study. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose testing their algorithms against methods developed for less-dense graphs and analyzing their time and memory costs. They note that the sparse conjugate-gradient solve is the most costly step in their algorithms.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the selected designs in real polymer experiments and measure whether they improve estimation of polymer-property effects. Further work could also assess other design criteria and practical constraints, and evaluate sequential use in which each batch of results informs the next selection.

narrate.summary: The paper develops finely stratified rerandomization, a hybrid design for randomized experiments that combines tight matching on a few important covariates with rerandomization to balance additional covariates. It develops estimation and inference for causal parameters defined through generalized method of moments (GMM), including both finite-population and superpopulation targets. The design forms small matched groups using the stratification covariates, assigns treatment within groups, and accepts an assignment only when the additional covariates meet a balance criterion. The paper also studies post-assignment linear adjustment and methods for constructing confidence intervals. Its theory shows how the design can reduce estimation variance, while simulations and an application to a student incentive experiment show efficiency gains over several comparison designs.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with sample sizes of 300 and 600 and covariate dimensions of 5 and 20, stratified rerandomization weakly minimized mean squared error (MSE) among the three studied designs—complete randomization, fine stratification, and stratified rerandomization—for both adjusted and unadjusted estimators across the reported specifications. At sample size 300 and dimension 20, the unadjusted rerandomized estimator had lower MSE than the adjusted complete-randomization estimator in every outcome model. In the application with 1,203 students, rerandomizing the original coarse strata reduced adjusted normalized root mean squared error for financial-stress treatment-effect heterogeneity from 0.98 to 0.89; rerandomizing the fine-grade-point-average design reduced it from 1.02 to 0.84 for grade-point-average heterogeneity. Application-wide mean coverage was 0.95 for superpopulation intervals and 0.98 for finite-population intervals; the finite-population intervals were slightly shorter on average.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that tight matching becomes implausible as the number of matching covariates grows, and that making the acceptance region very small can make rerandomization computationally infeasible or undermine the asymptotic approximation. narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical results rely on asymptotic regularity conditions and do not establish performance for arbitrary high-dimensional settings or for covariate dimensions growing with sample size. narrate.summary: This paper develops ways to construct almost orthogonal arrays (AOAs) for fixed-level experimental designs, focusing on strength two and indices of one or two. The objective is to make level combinations across every pair of factors as evenly represented as possible, minimizing either the largest count deviation, called tolerance, or an aggregate deviation, called unbalance. The authors search with integer programming (IP) and local-search heuristics, and also give constructions based on finite fields for prime-power numbers of levels. They compare the resulting arrays with simple repeated-factor constructions and arrays from earlier studies. The methods produce competitive arrays, with different approaches performing best for different criteria and parameter settings.
narrate.key_results: The reported search focuses mainly on strength two, at most 10 levels, and indices of one or two; the authors report comparisons using tolerance, unbalance, and several other non-orthogonality measures. For index one with six levels and four factors, the IP search obtains 1-unbalance 4, compared with 60 for the repeated-factor baseline. For index two with three levels and eight factors, the algebraic construction has 1-unbalance 12, compared with 24 for the baseline; the IP search reports 18 and reaches tolerance 1. For index two, the local-search heuristic finds the best tolerance in the reported comparisons, while the algebraic constructions give infinite families for prime-power level counts. The authors report that their arrays generally improve on earlier results for the balance-based criteria and are often close to earlier results on discrepancy measures.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their computational searches were limited to a maximum of 100 GB of memory and 72 hours per search, restricting the array sizes they could examine. Their main numerical study focuses on fixed-level arrays of strength two, indices one or two, and at most 10 levels. The algebraic constructions apply only when the number of levels is a prime power.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The methods are not demonstrated for higher-strength arrays, mixed-level factors, or design requirements such as restricted randomization and run costs, so their practical reach beyond the studied cases is uncertain. The numerical comparisons concern constructed arrays and previously published arrays, rather than performance in real experiments or measured effects on estimation and prediction.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify exploring new algebraic constructions as a promising direction, particularly because algebraic methods scale better than their integer-programming search. They also provide the arrays they found in a public repository.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could extend the searches to higher strengths and mixed-level designs, and incorporate practical constraints such as randomization restrictions or unequal run costs. Testing the designs in real experiments and assessing their effects on estimation or prediction would help establish their applied value.

narrate.summary: The paper develops asymptotic inference for treatment effect estimators when experiment assignments are restricted by rerandomization or by stratified rerandomization. It studies estimators defined by estimating equations, common regression-based approaches, estimators for missing outcomes, and efficient estimators using machine learning. The authors show that the influence function is unchanged by rerandomization, although the limiting distribution can be non-normal. Adjusting the analysis for the variables used in rerandomization can make the usual normal approximation valid; the paper extends this result to stratified rerandomization. Simulations and an analysis of a cluster-randomized health study illustrate the theory.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 400 individuals and 1,000 generated data sets, the unadjusted estimator’s empirical standard error was about 20% smaller than the standard error calculated as if simple randomization had been used under rerandomization and stratified rerandomization. For adjusted estimators, including regression and machine-learning approaches, reported coverage was generally close to 0.95, and their performance was similar across randomization procedures when the adjustment included the rerandomization variables. The real-data application involved 72 wards and 609 individuals in a Nepal health study. The estimated effects and standard errors were -1.25 and 0.78 for the unadjusted estimator, -1.45 and 0.56 for regression adjustment, -1.35 and 0.62 for mixed-model regression adjustment, and -1.44 and 0.64 for the machine-learning estimator; the authors note that the unadjusted standard error was conservative because the exact design parameters were unavailable.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their theory uses a super-population framework and first-order asymptotics, which may not capture finite-sample trade-offs that motivate rerandomization. They note that constraints on model form, pre-specification, or sample size can affect practical performance beyond what these asymptotic comparisons describe.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations use a limited set of generated data settings, and the real-data illustration is one cluster-randomized health study with 72 wards, so the practical results have limited empirical breadth. The machine-learning guarantees depend on nuisance estimates meeting stated convergence and boundedness conditions, which may be difficult to verify in small or complex experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing refined asymptotic approximations that better retain finite-sample features. They suggest local asymptotic regimes that jointly represent changes in populations, the strength and dimension of imbalance, and misspecification or regularization in covariate adjustment.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess the methods across more real experiments, especially those with few clusters or substantial allocation constraints. It could also develop practical guidance and software for selecting balance variables and thresholds under operational constraints, then validate that guidance in prospective experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Bayesian Adaptive Calibration and Optimal desigN (BACON), a sequential method for calibrating computer simulators while choosing where and at what parameter settings to run simulations. Its objective is to maximize expected information gain (EIG) about unknown calibration parameters, using a Gaussian process (GP) to link simulation outputs, real observations, and calibration parameters. At each iteration, it jointly selects simulation inputs and trains a variational approximation to the parameter posterior by maximizing a lower bound on information gain. The authors evaluate the method in synthetic problems, a hidden-source location problem, and soft-robotic gripper calibration. BACON generally produces informative simulations and competitive or closer posterior estimates, although performance depends on the problem and the comparison method.
narrate.key_results: In the synthetic bimodal experiment, after 50 iterations with batches of 4, BACON's information-gain indicator was 0.40 ± 0.03 and its divergence from the full-knowledge posterior was 0.45 ± 0.06; the corresponding values for random selection were 0.28 ± 0.07 and 0.54 ± 0.07. In the hidden-source problem, after 30 iterations with batches of 4, BACON obtained 0.37 ± 0.09 for the information-gain indicator and 0.07 ± 0.06 divergence from the reference posterior, compared with 0.22 ± 0.11 and 0.45 ± 0.21 for integrated mean squared prediction error selection. In the soft-robotics experiment, each method started with 123 random simulations and ran for 10 iterations with batches of 16; BACON's divergence from the reference posterior was 1.32 ± 0.05, versus 1.56 ± 0.08 for integrated mean squared prediction error, 1.50 ± 0.05 for D-optimal selection, and 1.48 ± 0.07 for random selection. Soft-robotic simulations took from minutes to a few hours each, and the paper does not report a measured total runtime or a quantified simulation-count saving against the baselines.

key_equations.explanation: The real process is f, the design input is x, the scale factor is rho, the simulator is h, the unknown calibration parameter is theta star, and the discrepancy function is epsilon.

key_equations.name: Sequential information-gain criterion
key_equations.explanation: The sequential expected information gain at iteration t is the mutual information I between the unknown calibration parameter theta star and a proposed simulated output y-hat, conditional on proposed design x-hat, simulation setting theta-hat, and data D from the previous iteration.

key_equations.name: Variational information-gain lower bound
key_equations.explanation: The lower bound is an expectation under the joint predictive distribution p of simulated output y-hat and unknown parameter theta star, given design x-hat, setting theta-hat, and previous data D; it compares the logarithm of the variational posterior q with the current parameter posterior p.

key_equations.name: Joint design and posterior construction
key_equations.explanation: At iteration t, the method jointly chooses design x-hat, simulation setting theta-hat, and variational posterior q to maximize the expected logarithm of q, where the expectation uses the predictive distribution p for output y-hat and parameter theta star conditional on the proposed inputs and previous data D.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that exact GP inference has cubic computational complexity in the data size, which limits scalability. They also note that the combined design and calibration search can be high-dimensional and that Gaussian assumptions may underestimate uncertainty for heavy-tailed errors, potentially causing under-exploration.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers a small set of synthetic and applied problems, and the soft-robotics comparison uses a reference posterior estimated from 1,024 simulations rather than a known exact posterior. The real-data demonstration uses 10 physical measurements and focuses on grasping a spherical object, so results may not transfer to other objects, simulators, or operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors discuss scaling the approach with sparse variational GP models and amortizing posterior inference by reusing learned variational distributions, with occasional posterior refreshes to limit degradation. They also note that the method can be adapted to vector-valued observations using multi-output GP models.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test robustness when the simulator or discrepancy model is misspecified and assess whether alternative stochastic-process models improve calibration under heavy-tailed errors. Broader validation on physical experiments, alternative design constraints, and comparisons that report total computational cost and simulation savings would help establish practical usefulness.

narrate.summary: The paper presents an informatics-driven design approach for nuclear waste forms, illustrated by phosphate-based ceramics intended to immobilize sodium and neodymium from salt waste. It links processing, material structure, measurable properties, and waste-form performance in a system design chart, then uses that chart to organize an iterative candidate-selection workflow. The workflow combines physics-based calculations, property-prediction models, domain knowledge, and laboratory synthesis and testing. Candidates are screened and ranked against objectives including waste-cation loading, storage volume, and mechanical performance. The authors synthesize and test selected candidates and report that the E2 composition meets the stated target criteria for loading, volume, and compressive strength.
narrate.key_results: The authors enumerated 12,341 compositions on a grid with 2.5 mol percent spacing in the sodium-neodymium-iron-phosphate design space, then used calculated phase mixtures and domain-knowledge filters to select candidates. For melting-temperature prediction, the reported random cross-validation results were an r-squared value of 0.77 and a mean absolute error of 202 kelvin; predictions in the target iron-phosphate system had errors above 400–450 kelvin in deep-eutectic regions, while adding 10–20 percent target-system data improved predictions. The experimentally tested E2 candidate had a reported sodium-plus-neodymium loading of 25.29 weight percent and an estimated storage volume of 54.36 cubic centimeters per 100 grams of nominal salt, exceeding the initial loading and volume targets. The paper’s text reports E2 compressive strength as 38.3–40.2 gigapascals and says the criteria were exceeded, while the corresponding figure labels its stress axis in megapascals; this is an inconsistency in the reported units.

key_equations.explanation: The probability-of-improvement score aPI integrates the normal predictive distribution N from baseline x0 to infinity, where x is the property value, mu(x) is its predicted mean, and sigma squared (x) is its predictive variance.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that phase predictions based on calculated energies can differ substantially from experiments because they omit finite-temperature and kinetic effects and can exclude phases with different or mixed oxidation states. They also note that thermodynamic databases for the target phosphate systems are incomplete and that large, well-curated datasets are lacking for important properties such as compressive strength and chemical durability. They identify the need for further work to bridge computational predictions and experimental material formation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstrated workflow covers a small number of laboratory-made candidates, and only one end-to-end iteration is reported; it therefore does not establish how much time or experimental effort the approach saves compared with conventional development. The property models and mixture-property estimates rely on simplifying assumptions, including estimating overall properties as phase-fraction-weighted means, and the demonstrated validation does not measure chemical durability or radiation stability. The reported compressive-strength units are inconsistent between the text and figure, which makes that result difficult to interpret without clarification.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors say that the characterization results will be used to refine the physics-based predictions, augment training data, and retrain models for a subsequent sequential-learning iteration, with those efforts to be reported later. They call for investment in collecting and curating waste-form property data and for further development of methods that connect computational phase predictions to experimental outcomes. They also identify process optimization and scale-up of promising waste forms as opportunities for the approach.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could run repeated design-and-test cycles and compare their total time, cost, and number of experiments against a conventional baseline. They could also validate candidate performance with standardized durability and radiation tests, clarify the compressive-strength units, and incorporate practical constraints such as processing limits and production-scale requirements into candidate selection.

narrate.summary: The paper presents an a priori design method for selecting training configurations for a Gaussian approximation potential, a kernel-based model of interatomic interactions. Its objective is to select a limited set of examples that is informative for the model and supports predictions beyond the most densely sampled configurations. The method first generates a large candidate pool, then greedily selects configurations to maximize the minimum pairwise squared kernel distance, using a distance based on the model's covariance function. The authors demonstrate the method on elastically deformed zirconium crystal structures, using a descriptor that combines pair interactions and smooth overlap of atomic positions. In their numerical study, the optimized sets gave better off-sample energy predictions than random subsets of the same size, while the authors note that the outcome depends on the candidate pool and distance measure.
narrate.key_results: For each of two independent candidate pools of 100,000 configurations, the authors selected an optimized set of 1,000 configurations and a random set of 1,000 configurations. In the cross-validation results, the model trained on the first optimized set had a 0.99 quantile of absolute energy error of 0.0367 on the second optimized set, compared with 0.0818 and 0.0783 for models trained on the two random sets. The model trained on the second optimized set had a corresponding 0.99 quantile of 0.0427 on the first optimized set, compared with 0.0737 and 0.0747 for the random-set models. The authors report that optimization improved transferability across the tested sets, with some trade-off in precision around the source-sampling distribution; they do not report a runtime comparison.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that success requires a sufficiently large candidate pool and a way to sample the domain adequately. The design can become unhelpful if it selects configurations that are nearly orthogonal under the kernel, and the authors identify choosing an appropriate distance measure as a key challenge. They also note that precomputed descriptors or kernel matrices can make memory a limiting factor for large candidate pools.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation is limited to elastic deformations of pure zirconium crystal structures, so it does not establish performance for other materials, chemical compositions, or configuration types. The comparisons use two candidate pools and one training-set size, and the procedure's effectiveness may depend strongly on the chosen descriptor parameters and candidate-generation distribution. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving the underlying sampling of configuration space, especially for many-body representations, to ensure adequate coverage of descriptor space. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the design across varied materials, chemical systems, and training budgets, and compare it directly with other design criteria and active-learning procedures. It would also be useful to assess the selected sets on independent experimental or simulation workloads and to develop practical guidance for choosing descriptor parameters and deformation constraints.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a human-in-the-loop sequential screening method for drug discovery, with the objective of finding as many molecules as possible that satisfy several property requirements. A transformer encodes peptide sequences, and Bayesian neural networks predict their properties and estimate uncertainty. Each round, the method recommends candidates both for their predicted promise and for their model uncertainty, while a human expert reviews the recommendations, selects the molecules to test, and can override the algorithm. Experimental results use a public therapeutic-peptide dataset and compare the method with algorithm-only and human-only approaches. The collaborative method achieves the highest hit rates in all three tasks and the paper reports that human expertise and access to uncertainty information contribute to its advantage.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used a search pool of 14,000 peptides, tested 50 peptides per round over 50 rounds, and repeated each policy 20 times. Across the three tasks, the method's final hit rates were 2.97%, 2.57%, and 0.76%; the active-learning-then-upper-confidence-bound baseline, the second-best method overall, achieved 1.65%, 1.59%, and 0.46%, respectively. The method's hit rate was at least three times the random baseline in every task, and its cumulative recall was highest across all three tasks. In the Task 1 collaboration comparison, human-algorithm collaboration improved recall by about 50% relative to human-only or algorithm-only decisions; the paper also reports more than 40% worse performance without uncertainty and search-score information for the expert, and more than 50% improvement for algorithm-to-human rather than human-to-algorithm delegation.

narrate.summary: This paper develops adaptive experimental input designs for estimating 9 parameters of a lithium-ion battery using a single-particle model (SPM). The method uses voltage sensitivities to build an information matrix, then selects currents that improve information about the parameters under a D-optimal criterion. The authors test both a collection of separate short current profiles and a continuous profile formed by joining optimized intervals. In virtual-data tests, both approaches support accurate parameter estimation, while tests using real battery measurements show that the joined profile can reduce experimental time while still producing a useful parameter fit. The paper reports implementation using Python and SciPy optimization routines.
narrate.key_results: With virtual data, the separate-profile design reached a relative parameter error of about 3.73 × 10^-10, and the concatenated design reached 9.74 × 10^-12. The concatenated profile lasted 6,480 seconds in the real-data tests, compared with 63,362 seconds for the collection-of-inputs test that included preparation and rest phases; their reported average parameter-optimization times were 450 and 154 seconds, respectively. For real data, the parameter proposed from the collection test had relative voltage errors on the order of 10^-3 for two inputs and 10^-2 for another, while the shorter concatenated test produced a fit the authors describe as comparable. Across the four real-data tests, the design helped parameter estimation in three, but the collection using only the current intervals did not identify the parameters with confidence.

key_equations.name: D-optimal uncertainty measure
key_equations.explanation: The uncertainty measure phi is the negative logarithm of the determinant of information matrix M, so minimizing it favors designs with greater information.

key_equations.name: Adaptive input objective
key_equations.explanation: The new input u is chosen from admissible set U to minimize the base-10 negative log determinant of accumulated information matrix M_acc at parameter vector mu, plus the input-size penalty weighted by gamma.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the single-particle model is simplified and may not reproduce real battery behavior in all operating conditions. They also note that the selected input shapes and lengths were restricted and chosen in an intuitive way, and that the adaptive stopping rule does not guarantee convergence.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data evaluation used two commercial cells and a single specified temperature range, so the results do not establish performance across other cell types or operating conditions. The real battery’s true parameter values are not known, and the proposed real-data parameter is judged through fit and optimization behavior rather than comparison with a known ground truth; moreover, the virtual-data design assumes noiseless model-generated observations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose applying the designs to more complex battery models and exploring alternative input choices, such as longer current jumps, longer pauses, or longer experiments. They also suggest imposing resource limits, such as time or energy budgets, directly in experiment design.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the designs on more cell types, temperatures, and independently repeated laboratory tests, with uncertainty estimates that account for measurement noise and cell-to-cell variation. It could also investigate constraints that reflect practical current and state-of-charge limits, and compare sequential updating with a fixed design when new measurements arrive.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential method for choosing experiments to estimate parameters and improve predictions for nonlinear models, including models defined by implicit equations. It demonstrates the method using a vapor-liquid equilibrium model for a narrow-azeotrope mixture of propanol and propyl acetate. At each step, the method estimates model parameters from collected measurements and selects a batch of new experiments by optimizing the combined information from the existing and proposed experiments. The design computation uses a finite set of candidate conditions and a locally linearized model, with a D-optimality criterion in the case study. The authors report that 15 sequentially selected experiments achieved prediction quality comparable to a 27-experiment factorial design.
narrate.key_results: For the propanol and propyl acetate case, the final sequential design contained 15 experiments, including four repeated conditions, compared with 27 experiments in the full factorial design. On the collected data, the vapor-composition prediction error was 59.61 times 10 to the power of minus 4 for the 15-experiment design and 59.86 times 10 to the power of minus 4 for the 27-experiment design; the corresponding temperature errors were 16.18 times 10 to the power of minus 2 and 15.75 times 10 to the power of minus 2. The reported worst-case sampling-based uncertainties were also similar: 5.60 times 10 to the power of minus 4 versus 4.49 times 10 to the power of minus 4 for vapor composition, and 1.94 times 10 to the power of minus 2 versus 1.36 times 10 to the power of minus 2 for temperature. The authors also report that the 9-experiment sequential design had prediction errors similar to those of the 27-experiment factorial design, although prediction-uncertainty measures continued to improve in later sequential stages.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their general method requires a finite candidate design space with information matrices that can be computed sufficiently quickly, including solving the defining equations for implicit models. Their method requires a differentiable design criterion and therefore excludes the E-criterion; the case study uses a finite grid of candidate conditions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical comparison concerns one binary mixture and one specific thermodynamic model, so it does not establish that the same run reduction will hold for other systems or model structures. The prediction errors are assessed against the same collected experimental data used to fit a reference model, rather than an independent held-out dataset, and the candidate conditions are restricted to a prespecified grid.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors plan to test the method on systems with liquid-liquid equilibria and chemical reactions, and to extend it to designs with practical constraints such as cost or location. They also plan to study design criteria based on sampling-based approximations to parameter or prediction uncertainty instead of the linearization-based criteria used here.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the approach on independent mixtures and held-out measurements, and examine how results change when the assumed thermodynamic model or measurement-error structure is inaccurate. It would also be useful to investigate sequential designs under operational constraints and to validate candidate-grid recommendations against achievable laboratory conditions.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential experimental design for estimating the average treatment effect (ATE) over a specified target population. Unlike designs that optimize treatment assignment alone, it chooses both which covariate profiles to sample and which treatment to assign. The choices are updated using past observations and estimated outcome variances, with an augmented inverse probability weighting estimator that adjusts for both treatment assignment and covariate sampling. The authors derive the design that minimizes the semiparametric efficiency bound and prove that their estimator reaches that bound under stated regularity and nuisance-estimation assumptions. Simulations generally show lower mean squared error than the comparison designs, but confidence-interval coverage is poor in the reported finite-sample experiments.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical result establishes that, as the number of experimental rounds grows, the proposed design’s estimator has asymptotic variance equal to the semiparametric efficiency bound minimized over both sampling density and treatment-assignment probability. In simulations with 2,000 rounds and 200 replications, the proposed design generally had lower mean squared error than deterministic and randomized control designs and an adaptive design that optimized treatment assignment but sampled covariates from the target distribution; the paper does not report exact mean squared error values in its text. For nominal 95% confidence intervals, coverage was 26.5% with Gaussian covariates and 44.0% with uniform covariates for the proposed design, compared with 95.5% for the randomized control design in both settings and 38.0% and 48.5% for the propensity-only adaptive design. A simulation using the Infant Health and Development Program benchmark, with 747 covariate records, also showed a qualitative mean squared error reduction compared with the control designs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The main setting assumes that the target covariate density is known; the authors describe rejection sampling as an extension for settings where it is unknown. The asymptotic result requires consistent estimates of conditional means and variances, and the authors note that high covariate dimension may make those conditions difficult to satisfy. In the finite-sample simulations, the adaptive designs’ confidence intervals had substantial undercoverage, which the authors attribute to bias that they expect to diminish as the sample size increases.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method relies on being able to recruit or select units from the adaptively changing covariate density, which may be impractical or costly when eligible units are scarce or sampling is constrained. The theoretical design also presumes stable outcome distributions and sufficiently well-behaved assignment and sampling probabilities; performance under model misspecification, operational constraints, or real-world experiments is not established by the reported evaluations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors describe extensions for rejection sampling when the target covariate density is unknown, batch designs, and multiple treatments. They also discuss estimating the target density from pilot data and note that results may need adjustment when the pilot sample size and experiment size grow at dependent rates.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could develop constrained versions that account explicitly for recruitment costs, limited availability of covariate profiles, and ethical or operational restrictions on treatment assignment. It would also be useful to test finite-sample inference and the design in real experiments, and to provide accessible software for fitting the nuisance functions and implementing the sequential sampling scheme.

narrate.summary: This paper designs an active-learning approach for online experiments that estimate treatment effects when people in a network can affect one another. The method models potential outcomes with Gaussian process regression, using each person’s own treatment, an integrated measure of neighbors’ treatment, and covariates. At each iteration, it selects the treatment condition with the greatest estimated uncertainty and uses a genetic algorithm to choose network-level assignments that generate useful data near that condition. The authors evaluate the approach with simulated networks and a mobile-game dataset. Their results show that the method can estimate effects using a subset of the available population, while also showing that its simulation comparison with random allocation is not uniformly favorable at every stage or for every effect.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation, experiments on 9 networks of 100 individuals each produced estimates for a population of 10,000 using 900 individuals, or 100 × 9 rather than 100 × 100. At 9 networks, the EISE for the overall effect was 31.74120205 with ACI and 39.42437691 with RTA; for the spillover effect it was 14.60991894 and 517.14218562, respectively. The comparison was mixed at earlier stages: for example, at 7 networks, the overall-effect EISE was 592.60175094 for ACI versus 34.5195497 for RTA, while the spillover-effect EISE was 51.28109163 versus 443.99716071. In the game study, the method used experimental data from 33,523 people in a population of 125,286; the estimated effect at own treatment 1 and neighbor-treatment level 0.612 was 2.681, compared with an estimated average treatment effect of −0.673 when interference was ignored.

key_equations.name: Average overall and spillover effects
key_equations.explanation: Tau with subscript 1 is the average overall effect and tau with subscript 0 is the average spillover effect; m with a subscript is the average potential outcome at that own-treatment level, and g is the integrated neighbor-treatment level.

key_equations.name: Uncertainty-based target selection

key_equations.name: Network assignment fitness
key_equations.explanation: For network q, the genetic algorithm chooses assignment vector A-q to maximize summed squared distances d between covariates X of units in S-q, the set receiving the target own treatment and falling within the chosen interval around the target neighbor-treatment level.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their method assumes static network structures, although real networks can change over time. They also note that their approach to integrating neighbors’ covariates and treatments may not extract neighborhood information effectively, and that some own-treatment and neighbor-treatment combinations are difficult to achieve and may require experiments across multiple networks.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The estimates depend on the stated exchangeability and positivity assumptions and on how neighbor treatments and covariates are reduced to integrated measures; violations or information loss from those reductions could affect causal conclusions. The simulation uses a specific generated outcome structure and network setup, and the real-data demonstration is a single game application, so the evidence does not establish performance across other network structures or business settings. The paper provides no reported runtime or operational details that would help assess the cost and feasibility of repeatedly optimizing assignments for large networks.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to dynamic networks and improving how information from neighbors is integrated, potentially with neural networks or other dimensionality-reduction methods. They also suggest developing ways to estimate effects for difficult-to-achieve treatment conditions from more attainable conditions, or by combining readily available treatment scenarios.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could evaluate the method under alternative causal models and design criteria, including explicit costs, capacity limits, or restrictions on which network members can be assigned treatment. Sequential validation in additional real experiments, together with published software and computational benchmarks, would clarify how well the approach transfers to routine quality and product experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a variance-reduction approach for ratio metrics in online A/B tests, with the goal of improving test sensitivity or reducing experiment cost. It studies one-day user retention on ShareChat and adapts control-variate methods to ratio outcomes. The authors compare pre-experiment values used in the CUPED approach with predictions from gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs), and with a combination of both. Their results indicate that GBDT-based control variates improve sensitivity more reliably than using pre-experiment values, even when the latter reduce variance more. The authors report that the GBDT approach improves statistical confidence in most of the tested experiments and can reduce the required data points while preserving confidence.
narrate.key_results: With GBDT-based predictions, 76.92% of the 13 experiments had a lower p-value, and the median relative z-score was 1.19. The authors interpret that z-score as allowing 30% fewer data points for the same confidence; the reported variance reduction for this approach was -45.66%, and its type-I error was 4.8%. By comparison, pre-experiment values alone had a lower p-value in 15.38% of experiments, while combining pre-experiment values with GBDT predictions did so in 30.77%; their reported variance reductions were -72.47% and -72.62%, respectively. Type-I error was assessed on 220 two-week A/A pairs, and the reported errors for all three approaches were close to the expected 5%.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors characterize the study as preliminary and evaluate 13 known A/B pairs for one-day retention. They do not provide a separate limitations section.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation covers only one platform, one ratio metric, and 13 historical experiment pairs, so the results may not generalize to other metrics, organizations, or experiment settings. The paper also does not give enough detail about GBDT training and validation to assess how readily the method can be reproduced or how it performs when predictions are less reliable.
