narrate.summary: The paper develops rerandomization for two-arm experiments that estimate the finite-population average treatment effect. In this design, treatment assignments are repeatedly randomized until the covariate imbalance, measured by Mahalanobis distance, meets a chosen threshold. The authors extend the theory to allow both the threshold to decrease and the number of balanced covariates to increase with sample size. They show that, under stated regularity conditions, a suitable decreasing acceptance probability can make the difference-in-means estimator asymptotically Gaussian and attain the precision expected with perfectly balanced covariates. The design retains randomized assignment rather than choosing a single allocation that minimizes imbalance.
narrate.key_results: The theory shows that the ideal precision is attainable when the logarithm of the inverse acceptance probability grows faster than the number of covariates, while the acceptance probability remains large relative to the Gaussian-approximation error. With fewer than logarithmically many covariates, the paper’s examples allow a polynomially decreasing acceptance probability and yield the ideal asymptotic precision; with a logarithmic number, rerandomization still improves precision over complete randomization but does not attain the ideal, and with polynomially many covariates the reported asymptotic gain disappears. The supplementary simulation used 974 units from the Student Achievement and Retention Project and 100,000 simulated assignments per design; in a constructed outcome scenario with 200 covariates and no trimming, reported 95% interval coverage ranged from 63.1% to 68.3%, compared with 92.5% to 92.8% after trimming. The authors also give an expected computational complexity of approximately order n times K times the sum of K and the inverse acceptance probability for obtaining an acceptable allocation.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that their derived Berry–Esseen-type approximation bounds are weaker than the rate conjectured in earlier work, leaving a gap for future theoretical improvement. narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical illustration is a simulation built around one real study dataset, with many covariates and some outcomes generated for the analysis; it is not a validation in a newly conducted experiment. The ideality results are asymptotic, so they do not by themselves establish that a particular finite-sample choice of threshold will deliver the claimed precision or interval coverage in a new application.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose pursuing tighter Gaussian-approximation bounds, including investigating whether the conjectured rate can be proved. They also identify extensions to other balance criteria, blocked, factorial, and sequential experiments, and superpopulation inference as directions for future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A practical design procedure could select covariates and the acceptance threshold jointly using pilot information while explicitly limiting the number of rejected assignments. Further validation could compare the method with alternative designs in prospective experiments across application areas and sample sizes.

narrate.summary: This paper develops synthetic control designs for experiments in which the units are large aggregate entities, such as markets, and only a few units can be treated. The design jointly chooses treated units, untreated control units, and their weights to estimate a population average treatment effect or an effect for the selected treated units. It constructs the groups by matching observed covariates and pre-experiment outcomes to population or treated-unit predictor values. The paper also develops tests and confidence intervals using unused pre-experiment periods as placebo periods. In the reported Walmart data and simulations, the designs generally produced smaller estimation errors than the randomized alternatives examined.
narrate.key_results: In a Walmart example with 45 stores and 143 weeks, the design with two treated units had a normalized out-of-sample root mean square error of 0.018, compared with 0.312 for random assignment, 0.299 for stratified random assignment, 0.070 for one-nearest-neighbor adjustment, and 0.063 for five-nearest-neighbor adjustment. In 1,000 simulations, the unconstrained design had a root mean square error of 0.97, compared with 3.45 for the constrained design with one treated unit and 6.35 for random assignment with one treated unit. With seven treated units, the constrained design's error was 0.97, compared with 3.01 for random assignment. In the Walmart placebo analysis, the test returned a value of 0.933 and did not reject the no-effect hypothesis; simulations under the null generally showed rejection rates near 0.05.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say that the perfect predictor-fit assumption is strong and may hold only approximately in practice. narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantees depend on the stated factor model and shock conditions, so departures from these assumptions in operational settings could undermine the bias or inference results. The empirical validation uses one observational retail dataset with a placebo intervention, while the simulations use a particular constructed setting; this leaves performance across other industries, outcome patterns, and operational constraints less established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors discuss extensions to include explicit experiment-budget constraints, additional regularization of the weights, bias correction, and clustering of units. They do not identify a separate future-work agenda.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the designs in actual prospective experiments and study how interference between aggregate units affects their estimates. It could also develop practical procedures for choosing the number of treated units and tuning parameters under real budget, eligibility, and operational constraints.

narrate.summary: This paper describes a community-focused process for optimizing the observing cadence of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) at Rubin Observatory. The design problem is to choose a 10-year survey schedule that supports the survey’s science goals while meeting technical and observing constraints, including those in the Science Requirements Document (SRD). The process uses simulated survey histories from the Operations Simulator (OpSim) and analysis metrics calculated with the Metric Analysis Framework (MAF). Community input was gathered through the Community Observing Strategy Evaluation Paper (COSEP), white papers, and cadence notes, with the Survey Cadence Optimization Committee (SCOC) guiding recommendations. The paper’s main finding is that open tools, sustained coordination, and broad scientific input made the optimization process possible, but the final cadence had not yet been selected when the paper was written.
narrate.key_results: The survey requirements described in the paper include a Wide-Fast-Deep (WFD) footprint of at least 18,000 square degrees, with a median of 825 nominal 30-second visits per 9.6-square-degree field. The community process included 14 simulated survey runs for the COSEP phase, 16 for the white-paper phase, and 173 for the cadence-note phase. The 2018 call received 46 white papers from 467 unique authors, and the cadence-note call received 39 notes from 218 unique authors. Comparisons of simulated strategies show that rolling cadence can improve supernova performance and yield small efficiency improvements, but the paper does not report numerical effect sizes or identify a final winning strategy.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the optimization effort was time- and labor-intensive, and that participation was selective without dedicated support. They note that the learning curve was substantial and that unpaid contributions could bias participation toward more senior, flexible, and well-funded scientists and toward better-funded areas of astrophysics.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper describes a decision process rather than a formally specified optimization method: it does not provide a single combined objective or a rule for resolving trade-offs among different science metrics. Its reported strategy comparisons are illustrative and the final cadence had not been chosen, so the paper does not validate the recommended design against actual survey operations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that the SCOC planned to select a cadence family by the end of 2021 and refine its recommendation by the end of 2022, with subsequent evaluation and revision during operations if needed. They also say that a later paper in the Focus Issue would describe the cadence choice and the considerations behind it, and that further experience could clarify how to incorporate community input effectively.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to define a transparent, reproducible approach for balancing metrics across science areas and to test how recommendations change under alternative metric priorities. The process could also be evaluated against actual observing outcomes after operations begin, including whether simulation-based predictions match delivered survey performance.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces UniCoRn, a randomized experiment design for measuring producer-side effects of recommender systems in two-sided marketplaces. It addresses the problem that a producer’s experience depends on which recommendation model serves that producer’s potential viewers. The method combines the rankings from control and treatment models, mixing selected items while preserving each group’s within-group ordering. A tuning parameter lets experimenters trade computation cost against ranking accuracy, and the paper proves that the maximum-mixing design minimizes its squared rank-inaccuracy criterion. Simulations and an industrial edge-recommendation deployment demonstrate the method’s performance and practical use.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that maximum-mixing UniCoRn minimizes expected squared rank inaccuracy among the designs considered. In simulations with 100 ranking positions, 50,000 sessions were used to assess ranking errors; in a separate comparison, 1,000-session datasets were repeated 100 times, with each iteration taking an average of 36 seconds on the reported computer. UniCoRn variants had lower treatment-effect estimation error than the modified score-based comparator, and the variants with tuning settings 1 and 0.2 outperformed the counterfactual-ranking comparator in the reported comparison. In two industrial experiments using 40% of viewer traffic, measured changes were 0.51% and 0.57% for weekly active unique users and sessions in the candidate-generation test, and 0.13% and 0.11% for those metrics in the ranking-model test; all results had reported p-values below 0.001.

key_equations.name: Squared rank inaccuracy
key_equations.explanation: The equation defines design inaccuracy as the expected squared difference between an item’s design rank and its ideal counterfactual rank, averaged over items and sessions.

key_equations.name: Mixed-item ranking score

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that UniCoRn does not capture treatment effects on viewer attention or session counts because viewers receive mixed treatment and control rankings. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate estimates against experiments with a defensible ground-truth comparison and test the method across additional real-world recommendation systems and response metrics. narrate.summary: This paper designs batches of experiments for learning causal structures when each experiment can perturb several variables at once. It considers directed acyclic graph models with no unobserved common causes and assumes the data are faithful to the graph; interventions are hard interventions that remove incoming edges to targeted variables. The design is constrained by a maximum batch size and a maximum number of perturbed variables per experiment. The authors develop algorithms for maximizing edge orientation and an infinite-sample information objective, using submodularity, stochastic continuous optimization, and separating systems. Their simulations and gene-network tests find that multi-variable interventions generally identify more edges than random selection or methods restricted to single-variable interventions.
narrate.key_results: For the edge-orientation objective, the authors prove that their Double Greedy Continuous algorithm achieves an expected value of at least (1 - 1/e) times the optimum, minus an error tolerance. Their Separating System Greedy method has a lower-bound guarantee for the sampled infinite-sample information objective, based on the size of its separating-system candidate set. The paper gives an example in which an optimal intervention targeting q variables can orient up to q times as many edges as an optimal single-variable intervention. In experiments, the proposed methods generally outperform random and single-variable greedy approaches on simulated graphs and five 50-node DREAM3 networks; the finite-sample study uses 800 observational samples and 3 samples per selected intervention, and reports improved information-objective and edge-prediction results for the proposed methods.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that a uniform sampler is available for sampling from an observational equivalence class, but not for essential graphs after prior interventions; their practical implementation therefore uses an efficient non-uniform sampler. They also note that the finite-sample algorithms do not have the theoretical guarantees established for the infinite-sample objectives, and that their infinite-sample information objective uses a sampled approximation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical objectives assume correct causal graphs, faithfulness, and no unobserved confounding, so the guarantees may not apply when these assumptions fail. The empirical comparisons cover selected synthetic graph families and DREAM3 subnetworks, and do not establish performance under practical restrictions such as unequal intervention costs, failed perturbations, or survival constraints beyond the per-intervention size limit.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors note that they suspect the infinite-sample information objective may be submodular when computed over the full equivalence class, and that proving this could support a direct algorithm without sampling a subset of graphs. They also describe extensions of their results to soft interventions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test these methods with intervention costs, limits on which combinations of variables can be perturbed, and perturbations that fail or have uncertain effects. Evaluating the designs in real experiments and developing sequential versions that update the graph distribution after each batch would also clarify their practical value.

narrate.summary: This paper develops experimental designs for collecting data to improve variable selection with the Lasso in sparse linear models. It proposes using nearly orthogonal Latin hypercube designs, which combine stratification across predictor ranges with small correlations between predictor columns. The paper presents two systematic construction approaches, one based on orthogonal arrays and another based on a generalized Kronecker-product construction. The authors compare these designs with two-level designs, random Latin hypercube designs, and independently sampled designs in simulated studies. Across the reported examples, the proposed designs yield fewer false variable selections, with the advantage increasing in the higher-dimensional examples.
narrate.key_results: Across 50 replications with 50 runs and 48 predictors, the median number of false selections was 13 for the nearly orthogonal Latin hypercube design, compared with 18 for the two-level design, 18 for the random Latin hypercube design, and 20 for the independent sample. With 49 runs and 96 predictors, the respective medians were 17.50, 27, 25, and 27; with 64 runs and 192 predictors, they were 27, 42.50, 43, and 41. The authors report that the advantage of the proposed designs grows as the predictor-to-run ratio increases. The paper does not report computational-time or other runtime efficiency measurements.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a way to choose pilot experiments when the generalized linear model (GLM), including its link, basis functions, and coefficients, is not yet known. It shows theoretically that a design with small discrepancy from a chosen target distribution has a lower bound on its efficiency across a broad class of model specifications. The authors propose constructing pilot designs by using low-discrepancy points, with either a uniform or arcsine target distribution on the experimental region. They assess the proposal through numerical comparisons of space-filling designs for logistic, probit, and linear models, focusing mainly on coefficient estimation. The main finding is that smaller discrepancy generally accompanies better worst-case efficiency, while the preferable target distribution varies by model type.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical result bounds estimation efficiency, and also prediction efficiency, below using the design’s discrepancy and a measure of model-function variation. In the logistic-regression example, designs used 16 distinct points in four dimensions and were evaluated over 16,807 coefficient values; uniform low-discrepancy designs had better worst-case A-optimality efficiency than the compared alternatives. In the probit example, 32 points in six dimensions were assessed over 1,024 coefficient samples, and arcsine-target designs—especially the transformed scrambled Sobol and maximum-projection Latin hypercube designs—performed best or comparably best. For linear regression, the study used 128 points in seven dimensions and evaluated 174 basis functions; the arcsine-transformed scrambled Sobol design had the best worst-case A-optimality efficiency among the compared designs. The comparisons also show that maximum-projection Latin hypercube designs can have low discrepancy at small design sizes, while scrambled Sobol designs are easy to construct and become more advantageous as design size increases.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that inverse-transforming a uniform low-discrepancy design may not retain low discrepancy for a non-uniform target distribution. They also state that constructing designs by directly minimizing discrepancy is beyond the scope of their study, so their numerical comparisons use readily available designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence covers a limited collection of model types, coefficient spaces, target distributions, and designs on the bounded region from minus one to one in each dimension; it does not establish performance across other practical constraints or model spaces. The study reports design-based numerical evaluations rather than validation in real experiments, and it gives no run-size guidance for practitioners beyond the selected examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying pilot designs for combined quantitative and qualitative responses, mixture experiments with constrained design spaces, and recommender-system applications. They also suggest investigating how low-discrepancy designs relate to robust designs and whether they regulate prediction bias and variance under generalized-linear-model misspecification.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could develop methods that directly optimize discrepancy while handling practical restrictions such as factor bounds, categorical settings, and costs, and compare them with the ready-made sequences in the paper. Sequential pilot designs and implementation tools would also be useful, as would prospective validation in industrial or health-care experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an adaptive sampling strategy for estimating first-order Sobol’ sensitivity indices of computational models. It combines two estimator classes, Oracle 2 and Oracle 1, with replicated Latin hypercube designs. Two initial designs provide estimates for all inputs; selected small or moderate estimates can then be checked using an averaged version of Oracle 1, constructed through row permutations and additional runs. Numerical examples show that this can improve estimates when inputs have mainly individual effects, while results for a model with strong interactions are comparable to a one-shot approach. The strategy is also demonstrated on a nuclear thermal-hydraulic simulation, where it changes the interpretation of which parameters are influential.
narrate.key_results: In the modified three-input benchmark, Oracle 1 performed better for the small and moderate indices, while Oracle 2 performed better for the large index; averaging three Oracle 1 estimates improved accuracy over the simple estimator. In a ten-input additive example with run size 200, at least one negligible index was estimated above 0.10 in 40.4% of the initial Oracle 2 estimate sets; re-estimating the nine small and moderate indices used 2,200 runs and removed this observed problem. For the ten-input interaction benchmark, the adaptive method and one-shot Oracle 2 each used 1,200 runs and had broadly comparable root mean squared errors: the reported per-index values ranged from 0.047 to 0.057 for the adaptive method and from 0.045 to 0.053 for the one-shot method. In the nuclear application, with 200 locations in each of the two initial designs, the initial estimates for the subcooled-condensation parameter, turbulent forced-convection heat transfer, and gap were 0.77, 0.25, and 0.29; re-estimation changed the latter two to 0.018 and 0.22, respectively.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that there is no theoretical justification for using Oracle 1 to re-estimate small and moderate indices when the corresponding inputs have interactions with other inputs. Their numerical results for an interaction-rich example show that the adaptive strategy is comparable to, rather than clearly better than, one-shot Oracle 2.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The strategy depends on screening estimates to decide which indices to re-estimate, so an initially misleading estimate could affect the sequence of additional runs or leave an index unchecked if the user stops early. The paper’s comparisons use a small set of benchmark functions and one nuclear application, so performance across other model structures, input distributions, and practical run constraints is not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose constructing optimized replicated Latin hypercube designs to improve coverage of the input space. They also suggest adapting Correlation 2 estimators for the second stage and extending the approach to replicated orthogonal arrays, including estimation of closed second-order indices.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test rules for selecting which indices to re-estimate, especially when the initial estimates are uncertain or interactions are substantial. They could also validate the procedure in additional real experiments and assess how it handles practical constraints such as correlated inputs or limits on the number of feasible simulation runs.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a task-driven framework for assessing and comparing diffusion magnetic resonance imaging experimental designs. It is intended for quantitative tasks such as classifying tissue as healthy or diseased, where good parameter estimates do not necessarily mean good classification. The framework simulates data generation, parameter estimation, and task evaluation for each candidate design, then assesses classification using receiver operating characteristic curves and their area under the curve. The authors validate the predictions against clinical results for spondyloarthritis and use simulated tasks to compare models and fitting methods. The results show that the best design choice can depend on the task, and that a biased model can sometimes classify better than the model used to generate the data.
narrate.key_results: For validation, the authors used an in-house dataset of 28 patients and an external dataset of 41 patients, and found that simulated and clinical receiver operating characteristic curves had similar forms and relative performance. Simulations used populations 1,000 times the clinical dataset size, followed by repeated subsampling to the clinical sample sizes; the resulting area-under-the-curve distributions agreed numerically with the clinical results. In the first illustrative task, the area under the curve was 0.567 for the apparent diffusion coefficient model, 0.642 for the intravoxel incoherent motion model with bound-constrained fitting, and 0.650 with segmented fitting. In the second task, the corresponding values were 0.796, 0.734, and 0.729, respectively, so the model and fitting method with the best classification performance differed by task.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a way to decide how to divide a limited simulation budget between low- and high-fidelity evaluations when building a hierarchical surrogate model. Its objective is to improve prediction of the high-fidelity response, supporting later optimization. The authors first compare model error across many combinations of high- and low-fidelity sample counts, then propose estimating the error trend by subsampling an initial design rather than running new evaluations for every combination. A fitted trend is used to estimate how additional evaluations should be divided given their relative costs. On benchmark functions, the subsampling method generally captures the trend and the budget-splitting heuristic works well in most tested cases, though not when the error trend changes across the sample-count range.
narrate.key_results: The full enumeration used 50 independent designs for each sample-count combination and, in the example configuration, required 250,000 designs; the authors note that the associated high-fidelity evaluations reach the millions. The subsampling approach reuses evaluations from one initial design, and its estimated error-gradient angles were generally within about 5 to 15 degrees of the full-enumeration estimates across the tested comparisons. In an illustrative budget-splitting comparison, the predicted allocation roughly matched the lowest observed error for three of four benchmark functions; the fourth showed that a global trend fit can mislead when the local error trend changes. The authors report that adding low-fidelity samples can even worsen prediction for weakly correlated functions, with this adverse behavior occurring for correlations up to about 0.8.

narrate.limitations_stated: The study uses a simplified additive model with its regression parameter fixed at one, and evaluates a Kriging model with a Matérn kernel. narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from benchmark functions rather than real engineering experiments, so the reported allocation behavior has not been validated under practical simulation constraints. The method also assumes a nested design in which high-fidelity sample locations are included among low-fidelity locations, which may not suit every simulator or operational sampling constraint.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose experiments on additional benchmarks and real-world problems, investigation of other multi-fidelity models, and evaluation of error grids and the allocation scheme in optimization applications. narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method under practical constraints such as limits on paired evaluations, parallel simulation capacity, or restricted operating regions. It would also be valuable to compare repeated budget updates against a one-time allocation and to validate prediction accuracy and optimization outcomes in real engineering studies.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an optimal-design method for estimating parameters in linear regression models with correlated errors on a finite set of candidate design points. It modifies the virtual-noise approach so that optimizing a concave criterion, including D-optimality or A-optimality, becomes a convex problem when the tuning constant is below a stated covariance-matrix bound. The authors use a linear-programming procedure to find a design measure and prove an equivalence theorem that supplies an upper bound for evaluating exact designs. They also describe converting the measure into exact designs by selecting quantiles or by random sampling. Numerical examples and a weather-station application show that the method gives a useful performance bound, although another compared method often constructs slightly more efficient exact designs.
narrate.key_results: In a four-point example, the paper reports a D-efficiency of 0.8316 for the virtual-noise quantile design, 0.9075 for the approximate-sensitivity method, and 0.9158 for exhaustive search. In a five-point polynomial example, the virtual-noise quantile design reached 0.9251, compared with 0.9270 for the approximate-sensitivity method and 0.9308 for exhaustive search. For the weather-station application, involving 445 municipality locations and a 36-point design, the best of 100 random designs drawn from the virtual-noise measure had D-efficiency 0.9915; the approximate-sensitivity method had 0.9965, while the median of 100 uniform random designs had 0.6689. The paper reports that efficiency generally improves as the number of design points increases, and that its equivalence theorem provides a bound against which exact designs can be evaluated.

narrate.summary: The paper develops clinical trial designs for learning personalized treatment rules: rules that select a treatment using a patient's covariates. The paper reports that the same regret as balanced allocation with 164 participants could be achieved with 143 participants under the optimized design, a 13% reduction in sample size. In numerical examples with three treatments, optimized covariate-dependent allocation reduced regret by 18.8% to 41.9% relative to balanced allocation across the reported scenarios with four covariate distributions and two variance settings.

narrate.summary: This theory paper studies random point designs in a multidimensional unit cube and seeks bounds on how evenly their points fill the space, measured by star discrepancy. They find that the bounds apply to both Monte Carlo and Latin hypercube samples and have the order of the square root of dimension divided by sample size. The probability that the star discrepancy is at most 3 times that square-root rate is at least 0.987256 for Monte Carlo and 0.965358 for Latin hypercube samples; for a multiplier of 4, the probability is at least 0.999999 for both. The Monte Carlo constant improves on the earlier constant of 9.65 reported in the paper. The stated run-size bound is at most 6.3944 times dimension divided by the square of the target discrepancy.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a design of experiments (DoE) framework for choosing measurements that estimate unknown quantum states. It derives optimal measurement designs for general qubit models under A-optimality, D-optimality, E-optimality, and a broader family of criteria. The construction represents qubit Fisher information through the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) Fisher information and mixtures of measurements in orthogonal parameter directions. The paper also proves a qubit equivalence result linking D-optimality to a weighted form of A-optimality. Its comparisons show that a design optimal for one criterion can perform poorly for another, especially near pure quantum states.
narrate.key_results: For qubit models with two or three parameters, the paper derives analytic A-, D-, E-, and gamma-optimal designs; the optimal designs can be implemented as randomized mixtures of projection measurements. For these models, the Fisher information region attainable by general measurements equals the region attainable by mixtures of projection measurements. The qubit D-optimal design is also A-optimal when the A criterion uses the SLD Fisher information as its weight matrix. In the standard three-parameter qubit example, the A-efficiency of the D-optimal, E-optimal, and standard tomography designs approaches two-thirds at the pure-state limit, while their D-efficiencies approach zero; the paper's comparisons are theoretical rather than based on observed experimental run sizes.

It uses a separate Gaussian process (GP) model for each output and proposes the cross-validation-high (CVH) strategy to choose which output model leads each next measurement. CVH leads with the output having the highest filtered 10-fold cross-validation error, then selects an input where that model's predicted variance is highest. The authors compare CVH with sequential, round-robin, global, and sequential space-filling designs using noisy simulated examples and a public geostatistics dataset. CVH often reduces measurements compared with the space-filling baseline, but it is less effective when one output is both highly noisy and another is highly complex.
narrate.key_results: In the first simulated setup, CVH reduced the measurements needed to reach the space-filling design's final error by 15 percent; in the second setup, it reduced them by 30 percent and outperformed the other active strategies. In the setup combining a very noisy output with a very complex output, sequential and round-robin strategies performed best, and the space-filling design also outperformed CVH at the reported final comparison. On the Jura public benchmark, CVH had the lowest mean error during the measurement sequence, but its final accuracy was not significantly better than the space-filling design; the strategies were averaged over 50 test runs. Overall, the results show that active learning does not always outperform a passive space-filling design.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that CVH can be less robust in noisy environments, particularly when outputs differ in noise and complexity. They also note the lack of a public benchmark dataset suited to drivability calibration and say that a more suitable dataset would make comparisons easier.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses three-output toy examples with two input dimensions and a geostatistics benchmark, rather than measurements from an actual vehicle test bench. The results also concern equal-priority outputs measured together, so they do not establish performance when outputs have different priorities, measurement costs, or missing observations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving CVH, including by considering estimated generalization error, and applying it to a real-world example. They also propose testing different numbers of input dimensions, different modeling approaches, and single-model active learning methods; they note that a public drivability-calibration benchmark would support future comparisons.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the strategy with correlated outputs, unequal output priorities, and practical constraints on where measurements can be taken. Prospective validation on a real test bench, including a direct comparison of measurement savings and model quality under changing operating conditions, would show whether the simulated benefits transfer to engineering use.

narrate.summary: This paper examines whether temporal correlation in electroencephalography (EEG) can make classification results from block-designed visual experiments misleading. The authors compare data from a previously published block-design experiment with recordings made during blank screens and a new rapid, interleaved experiment. They filter the EEG data and assess several classification methods, including analyses that pool participants and analyses performed separately for each participant. Their results indicate that temporal correlation has little effect on classification in the properly filtered block-design data, while the rapid experiment with block-level labels is only modestly above chance. They argue that the much larger bias reported in the paper they respond to may reflect differences in experimental duration, breaks, and analysis choices rather than a general problem with block designs.
narrate.key_results: On the block-design visual dataset, the best reported result was 48.8 percent accuracy across 40 classes using the 55 to 95 hertz band; chance accuracy was 2.5 percent. Blank-screen classification was near chance, with reported results from 3.8 to 9.1 percent against a 5 percent chance level. In the rapid experiment with incorrect block-level labels, the highest reported result was 11.4 percent, far below the 53.3 percent reported by the criticized study for its one-dimensional convolutional network. With correct class labels, rapid-experiment results were at chance.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors describe both their study and the criticized study as small-scale, and say that further examination is needed before drawing firm conclusions. They also report that the other study's code and sufficient experimental metadata were unavailable to them, so their replication used their own implementation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The experiments do not independently manipulate session duration, breaks, and participant pooling while holding other conditions constant, so the proposed causes of the differing results are not cleanly separated. The evidence also comes from six participants and a limited set of datasets and classification methods, which restricts how broadly the conclusions can be applied.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for further examination of temporal-correlation effects and for closer collaboration between machine-learning and cognitive-neuroscience researchers. They recommend keeping recording sessions under 8 minutes and pooling data across participants.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A follow-up study could vary session length, breaks, and analysis strategy systematically in a matched experiment, with enough participants to estimate each factor's contribution. Replication across laboratories and release of the full code, protocol, and data metadata would help assess whether the findings generalize.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces a sequential design method for safely identifying parameters in nonlinear kinetic models. The method combines Gaussian processes to learn the difference between the process and its model, and to estimate the information objective under parameter uncertainty. It uses adaptive trust regions to keep new experiments close to conditions where the process approximation is considered reliable, and a probabilistic constraint bound to select feasible conditions. The authors evaluate the method in two simulated flow-reactor studies using a D-optimal criterion. In both studies, the proposed method keeps the experiments feasible, while the two comparison methods violate constraints.
narrate.key_results: In the first study, the method remained feasible over the 20 displayed experiments; Monte Carlo-based design and disturbance-estimation design did not. The reported final chi-square statistics were 2018 for the proposed method, 1965 for the Monte Carlo method, and 1888 for disturbance estimation, against a reference of 74.47. In the second study, the proposed method remained feasible over the 23 displayed experiments, and its chi-square statistic was 1805, compared with 3892 and 3079 for the two alternatives, against a reference of 132.14. Average computation times for the two studies were 42 and 121 CPU seconds for the proposed method, 250 and 500 for the Monte Carlo method, and 20 and 62 for disturbance estimation. The results are from simulations, and the reported parameter-estimation tests show the proposed method’s final parameter t-values exceed their reference values in both studies.

narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the method in controlled physical experiments and test whether its probabilistic feasibility claims hold under measurement drift and operating constraints not represented in the simulations. Further work could also compare alternative information criteria and uncertainty-propagation methods, and test sequential strategies when experiments have cost, batch, or equipment constraints.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a way to use transformations and symmetries to simplify optimal design problems for generalized linear models, illustrating the approach with gamma responses and an inverse link. It focuses on designs for parameter estimation using the determinant-based D criterion and for prediction using integrated mean squared error. The method transforms experimental settings together with model parameters so that optimal designs can be transferred between regions, and it also uses symmetry to reduce the search to designs with equal weights on symmetry-related settings. For the gamma model, scaling the parameters provides a further reduction in the optimization problem. The paper derives results and gives examples, including a numerical maximin efficiency design for a two-factor model.
narrate.key_results: The authors show that locally optimal and maximin-efficient designs for both the D criterion and integrated mean squared error can be transferred under suitable transformations; symmetry can also restrict the search to invariant designs. For simple linear regression on an interval, the paper derives endpoint-supported locally optimal prediction designs for three weighting measures, with the weights depending on the measure and, in some cases, on the parameters. In the two-factor gamma model with equal slopes, the proposed invariant maximin D-efficient design has minimum D-efficiency 0.8660, compared with 0.8585 for the uniform design on the four vertices. Numerical integrated mean squared error designs are also reported for selected parameter values in that model, but the paper does not report an exact run-size comparison or a general performance ranking.

Its approximate designs allow continuously chosen weights, and the paper does not assess how well those weights translate into feasible exact run allocations under practical constraints.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the transformation and symmetry methods in higher-dimensional models, other response distributions, and criteria beyond the two emphasized here. It could also study constrained exact designs, sequential updating when parameter guesses change, and validation in real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops experimental designs for choosing treatment policies when individuals can affect one another and the interaction network is unknown. It assumes a finite number of large clusters, negligible spillovers across clusters, and comparable average policy responses across clusters. In the single-wave design, clusters are paired and assigned treatment probabilities just above or below a baseline; their outcome differences estimate the marginal policy effect (MPE), which includes direct and spillover effects. The authors also propose a sequential design that uses MPE estimates from other cluster pairs to update the policy over repeated waves. A field experiment with weather forecasts for farmers in Pakistan finds evidence for increasing treatment near a 50% treatment rate, but little evidence for increasing it near 70%, illustrating how local estimates can guide policy and reduce costs.
narrate.key_results: In the Pakistan experiment, 25 tehsils and 287,487 farmers were assigned to local perturbations of 10 percentage points around treatment rates of 50% and 70%. For the outcome measuring incorrect temperature beliefs, the estimated MPE was -3.39 at 50% treatment, with a one-sided p-value of 0.03; at 70%, it was -0.93, with a p-value of 0.22. At 50%, the estimated marginal spillover effect on untreated farmers was -6.41, with a p-value of 0.04, while the corresponding estimate at 70% was 0.78, with a p-value of 0.42. The authors estimate that treating 70% rather than 100% of farmers could save approximately USD 1,000,000 per year at scale in Pakistan; a simple grid design using treatment rates of 0%, 50%, and 100% would instead recommend treating everyone and would not identify the declining marginal effects near 70%. The theoretical analysis gives regret that decreases at about 1 divided by the number of iterations, up to logarithmic factors, when the number of clusters grows proportionally with iterations; an exponential out-of-sample rate is also derived under stronger smoothness conditions and a much larger sample size, and calibrated numerical studies compare the adaptive procedure with model-based and grid-based alternatives over 200 replications.

key_equations.name: Sequential policy update
key_equations.explanation: The center policy parameter for pair g at the next iteration is its current value plus learning rate alpha_t times the estimated marginal effect from the next pair, projected onto the allowed policy set B; the paper uses circular pairing so the update does not use that pair's own outcomes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that inference relies on comparable cluster-level policy responses and limited within-cluster dependence, and assumes negligible interference across clusters. They also note that comparisons of marginal effects across waves require no carryover effects; with unobserved cluster heterogeneity or strong within-cluster dependence, optimal policies cannot generally be learned without network information or many independent clusters.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main field application has only 25 tehsils, and its principal estimates rely on the authors' stated comparability assumptions; balance on observed characteristics cannot establish that unobserved policy responses are comparable. The outcome is accuracy of beliefs about forecast temperatures, not farmer income or overall welfare, and the estimated national cost saving is an extrapolation rather than a measured full-scale outcome.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify as future work designs for clusters that are not fully disconnected, methods for estimating clusters from data, and analysis of matching clusters on observed characteristics. They also propose studying cases where interference grows with sample size and policies when networks are only partly observed, including the costs and benefits of collecting network data.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate whether the design remains reliable when cluster comparability is imperfect, using pre-specified adjustments or sensitivity analyses for unobserved differences. Field validation could also connect the temperature-belief outcome to behavioral and economic outcomes, and test whether the recommended treatment rates perform well when deployed at scale.

narrate.summary: This paper develops two rerandomization methods for stratified randomized experiments that aim to improve estimation of the average treatment effect by balancing additional covariates. The methods use fixed potential outcomes and randomization-based inference, without assuming a model for the outcomes. The overall Mahalanobis-distance method (SRRoM) evaluates covariate imbalance across all strata together, while the stratum-specific Mahalanobis-distance method (SRRsM) rerandomizes independently within each stratum. The authors derive asymptotic distributions, variance estimates, and conservative confidence intervals for both methods. Their results show that rerandomization can improve precision over stratified randomization, with the overall method particularly useful when some strata are small.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, SRRoM reduced root mean squared error by 2.6% to 56.0% and confidence-interval length by 3.6% to 40.7% compared with stratified randomization. The authors recommend SRRoM when there are small strata and SRRsM when there are only a few large strata; in simulations with two large heterogeneous strata, fair SRRsM reduced root mean squared error by 27.6% to 38.9% relative to SRRoM. In the Opportunity Knocks example, SRRoM had a standard deviation of 0.3935, root mean squared error of 0.3935, and mean confidence-interval length of 1.9739, compared with 0.5283, 0.5283, and 2.4095 under stratified randomization. The example used 16 strata, with 382 treated and 821 control students; the reported empirical coverage probabilities for the methods were all above the nominal confidence level.

key_equations.explanation: The estimated average treatment effect tauhat is the sum over strata k from one to K of each stratum's share pi_k times the observed mean outcome for treated units, Ybar k1, minus the observed mean outcome for control units, Ybar k0.

key_equations.name: Rerandomization acceptance criteria
key_equations.explanation: The overall distance M_X is the covariate-difference estimate tauhat_X multiplied on both sides of its inverse covariance matrix and is accepted when below threshold a; the stratum-specific distance M_X,k is accepted when below its stratum threshold a_k for every stratum k among K strata.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on binary treatments and continuous potential outcomes, and assume that the number of additional covariates is fixed. They also note that choosing the acceptance probability remains an open issue.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The recommended acceptance probability of 0.001 may require generating many assignments, and small strata may have too few possible allocations for strict stratum-specific thresholds to accept any assignment. The numerical evidence uses a limited set of simulated settings, while the real-data analysis imputes unobserved potential outcomes and evaluates repeated simulated assignments rather than an implemented rerandomized trial.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying how to pool small strata before applying stratum-specific rerandomization. They also identify extensions to multiple treatments, factorial experiments, binary potential outcomes, and high-dimensional covariates as future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could measure the computational burden and acceptance rates across realistic combinations of stratum sizes and thresholds, and provide practical guidance for settings with allocation constraints. Prospective evaluations in operational experiments would also help assess whether the theoretical and simulated precision gains hold when rerandomization is implemented in practice.

narrate.summary: This paper develops experimental-design methods for overparameterized regression, where the number of model parameters can exceed the number of labeled examples. Its objective is to improve prediction by accounting for both bias and variance, rather than using the variance-focused criteria commonly used for underparameterized models. The authors bound the bias term to create a practical design criterion, then construct a pool-based selection method that greedily adds the example that best improves the criterion. They extend the method to kernel regression and use it to select examples for single-shot deep active learning through a neural tangent kernel. Their experiments report better results than random selection in the tested settings, including a reduction in the number of labeled examples needed to reach a reported accuracy level.
narrate.key_results: On the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology handwritten-digit dataset, the authors report that their design with 400 examples achieved accuracy comparable to random selection with 600 examples for the widened LeNet5 network; the same approximate comparison held for the standard LeNet5 network. In a comparison across 112 classification datasets from the University of California, Irvine repository, with 50 selected examples, the bias-oriented criterion performed better on 68 datasets at ridge parameter lambda 10, while the variance-including alternative performed better on 19 and tied on 25. In kernel regression experiments on the handwritten-digit dataset, the authors report that the bias-only choice of the tradeoff parameter performed better than the tested alternatives and better than random selection. They also report that incremental matrix updates reduce the cost of greedy selection; the stated overall cost scales quadratically with pool size and with the square of design size, plus the feature dimension.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical validation is concentrated on handwritten-digit data and a collection of classification datasets, so it does not establish performance across a broad range of industrial response types or experimental settings. The design criterion assumes a linear or kernel-regression representation and relies on a pool of unlabeled examples; the paper does not test how sensitive the selected designs are to model misspecification, operational restrictions on which runs can be made, or label costs that differ among examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors explicitly leave sequential experimental design for future research and suggest dynamically refining the bias-variance tradeoff as labels are acquired. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the criterion under industrial constraints such as batch structure, restricted factor combinations, unequal labeling costs, and required randomization, then validate it in real physical experiments. It would also be useful to test alternative response models and prediction criteria, and to compare sequential versions of this method against sequential baselines across datasets beyond handwritten digits.

narrate.summary: The paper derives the dual of approximate D-optimal design for multivariate polynomial regression on a compact semi-algebraic domain. It formulates the design through moments and moment matrices, then uses convex analysis to obtain the dual problem. For the logarithm-of-determinant objective, the dual constraint is a polynomial bound over the design domain. The polynomial at the optimum is the Christoffel-Darboux polynomial. The paper proves that the optimal moment vector is unique and that an optimal design can be supported on the polynomial's specified level set.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves strong duality between its general primal and dual optimal-design problems. For the logarithm-of-determinant criterion, it proves that the optimal moment vector is unique and that the Christoffel-Darboux polynomial equals n_d at points supporting an optimal measure. The dual maximizes the logarithm of the determinant of a positive definite matrix subject to a polynomial being bounded by n_d throughout the domain. When d equals 1, the dual has the interpretation of finding a minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid, extending the Loewner-John ellipsoid problem to the paper's broader setting.

key_equations.explanation: H is the positive definite dual matrix, log det is the logarithm of its determinant, n_d is the number of basis elements, v_d(x) is the polynomial basis vector at predictor value x, and X is the design domain over which the constraint holds.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say it is unclear whether their variational characterization of the Christoffel-Darboux polynomial will help study how that polynomial or its maximizers change when the design domain is perturbed.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for choosing measurements in Bayesian experimental design for parameter estimation in subsurface flow models. Its objective is to select design settings, especially the locations of additional wells and measurements, that maximize expected information gain. The method builds a polynomial chaos expansion for information gain by fitting divergence values sampled over parameters, measurement noise, and design settings, then uses polynomial orthogonality to obtain the design-dependent objective. It also uses polynomial surrogates of reservoir permeability and pressure to avoid repeatedly running the expensive flow simulator. The numerical examples show that the method approximates the objective and its maximizing designs well, with better objective-surface accuracy for smoother problems.
narrate.key_results: In the analytical test cases, the polynomial chaos response surfaces closely match reference utility curves, especially for small noise and smooth models; for a nonsmooth model they do not reproduce a derivative discontinuity, but the maximizing design is still accurately approximated. For the reservoir example, the forward surrogates were trained using 4,000 of 5,000 flow simulations and validated using the remaining 1,000, with reported accuracy around 3%. For the well-design calculations, the authors sampled 200,000 design settings in each case and estimated each divergence using a 50,000-step Markov chain Monte Carlo chain; the resulting design objective used a polynomial expansion of total degree 5. The paper describes the computational cost as comparable to several dozen conventional utility-function evaluations in its conclusion, while its abstract characterizes the budget as comparable to several single-point evaluations; it does not provide a direct timed comparison with a competing method. In the reservoir example, high-information locations tend to be at domain corners away from existing injector and producer wells, and adding pressure measurements shifts the preferred location toward areas of higher pressure variance.

narrate.summary: The paper develops robust optimal designs for predicting responses when the assumed regression model may be misspecified and some responses may be missing completely at random. It considers linear and nonlinear regression, with complete-case analysis for missing responses. The design criterion averages prediction error across the design space and over missingness, then finds the largest criterion value across a bounded neighborhood of possible model discrepancies. The design is selected to minimize that worst-case loss; for nonlinear models, the loss is averaged over a prior distribution on unknown parameters. In the examples, increasing the allowed model discrepancy generally spreads design points more widely, while larger response variance increases the reported loss.
narrate.key_results: The authors used a genetic algorithm with a population of 40 designs and stopped it when the best loss had not changed for 200 consecutive generations. In the polynomial example, at response variance 0.01, the reported loss components in the table's times-10-to-the-third scale rose from 0.7304 at neighborhood size 0.3 to 1.1703 at size 2.5; at response variance 0.1, they rose from 6.7437 to 7.2155 over the same sizes. The authors report that the robust designs become more dispersed as the neighborhood grows, compared with the classical designs that assume no model discrepancy. In the nonlinear example, at neighborhood size 0.5, the reported loss components were 0.4875 for the uniform prior, 0.3406 for the symmetric Beta prior, and 0.3275 for the right-skewed Beta prior; the designs themselves were described as not dramatically different across these priors.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to evaluate a boosted decision-tree classifier for labeling shipboard bathymetry measurements as good or bad. The objective is to predict measurement quality and provide confidence scores to support computer-assisted editing. The authors analyze more than 400 million measurements from 17 organizations and show that measurements are dependent within ship cruises and differ across data sources. They compare random splits of individual measurements with splits by cruises or long sequence segments, and compare models trained on one region with models trained on data pooled across regions. Their main finding is that evaluation and training data should reflect the sequence structure and the source expected at deployment; otherwise, reported predictive performance can be misleading.
narrate.key_results: A random split of individual measurements produced an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.9975, but the paper reports lower and more realistic AUROC values of 0.883 when splitting by whole cruises and 0.943 when splitting by segments of 100,000 measurements. These results indicate that randomly separating neighboring measurements can make test performance overly optimistic. For each of the nine regions in the table, a model trained on that region outperformed a model trained on all data, with reported AUROC improvements ranging from 0.73% to 6.94%. In the three detailed regional comparisons, the same-source model achieved AUROC values of 0.968 for AGSO, 0.994 for JAMSTEC, and 0.932 for NGDC, while the pooled model achieved 0.925, 0.968, and 0.888, respectively.
narrate.limitations_stated: None stated.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is specific to one bathymetry-labeling application and its data sources, so the results may not generalize to other operational settings. The paper reports selected split and regional comparisons but does not give uncertainty estimates or repeated-split variability for the reported performance differences.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test evaluation splits and training strategies across additional environmental monitoring applications, and assess models against future cruises and changing regional data mixes. It could also investigate practical ways to combine region-specific models or adapt them as new labeled data becomes available.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an optimal experimental design strategy for uncertain systems described by coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The authors use non-homogeneous Kuramoto oscillator models, where pairwise coupling strengths are uncertain, and aim to reduce the cost of robustly synchronizing the system. The strategy scores candidate pairwise synchronization experiments by their expected effect on the mean objective cost of uncertainty (MOCU), then selects the experiment expected to leave the least MOCU. Each experiment tests whether two oscillators synchronize in isolation, and its binary outcome narrows the interval for their coupling strength. Simulations show that this objective-based strategy reduces uncertainty in fewer experiments than random or entropy-based selection.
narrate.key_results: In the five-oscillator simulation, the MOCU-based design nearly reached the minimum attainable uncertainty after three updates, earlier than random selection or selection based on the largest parameter interval. In the nine-oscillator simulation, it reached the minimum attainable uncertainty after nine updates, compared with 36 possible pairwise experiments; the other strategies had not reached that level by 18 updates. The authors estimated a MOCU-computation runtime of about 2.87 seconds for five oscillators, a time horizon of 4, and a Monte Carlo sample size of 20,000, using PyCUDA on an Nvidia GTX 1080-Ti. The simulations used a fourth-order Runge-Kutta solver, and the reported relative L2 error for the five-oscillator case was between 10 to the power of negative 10 and 10 to the power of negative 9 at the final time.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how sampling designs affect exploratory landscape analysis (ELA), which estimates features of black-box optimization problems from sampled points and function evaluations. The authors use 46 features to classify 24 Black-Box Optimization Benchmark (BBOB) functions in five dimensions, comparing uniform random sampling, two Latin hypercube designs, and Sobol sequences. They repeat feature estimation at run sizes of 30, 300, and 3,125 points and assess classification accuracy with decision trees and K-nearest neighbors. They find that feature estimates from different sampling strategies can converge to different values, so estimates and classifiers depend on the strategy used. Sobol sequences give the highest median classification accuracy when training and testing use the same strategy.
narrate.key_results: Across all six combinations of classifier and run size, Sobol sampling had the highest median and average accuracy when training and testing used the same strategy; its matched-strategy accuracy at 3,125 points was 98.0% for K-nearest neighbors and 99.6% for decision trees. At 300 points, the corresponding matched Sobol results were 96.6% and 99.2%. Training and testing with different strategies could sharply reduce accuracy: for example, at 3,125 points, a decision tree trained on Sobol features and tested on LHS features reached 29.7%, compared with 99.6% when tested on Sobol features. The two uniform random-number generators, Mersenne Twister and RANDU, gave comparable results, while centered LHS generally performed worse than improved LHS.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on classification accuracy and do not optimize the default classifier implementations. They note that the choice of dimension and benchmark instance was not further motivated, and that a detailed analysis of feature approximations remains to be done.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The experiment uses only the first instance of the 24 benchmark functions at five dimensions, so it does not establish that the results generalize across instances, dimensions, or real engineering problems. Classification accuracy is an indirect measure of feature usefulness and does not show whether the designs improve the performance of an optimizer in practice; the largest run size may also be impractical when function evaluations are costly.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors plan a more detailed analysis of how sampling strategies relate to feature estimates, with the aim of developing corrections that translate estimates between strategies. They also propose investigating other low-discrepancy designs and feature-extraction tasks beyond ELA, examining links to one-shot optimization, and using confusion matrices to study similarities among benchmark functions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the sampling strategies across more dimensions, benchmark instances, and real optimization problems, including cases with costly evaluations and practical input constraints. Compare their effects on downstream optimization or algorithm selection, and test whether sequential or adaptive sampling can obtain useful features with fewer evaluations.

narrate.summary: This theory paper constructs locally D-optimal designs for Poisson regression with a synergetic interaction between two nonnegative predictors. The two-predictor model includes an intercept, two main effects, and their interaction, and the objective is precise estimation of these parameters. The authors choose a design with four equally weighted settings: the origin, one setting on each axis, and a setting on the diagonal whose position depends on the interaction strength. They prove optimality by examining the sensitivity function along contours of constant intensity and showing it is enough to check the axes and diagonal. They also give extensions to higher-dimensional models under specified interaction assumptions and discuss situations where the results do not establish an optimum.
narrate.key_results: For two predictors with negative main effects and a nonpositive interaction coefficient, the paper proves that four settings with weight one quarter each are locally D-optimal on the nonnegative quadrant. In the standardized model, the diagonal coordinate is the square root of one plus eight times the synergy strength, minus one, divided by twice the synergy strength; when the synergy strength is zero, the coordinate is two. The paper also establishes minimally supported designs for higher-dimensional models with zero interaction parameters and a design on the union of two-dimensional faces for nonnegative synergetic interactions. Its efficiency comparison shows that the design with diagonal coordinate two loses efficiency quickly as synergy increases, while the design with coordinate one is comparatively robust; the paper provides curves rather than tabulated efficiency values.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes balance-subsampled stable prediction (BSSP), a method for predicting across unknown environments when the training and test data distributions differ. It assumes the relationship between stable predictors and the outcome remains invariant, while noisy predictors can become spuriously associated with the outcome as distributions change. The method matches observed binary predictor patterns to a fractional factorial design (FFD), selecting a subset intended to reduce confounding among predictors and their interactions. It then fits a prediction model on the selected data, using regression or classification models. The authors report more accurate parameter estimates and more stable predictions than their comparison methods in synthetic and real datasets, while training on fewer observations.
narrate.key_results: The method uses a resolution-5 design with 128 runs, which the paper says removes confounding through interaction order 3 when the design is fully matched. In the synthetic regression experiments, the authors use 10 predictors and 2,000 observations after biased selection, and repeat training 50 times; they report that BSSP estimates parameters more precisely and gives the best stable predictions compared with ordinary least squares and the global balancing method. In synthetic classification experiments, BSSP’s root mean squared error is reported as more stable across test environments than logistic regression and global balancing. On the WeChat advertising and Parkinson’s telemonitoring datasets, BSSP is reported to perform comparably to the standard baselines in the training environment and better in the other test environments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for optimizing Bayesian experimental designs to maximize expected information gain about hidden parameters. The method applies randomized multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) to construct unbiased estimates of the design gradient, which is difficult to estimate because it contains nested expectations. It uses antithetic corrections across increasing inner sample sizes and draws levels randomly, allowing the gradient estimate to have finite expected squared size and finite expected computational cost under stated assumptions. The authors combine this estimator with stochastic gradient optimization and test it on a simple example and a pharmacokinetic (PK) design problem. The simple example shows that fixed-size inner Monte Carlo estimates can lead optimization away from the true optimum, while the proposed method reaches it; in the PK example, it produces a different sampling-time allocation and a slightly higher estimated information gain than the standard Monte Carlo comparison.
narrate.key_results: In the simple test case, the estimated decay rates for the squared MLMC corrections were 1.64 and 1.63 at the tested design points, and the randomized estimator used an expected 2.21 inner samples per gradient sample. With the same computational-cost comparison, fixed inner sample sizes from 1 to 64 either moved toward the wrong design or leveled off away from the optimum, whereas the proposed method continued to converge; the reported mean squared error decayed approximately as iteration count to the power of minus 1.12. In the PK problem, the proposed method used an expected 1.34 inner samples and yielded three clusters containing 3, 6, and 6 sampling times, compared with 3, 5, and 7 for standard Monte Carlo. Across 10 runs, the estimated information gain was 4.544 for the proposed method and 4.535 for standard Monte Carlo, versus 3.774 for the initial design.

narrate.summary: The paper develops the cumulative Aalen survival analysis-of-variance approach, called CASANOVA, for comparing groups in factorial studies with possibly right-censored survival times. It tests hypotheses about cumulative hazards, including main effects and interactions, without requiring proportional hazards. The method forms weighted Nelson–Aalen-type integrals and combines weights to address both proportional and crossing hazard patterns. A studentized permutation procedure is used to obtain critical values, with theoretical results establishing its asymptotic validity. Simulations and a lung cancer data analysis show that the combined permutation test can control false positive rates and detect different hazard patterns without selecting just one weight in advance.
narrate.key_results: In the simulations, each setting used 5,000 runs and 1,999 permutation iterations, with a nominal false positive rate of 5 percent. For the two-by-three factorial layout, only 4 of 72 permutation-test scenarios fell outside the reported 95 percent interval of 4.4 to 5.6 percent; asymptotic tests were often conservative, with rates around 3 percent for main effects and 2 percent for interactions. In the additional one-way simulations, asymptotic false positive rates reached 25.9 percent, while permutation rates were generally close to the target. In the lung cancer analysis, the permutation combined test gave a treatment p-value of 1.0 percent, compared with 2.8 percent for the log-rank test and 79.1 percent for the crossing-weight test; the reported interaction p-value was 75.0 percent.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that it is unclear whether the permutation method remains valid with more complex filtering mechanisms, such as truncation or certain interval-censoring settings. They also report that implementation in the GFDsurv software package was still in progress.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations cover selected distributions, censoring patterns, sample sizes, and weight choices, so they do not establish performance across the full range of factorial survival studies. The method tests cumulative-hazard contrasts, but the paper does not provide a general procedure for translating a rejection into an estimated, practically interpretable treatment effect.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to more complex filtering mechanisms, while noting that multiplier resampling would be their first choice for approximating critical values beyond ordinary right-censoring. They also state that they are working on implementing the combination test in GFDsurv and on encouraging medical and epidemiological applications.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the method with additional factorial structures, censoring mechanisms, and weight combinations, and provide guidance for choosing contrasts and planning sample sizes. Testing the procedure prospectively in real factorial clinical studies would also help assess its practical performance.
