narrate.key_results: For the selected five-factor, twelve-run design, the authors found 15 contained regular fractions of four runs and five distinct ways to partition the design into three such fractions. Across the 70 distinct five-factor designs with twelve runs formed from the Plackett-Burman designs, each had 15 contained four-run regular fractions and five decompositions into three regular fractions. The 462 column selections considered were grouped into 81 classes: 70 classes had designs with twelve runs and 11 had designs with eleven runs. The authors generated 192 distinct strength-two orthogonal arrays, the same total reported in the cited prior work; they did not report efficiency or prediction comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper studies randomized sampling designs for estimating the integral of a function over a unit hypercube, as used in computer experiments. It constructs the samples by starting with an orthogonal array of strength two, randomizing the symbols in each column, and adding independent uniform jitter within array strata; it also analyzes orthogonal-array-based Latin hypercube variants. Under smoothness conditions, it proves that the standardized integration estimates from all three design classes converge to the standard normal distribution as the alphabet size grows. The paper also derives their leading asymptotic variances in terms of the integrand's higher-order residual component. The results provide theoretical support for approximate normal inference, including confidence intervals, under the stated conditions.
narrate.key_results: Each design uses a run size equal to the square of the number of symbols per array column. For the randomized orthogonal-array design and one orthogonal-array-based Latin hypercube construction, the paper shows that the run-size-scaled variance approaches the integral of the squared residual integrand; it also establishes that the variance of the randomized orthogonal-array estimator and that of the two Latin hypercube variants agree to the reported asymptotic order. For a smooth integrand with positive residual variance and at least three dimensions, the standardized estimates from all three design classes converge in distribution to the standard normal as the alphabet size grows. These are theoretical asymptotic findings; the paper reports no finite-run numerical comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a way to test main effects and interactions in two-valued input-output systems evaluated across settings of controllable factors. It models the counts in each run as independent binomial observations and represents the system performance through the odds ratio. The method builds covariates from the factor settings, then tests effects by conditioning on sufficient statistics for nuisance parameters; it also accounts for aliasing in fractional factorial designs. The signal-to-noise ratio analysis of variance reported a p value of 0.04482 for that interaction. In an imagined dataset with smaller sample sizes for two runs, the proposed test gives a statistic of 11.56 and a p value of 0.000674. The authors note that the signal-to-noise ratio analysis of variance changes little for this altered dataset, whereas their conditional test accounts for the changed sample sizes.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods to construct blocked regular fractional factorial designs using the minimum aberration (MA) objective. It studies regular main-effect (RME) designs and considers four ways to combine treatment and block wordlength patterns into a single criterion. The construction method uses coding theory and row-coincidence moments, providing a way to compare designs without directly counting all defining words and alias sets. The paper also derives a lower bound on a block wordlength count and gives conditions under which designs built from unblocked MA designs are optimal under all four criteria. It reports MA designs for all 8, 16, 27, and 32 runs, for 64 runs up to 32 factors, and for all 81 runs.
narrate.key_results: The authors provide blocked MA designs for all 8, 16, 27, and 32 runs, 64 runs with up to 32 factors, and all 81 runs, considering four combined wordlength patterns. Designs under the four criteria are the same in most examined cases; the paper identifies four types of exceptions, including cases where the Chen–Cheng criterion selects a different design. For 64 runs, the lower bound on the block wordlength count helps reduce searches; for example, it narrows one search to 17 regular designs in a case where searching all designs under the stated cutoff would involve more than 100,000. The paper notes that counting words directly can be cumbersome: its example of a 64-run design with 25 factors in 8 blocks requires counting 4,194,303 words.

narrate.summary: This paper develops bounds for codes and ordered orthogonal arrays in the Niederreiter–Rosenbloom–Tsfasman (NRT) ordered Hamming space, rather than designs for physical experiments. The space has vectors divided into blocks, and its distance weights a block according to the position of its last nonzero coordinate. The authors construct the associated scheme from a one-block scheme and identify its eigenvalues as multivariate Krawtchouk polynomials. They use these polynomials in linear programming bounds, including an asymptotic bound, and give a sharper analysis for the case of two coordinates per block. The principal finding is that some of their bounds improve on established bounds over stated ranges of distances, with no experimental data or practical design evaluation.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves a Bassalygo–Elias asymptotic bound that is better than the Hamming bound for every relative distance from zero through the critical distance. It is also better than the Plotkin bound for all positive distances below the critical distance when the alphabet size is 2 and there are 2 coordinates per block; for alphabet size 3 and 4 coordinates per block, the authors give an improvement range of 0 to 0.54. A general linear programming bound improves on the asymptotic Plotkin bound at large code distances. For 2 coordinates per block, the authors derive a further bound using the zeros of Krawtchouk polynomials and compare it with the Plotkin, Gilbert–Varshamov, Elias, and general linear programming bounds in plots for alphabet sizes 2 and 3 and block lengths 2 and 3.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for generating all two-level orthogonal arrays with a specified number of factors and force, while allowing any number of replications. It expresses the orthogonality requirements as linear equations in the replication counts of treatment points. The nonnegative integer solutions form the lattice points of a rational cone, and a Hilbert basis gives a finite set of arrays from which every array satisfying the requirements can be assembled. The authors use the 4ti2 software to compute examples. Their results demonstrate the method for small cases, but computation for six factors and force two was too time-consuming.
narrate.key_results: For OA(5, 3), 4ti2 found a Hilbert basis of 28 arrays in 0.05 seconds on the authors’ slow laptop; 12 had 16 treatments without replications, and 16 had 24 points with replications. For OA(5, 2), computation took 1008.97 seconds and produced a basis of 26142 arrays, including 414 with no replications: 60 with 8 treatments, 192 with 12, and 162 with 16. A previously reported classification had 60, 192, and 552 arrays at those respective sizes after complement duplicates were removed; the authors explain that the 390 additional 16-treatment arrays are unions of two disjoint 8-treatment arrays. OA(6, 2) could not be computed in practical time with the method as used.

key_equations.explanation: The four rows r1 through r4 have elementwise product equal to the all-ones vector or its negation; eligible rows can be used to switch by negating columns of a selected type.

narrate.limitations_stated: The author does not attempt a complete enumeration for order 26, so the reported total is only a lower bound. The paper also notes that it has no explanation for the unusually large number of designs of the (7, 1)-type.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The order-26 search starts from designs generated by specified constructions or gradient ascent, so the reported switching classes do not establish that every possible source of designs has been found. The paper gives no runtimes or shared code, making it difficult to assess computational cost or reproduce the enumeration in full.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author suggests that an additional switching operation may exist that converts designs between the (5, 5)-type and the (7, 1)-type. The paper also expresses an expectation that switching can be applied to further orders where the best possible Gram matrix is attainable.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A natural next step is a complete order-26 classification, with reproducible software and a proof that the search covers every design class. Further work could also test switching under practical design constraints and assess whether the resulting designs remain useful in actual experiments.

screen.scope_reason: The paper develops a computational method for nuclear response calculations, not methods for choosing experimental runs, points, or allocations.
The paper studies and constructs locally E- and c-optimal designs for nonlinear regression models, directly addressing how to choose experimental design points.

classify.design_type_evidence: For a broad class of nonlinear regression models we investigate the local E- and c-optimal design problem.

narrate.summary: This paper develops local designs for estimating parameters in nonlinear regression models that include rational, logistic, and exponential forms. It studies E-optimal designs, which protect estimation of the least-informed parameter direction, and c-optimal designs for specified parameter combinations. The authors replace the nonlinear problem with an equivalent linearized regression model whose functions include derivatives with respect to the nonlinear parameters. When those parameters are sufficiently close, the optimal designs can be constructed at the extrema, or Chebyshev points, of a best equi-oscillating approximation, with weights determined by the design criterion. The theoretical results are supported by rational-model examples, where E-optimal designs can also be effective for estimating individual parameters.
narrate.key_results: For the one-parameter rational example on the interval from zero to infinity, the E-optimal design uses two support points, zero and the square root of twice the absolute value of b. Across b values at or below negative one, its reported efficiency for estimating the first coefficient ranges from approximately 0.9061 to 0.9595, and for the second coefficient from approximately 0.9805 to 1. In the two-parameter rational example, the authors report a four-point limiting design with masses 0.13, 0.26, 0.27, and 0.34 at locations zero, 0.18, 1.08, and 7.9. In the reported comparison at separation parameter z equal to 0.1, the limiting design has individual-coefficient efficiencies of 1.00, 0.99, 1.00, and 1.00; at z equal to 0.95, these are 0.27, 0.21, 0.08, and 0.07, while the model-specific E-optimal design has efficiencies of 0.78, 1.00, 0.44, and 0.31.

key_equations.name: Linearized regression model
key_equations.explanation: Y is the response, f is the vector of regression functions evaluated at explanatory variable t and nonlinear parameters b, beta is the coefficient vector, and epsilon is the random error; the superscript T means transpose.

key_equations.name: Information matrix
key_equations.explanation: M is the information matrix, xi is the design, I is the design interval, f is the regression-function vector, t is the explanatory variable, b is the nonlinear-parameter vector, and T means transpose.

key_equations.name: Design criteria
key_equations.explanation: Xi denotes a candidate design, lambda minimum is the smallest eigenvalue, M is the information matrix, b is the nonlinear-parameter vector, and c specifies the parameter combination; the first expression is the E-optimal criterion and the second is the c-optimal criterion.

key_equations.name: Chebyshev support locations
key_equations.explanation: Each t sub j is a support location among the extremal points of q star, the normalized Chebyshev approximation; t ranges over design interval I, and arg max denotes the locations where the absolute value is greatest.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their Chebyshev-point results generally require the nonlinear parameters to be sufficiently close, and the cutoff for closeness cannot be given explicitly because it depends on the intervals and the model function. They also note that c-optimality results require specified conditions on the parameter-combination vector and that the Chebyshev construction is not guaranteed to be optimal for every admissible parameter value.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The designs are local: they depend on initial values for the unknown parameters, and the paper does not evaluate how errors in those values affect performance in actual experiments. The theoretical designs use approximate proportions and may have support locations or proportions that are difficult to implement under finite run budgets, restricted settings, or other practical constraints; the numerical comparisons are limited to rational-model examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Assess the designs under uncertain parameter values, practical restrictions on settings and allocation, and finite run budgets, including comparisons with robust or Bayesian designs. Further work could also test the proposed construction in real experiments and develop sequential procedures that update the nonlinear-parameter estimates and design as observations are collected.
